mots-c::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: MOTS-c appears to activate cellular sensors and pathways that regulate energy metabolism, inflammation, and stress resilience. When injected, it circulates systemically and may enhance how efficiently cells produce energy, dampen excessive inflammatory responses, and improve the body's ability to handle metabolic stress. The exact receptor and full cascade of effects are still being mapped, but evidence suggests it works partly by optimizing mitochondrial signaling and reducing metabolic dysfunction.

proven_benefits.note: Human evidence from 14 studies supports improved insulin sensitivity and glucose metabolism, particularly in metabolic syndrome and obesity.
Human evidence from 34 studies indicates improvements in vascular function, blood pressure, and markers of heart disease risk.
Human evidence from 6 studies shows benefits in aerobic capacity and muscle fatigue recovery, though the effect sizes vary.

promising_benefits.note: 33 human studies suggest anti-inflammatory effects, but results are inconsistent and the clinical relevance remains unclear.
Only 1 animal study; human evidence is absent, so any anxiolytic benefit is unproven and speculative at this stage.

mots-c::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work is exploring MOTS-c's potential in neurodegeneration, longevity, and age-related muscle loss, as well as its interaction with circadian rhythms and cellular autophagy. Some studies hint at neuroprotective properties, but these remain in early-stage research with limited human data. Long-term effects and optimal dosing schedules are not yet established.
mots-c::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: MOTS-c is often supplied as a research chemical and is not approved by the FDA for clinical use; quality, purity, and sterility vary widely depending on source. Safety in long-term human use, optimal dosing, and potential off-target effects require further study; this is an injectable peptide best used under medical supervision, if at all.

nac::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: NAC (N-acetylcysteine) is a modified form of the amino acid cysteine. It is readily absorbed and serves as a precursor to glutathione, one of the body's most important antioxidants and detoxification molecules.
nac::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: NAC replenishes glutathione levels in cells, which neutralizes free radicals and supports the body's natural detoxification pathways. It also reduces inflammation by modulating immune signaling and improves mucus clearance in the lungs and gut. Additionally, NAC influences neurotransmitter balance—particularly dopamine and serotonin—which affects mood and stress resilience. By stabilizing blood sugar metabolism and supporting gut barrier function, it indirectly benefits multiple systems.

proven_benefits.note: 26 human studies show NAC improves depressive symptoms, likely through glutathione restoration and neurotransmitter support.
32 human studies demonstrate NAC reduces anxiety and stress-related symptoms, with effects on both inflammatory and neurochemical pathways.
36 human studies confirm NAC lowers inflammatory markers and supports immune regulation.
34 human studies show NAC improves glucose control and insulin sensitivity.
40 human studies indicate NAC supports gut barrier integrity and digestive function.

nac::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work explores NAC's role in respiratory health, autoimmune modulation, and liver support—areas with mechanistic plausibility but limited human clinical data. Some early evidence suggests potential benefits in cognitive resilience and heavy metal detoxification, though these remain investigational and require confirmation in larger populations.
nac::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: NAC is generally well-tolerated, but high doses or prolonged use warrant medical oversight, particularly in people with bleeding disorders or cysteine metabolism issues. Quality varies by brand; pharmaceutical-grade NAC is preferable to unregulated supplements. Long-term safety in all populations has not been exhaustively studied.

niacin::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Niacin, also called vitamin B3 or nicotinic acid, is an essential water-soluble B vitamin that your body uses to convert food into energy and to build and repair DNA. It's found naturally in foods like chicken, tuna, mushrooms, and peanuts, and is also available as a dietary supplement.
niacin::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Niacin works as a precursor to NAD+ (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide), a coenzyme central to energy metabolism in every cell. NAD+ is involved in hundreds of enzymatic reactions that govern glucose metabolism, fat breakdown, inflammation signaling, and DNA repair. By maintaining adequate niacin status, you support these metabolic pathways; supplementation at higher doses can further influence lipid profiles and inflammatory markers through effects on cell signaling and gene expression.

proven_benefits.note: Multiple large human studies (17 total) confirm niacin improves cholesterol profiles, blood pressure, and arterial health in people at cardiovascular risk.
Strong human evidence (22 studies) shows niacin improves fasting glucose, insulin sensitivity, and glycemic control in both healthy and diabetic populations.
Well-supported by 22 human studies demonstrating niacin lowers inflammatory markers and may benefit inflammatory conditions.
Moderate human evidence (10 studies) suggests niacin may help reduce anxiety and stress-related symptoms, though more research is needed to establish optimal dosing and populations.

promising_benefits.note: Despite 27 human studies, evidence remains preliminary; niacin may support gut barrier function and microbial balance, but clinical significance is not yet established.

niacin::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work is exploring niacin's role in cellular stress resistance and longevity pathways via NAD+ restoration, particularly in aging and neurodegenerative conditions. Some studies are investigating whether niacin supplementation enhances the effects of exercise on metabolic health. However, these directions are early and largely mechanistic; clinical benefits in these areas have not yet been demonstrated in humans.
niacin::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Niacin is a vitamin and generally safe at dietary amounts, but high-dose supplementation (>1.5 g/day) can cause flushing, liver issues, and interactions with medications—consult a healthcare provider before supplementing at therapeutic doses. Quality and purity vary between brands; choose products third-party tested.

nmn::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: NMN (nicotinamide mononucleotide) is a naturally occurring compound and a direct precursor to NAD+, a coenzyme found in every cell. It is the immediate chemical step before NAD+ is synthesized, making it a shortcut to boost cellular NAD+ levels.
nmn::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: NAD+ is critical for energy production (mitochondrial function), DNA repair, and cellular stress responses. As we age, NAD+ levels decline, which contributes to fatigue, reduced metabolic function, and age-related cellular damage. By supplying NMN, cells can rapidly regenerate NAD+ without having to manufacture it from scratch. This restored NAD+ then activates sirtuins and other longevity-associated proteins that regulate inflammation, energy metabolism, and cellular repair.

proven_benefits.note: 31 human studies support that NMN can help lower inflammatory markers, though the magnitude of effect varies.
34 human studies suggest NMN may support memory, focus, and mental clarity, likely through improved mitochondrial energy in brain cells.
29 human studies indicate NMN supports immune cell activity and response, though clinical relevance remains under investigation.

promising_benefits.note: 10 human studies are early-stage; NMN may support intestinal barrier integrity and gut microbiome balance, but evidence is not yet conclusive.
Only 4 human studies exist; preliminary findings suggest NMN may help modulate stress responses, but this requires confirmation in larger trials.

nmn::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work is exploring NMN's effects on vascular health, muscle recovery, and longevity markers in human aging. Some animal studies hint at lifespan extension and metabolic rejuvenation, but human longevity data remains limited. Clinical trials are ongoing to clarify whether NMN can slow aging or prevent age-related disease in humans—a promising but still-unproven frontier.
nmn::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: NMN is taken orally and is generally well tolerated, but long-term safety data in humans is sparse. Quality and bioavailability vary significantly between supplements; look for third-party tested products. NAD+ boosting is not a substitute for lifestyle (exercise, sleep, diet) and may not produce dramatic effects in younger, healthy individuals.

noopept::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Noopept is a synthetic peptide-like nootropic (cognitive enhancer) developed in Russia in the 1970s. It is structurally similar to piracetam but significantly more potent by weight, and works through distinct molecular pathways in the brain.
noopept::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Noopept is believed to enhance cognition by increasing brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), a protein critical for neuronal growth and plasticity. It may also modulate ion channels and reduce excitotoxicity—damage from excessive neuronal firing. Additionally, it may improve communication between brain hemispheres and enhance oxygen utilization by neurons. The exact mechanisms remain incompletely understood in humans.

promising_benefits.note: Human studies (26 total) show mixed but suggestive improvements in memory and executive function; evidence is not yet robust enough to claim established efficacy.
Animal studies (6) hint at potential glucose-lowering effects, but no human evidence exists.
Limited animal data (4 studies) suggest anti-inflammatory properties; human studies are absent.
Only 2 animal studies; human efficacy is completely unproven.
Minimal animal evidence (2 studies); no human data available.

noopept::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work has focused on noopept's neuroprotective potential in neurodegenerative disease models and its effects on synaptic density. Some researchers are investigating whether BDNF upregulation might support cognitive aging. However, all of these directions remain in early animal or small human pilot phases; large, well-controlled clinical trials are needed before any clinical claims can be made.
noopept::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Noopept is a research chemical not approved by the FDA and is not widely available in most Western markets; purity and quality of commercial sources are often unverified. The bulk of evidence comes from Russian and Eastern European research, which may reflect publication or methodological differences. Long-term safety in humans is not well characterized, and optimal dosing for cognitive benefit remains unclear.

nr::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Nicotinamide riboside (NR) is a form of vitamin B3 that serves as a precursor to NAD+, a coenzyme critical for cellular energy production and DNA repair. Unlike standard niacin, NR is absorbed efficiently and crosses the blood–brain barrier, making it a popular supplement for longevity and metabolic health.
nr::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: NR is converted in the body to NAD+, which fuels mitochondria (the cell's power plants) and activates longevity-related enzymes called sirtuins and PARPs that regulate stress responses, inflammation, and DNA repair. As we age, NAD+ levels naturally decline; supplementing NR aims to restore these levels and support cellular resilience. By boosting NAD+, NR may improve how cells respond to metabolic stress, sleep signals, and blood sugar regulation.

proven_benefits.note: Human evidence from 33 studies shows consistent improvements in sleep duration and quality.
28 human studies support improvements in memory, attention, and processing speed, though effect sizes vary.
32 human studies indicate NR helps regulate glucose metabolism and insulin sensitivity, particularly in metabolic contexts.
33 human studies show modest but measurable effects on testosterone and other hormonal markers.
19 human studies demonstrate anti-inflammatory effects, likely through NAD+-dependent immune pathways.

nr::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work has explored NR's role in mitochondrial biogenesis (building new energy-producing structures), cardiovascular endurance, and age-related muscle decline, though human evidence remains limited. Some studies suggest NR may enhance the benefits of exercise or caloric restriction, but these findings are still early and require larger confirmatory trials.
nr::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: NR is a dietary supplement and not FDA-approved as a drug; quality varies by manufacturer, so third-party testing is advisable. Long-term safety data beyond 3–5 years is incomplete, and optimal dosing for sustained efficacy remains unclear; individual response varies significantly.

omega-3::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Omega-3 fatty acids are essential polyunsaturated fats found in fish, algae, and plant sources like flaxseed. The most bioactive forms are EPA (eicosapentaenoic acid) and DHA (docosahexaenoic acid), which your body cannot synthesize on its own.
omega-3::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Omega-3s are incorporated into cell membranes throughout your body, where they improve cellular fluidity and function. They reduce the production of pro-inflammatory molecules called cytokines and eicosanoids, helping lower systemic inflammation. In the brain, DHA in particular is a structural component of neuronal membranes and supports neurotransmitter function. In blood vessels, omega-3s improve endothelial function, reduce triglycerides, and help prevent clot formation. They also promote a healthier gut microbiome and support muscle protein synthesis when combined with resistance training.

proven_benefits.note: Omega-3s reduce triglycerides, support healthy blood pressure, and lower cardiovascular disease risk across multiple large human studies.
DHA supports memory, attention, and processing speed; evidence is particularly strong for maintenance of cognitive function with age.
Omega-3s measurably lower inflammatory markers like CRP and IL-6 in human studies across diverse populations.
Omega-3s improve gut barrier function and support beneficial bacteria; evidence is solid but less extensive than cardiovascular data.
Omega-3s enhance muscle protein synthesis and support strength gains when combined with resistance training, though effects are modest.

omega-3::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work explores omega-3s' role in mood regulation, eye health, and bone density, though human evidence remains preliminary in these areas. Some studies suggest omega-3 supplementation may support metabolic health and insulin sensitivity, but larger trials are needed to confirm clinical significance.
omega-3::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Quality and EPA/DHA content vary widely among supplements; third-party testing is recommended. Fish oil supplements may cause mild gastrointestinal upset or fishy aftertaste, and very high doses can have mild blood-thinning effects—discuss with a doctor if on anticoagulants.

phosphatidylserine::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Phosphatidylserine (PS) is a phospholipid—a fatty molecule with a phosphate group—that is a structural component of cell membranes, particularly abundant in brain and nerve cells. It is found naturally in foods like soy, fish, and leafy greens, and is also available as a supplement derived from plant or animal sources.
phosphatidylserine::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: PS integrates into cell membranes and helps maintain their fluidity and integrity, which is essential for cell signaling and function. In the brain, it supports neurotransmitter release and receptor sensitivity. It also appears to modulate the stress response by influencing cortisol levels and may help regulate immune and inflammatory signaling pathways through effects on cell membrane properties and intercellular communication.

proven_benefits.note: Human evidence from 26 studies suggests PS supports memory, attention, and cognitive function, particularly in aging populations.
28 human studies indicate PS may support healthy blood pressure, cholesterol profiles, and endothelial function.
21 human trials show PS may help reduce markers of systemic inflammation and support a balanced inflammatory response.
5 human studies suggest PS may reduce cortisol response to stress and support mood resilience under psychological strain.

promising_benefits.note: 25 human studies show early promise for PS in supporting immune cell activity and response, though effects require further confirmation.

phosphatidylserine::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work is exploring PS's role in cellular senescence (aging), gut barrier integrity, and its potential synergy with other phospholipids for neuroprotection. Some early studies suggest benefits in neurodegenerative contexts, though human evidence remains limited and preliminary in these areas.
phosphatidylserine::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: PS is generally well-tolerated; most common sources (soy-derived or bovine) are safe for most people, though those with soy allergies should seek non-soy alternatives. Quality and purity vary among commercial products, and most human studies used doses of 100–300 mg daily; optimal dosing and long-term safety in all populations are not fully established.

piracetam::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Piracetam is a cyclic derivative of the amino acid GABA, synthesized in 1972 as one of the first 'nootropic' compounds. It is a small, water-soluble molecule that crosses the blood-brain barrier and is structurally distinct from stimulants or sedatives.
piracetam::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Piracetam's exact mechanism remains incompletely understood, but evidence suggests it enhances neuronal membrane fluidity, improves mitochondrial function, and may stabilize cell membranes across the brain and body. It appears to modulate neurotransmitter activity and increase cerebral blood flow without acting as a direct agonist or antagonist of known receptors. This broad cellular effect may explain why it influences cognition, stress response, and systemic health markers simultaneously.

proven_benefits.note: Supported by 21 human studies showing improvements in memory, learning, and processing speed, particularly in aging and cognitively impaired populations.
21 human studies indicate piracetam may reduce subjective anxiety and stress markers, though effects are modest and most pronounced in clinical populations.
30 human studies show improvements in blood viscosity, platelet aggregation, and microcirculation, potentially beneficial in vascular health.
23 human studies report enhancement of immune markers and resilience to infection, though mechanistic details remain sparse.

promising_benefits.note: 36 human studies suggest piracetam may lower inflammatory markers, but evidence is inconsistent and clinical significance unclear.

piracetam::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work has explored piracetam's role in neuroprotection against aging, recovery from stroke, and cognitive decline in neurodegenerative disease, though these remain early-stage findings. Some studies hint at effects on synaptic plasticity and neurogenesis in animal models, which could underpin its cognitive benefits, but confirmation in humans is limited. Long-term safety and optimal dosing strategies continue to be defined.
piracetam::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Piracetam is prescription-only in some countries and available over-the-counter in others; regulatory status varies widely. While generally well-tolerated in studies, individual responses vary, quality and purity of commercial products may differ, and it is not a substitute for medical treatment of neurological or psychiatric conditions. The mechanism of action remains only partially understood, and rare adverse events are not fully characterized.

potassium::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Potassium is an essential mineral and electrolyte found naturally in foods like bananas, leafy greens, and beans. It plays a fundamental role in nerve signaling, muscle contraction, and maintaining fluid balance in the body.
potassium::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Potassium works by regulating the electrical gradient across cell membranes—a difference in charge that drives nerve impulses and muscle contractions. It helps counterbalance sodium to maintain healthy blood pressure and supports the heart's rhythm and force of contraction. Adequate potassium also influences how cells respond to insulin, affecting glucose metabolism and blood sugar stability.

proven_benefits.benefit: Cardiovascular health and blood pressure regulation
proven_benefits.note: Evidence from 21 human studies shows potassium supports healthy blood pressure and heart function, likely through its effects on blood vessel relaxation and sodium balance.

proven_benefits.benefit: Blood sugar control and glucose metabolism
proven_benefits.note: Data from 27 human studies indicate potassium helps maintain healthy blood sugar levels, possibly by enhancing insulin sensitivity and glucose uptake in cells.

promising_benefits.note: Early evidence from 23 human studies suggests a role in digestive function, but the mechanism and clinical significance remain to be fully clarified.

potassium::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work is exploring potassium's effects on bone health and its interactions with gut microbiota, though these areas remain preliminary. Some studies are examining whether potassium status influences inflammation markers, but results are not yet conclusive. More research is needed to establish robust clinical applications beyond cardiovascular and metabolic health.
potassium::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Potassium balance is tightly regulated by the kidneys; excessive supplementation without medical supervision can be dangerous, especially in people with kidney disease or those taking certain medications. Most people can meet potassium needs through food; supplementation should be guided by a healthcare provider and regular monitoring.

progesterone::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Progesterone is a steroid hormone naturally produced primarily by the ovaries in women and, in smaller amounts, by the adrenal glands and testes. It is essential for reproductive function and exists throughout the body in tissues including the brain, immune cells, and inflammatory mediators.
progesterone::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Progesterone acts by binding to progesterone receptors distributed across multiple organ systems. In the brain, it modulates neurotransmitter activity and can affect mood-regulating pathways. It influences immune cell development and function, helping to regulate inflammatory responses. It also interacts with other hormonal systems, including effects on testosterone and cortisol balance. These wide-ranging receptor interactions explain why progesterone affects cognition, mood, inflammation, and immune regulation simultaneously.

proven_benefits.note: Multiple human studies (n=24) show progesterone supports cognitive function, including memory and processing speed.
Evidence from 28 human studies indicates progesterone plays a role in hormonal homeostasis and testosterone regulation.
14 human studies support a moderately strong link between progesterone levels and mood regulation, particularly across the menstrual cycle.
26 human studies demonstrate that progesterone modulates inflammatory pathways and immune signaling.
28 human studies show progesterone influences immune cell populations and responses, supporting immune regulation.

progesterone::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent studies are exploring progesterone's neuroprotective role in traumatic brain injury and neurodegenerative conditions, as well as its potential in autoimmune disease modulation. Research is also investigating optimal dosing windows and receptor selectivity for therapeutic applications. These investigations remain early and are not yet established as clinical standards.
progesterone::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Progesterone supplementation or replacement should only be undertaken under medical supervision, as dosing, formulation (bioidentical vs. synthetic), and individual hormonal status significantly affect safety and efficacy. Quality and purity of commercially available progesterone products vary widely; pharmaceutical-grade forms are preferred over unregulated supplements.

psyllium fiber::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Psyllium is a soluble dietary fiber derived from the seeds of the Plantago ovata plant. It absorbs water in the digestive tract, forming a viscous gel that adds bulk to stool and slows gastric emptying.
psyllium fiber::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: When mixed with water, psyllium husk swells to create a thick, gel-like mass in your intestines. This slows digestion and nutrient absorption, which helps stabilize blood sugar spikes and keeps you feeling fuller longer. The gel also acts as a prebiotic, feeding beneficial gut bacteria and potentially reducing inflammatory markers. Additionally, by slowing cholesterol absorption in the small intestine, it can lower LDL and improve lipid profiles.

proven_benefits.note: 24 human studies show psyllium reduces postprandial glucose spikes and improves overall glycemic control.
11 human studies demonstrate improvements in LDL cholesterol, triglycerides, and other heart disease risk factors.
20 human studies confirm psyllium improves bowel regularity and stool consistency in both constipation and diarrhea.
20 human studies indicate psyllium lowers inflammatory markers like CRP in some populations.
7 human studies show modest support for weight loss, likely mediated by increased satiety and slower calorie absorption.

psyllium fiber::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work explores psyllium's role in microbiome diversity and its potential synergy with other fibers for metabolic syndrome. Some studies investigate whether chronic use improves insulin sensitivity beyond acute glucose control, though these findings remain preliminary and warrant confirmation in larger trials.
psyllium fiber::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Psyllium must be consumed with adequate water to prevent intestinal blockage; insufficient fluid intake can cause cramping or obstruction. Quality varies by brand; choose products that are third-party tested. Some people experience bloating or gas initially as their microbiome adjusts; gradual introduction minimizes this.

pt-141::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: PT-141 (bremelanotide) is a synthetic peptide that activates melanocortin receptors, primarily MC1R and MC4R, in the brain and body. It was originally developed as a sunless tanning agent but has been studied for effects on sexual function, inflammation, and tissue repair.
pt-141::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: PT-141 binds to melanocortin receptors in the hypothalamus and other tissues, triggering signaling cascades that influence sexual arousal, inflammatory response, and metabolic processes. In the central nervous system, it may modulate dopamine and other neurotransmitters involved in motivation and arousal. Peripherally, activation of these receptors can dampen inflammatory pathways and support tissue remodeling.

promising_benefits.note: Human evidence from 8 studies suggests PT-141 may lower inflammatory markers, though clinical significance and optimal dosing remain to be fully defined.
One human study reports cognitive benefits, but replication and mechanistic clarity are needed before firm conclusions.
Eight human studies indicate potential for accelerating tissue repair, but variability in protocols and outcomes warrants further investigation.
Three human studies suggest cardiovascular benefits, though sample sizes are small and long-term safety data are limited.
A single human study hints at hormonal effects; far more evidence is needed to establish whether PT-141 reliably influences testosterone or other hormones.

pt-141::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work has explored PT-141's role in metabolic regulation and systemic inflammation, with interest in autoimmune and inflammatory conditions. Animal models suggest broader neuroprotective potential, though human translation remains preliminary. Most clinical interest currently focuses on cardiovascular and tissue-repair applications, but these remain investigational.
pt-141::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: PT-141 is a research peptide often obtained outside regulated pharmaceutical channels; purity, sterility, and dose accuracy are not guaranteed. Injectable peptides carry infection and contamination risks if not properly prepared and administered. Long-term safety, optimal dosing, and effects on healthy individuals are not well established; use should be considered experimental and only under medical supervision where legally permitted.

quercetin::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Quercetin is a flavonoid—a plant pigment found in apples, onions, berries, and leafy greens. It belongs to a class of polyphenols known for antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties.
quercetin::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Quercetin works through multiple pathways. It scavenges free radicals that damage cells, reducing oxidative stress. It also blocks inflammatory signaling molecules (like NF-κB and cytokines) that drive chronic inflammation and immune overactivation. At the cellular level, it stabilizes mast cells and basophils, which reduces histamine release—relevant to allergy and stress responses. It may also enhance mitochondrial function and support barrier integrity in the gut and blood-brain barrier.

proven_benefits.note: Supported by 38 human studies; quercetin appears to modulate stress hormones and calm overactive immune/inflammatory pathways linked to anxiety.
Backed by 35 human studies; enhances immune cell activity and barriers against infection while helping prevent excessive inflammation.
Based on 30 human studies; shows consistent, mild-to-moderate reductions in inflammatory markers, particularly in chronic conditions.
Evidence from 29 human studies; supports endothelial function, blood pressure regulation, and atherosclerosis markers, though effect sizes are modest.

promising_benefits.note: Only 3 animal studies to date; shows promise in reducing inflammation around injured tendons, but human evidence is absent and healing outcomes remain unproven.

quercetin::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work explores quercetin's role in cellular senescence (aging cells) and its potential synergy with other polyphenols for longevity pathways, but these are early-stage observations mostly in cell and animal models. Some studies suggest it may enhance autophagy (cellular cleanup), though translation to human lifespan or healthspan remains speculative. Quality of supplement formulations varies widely; bioavailability is relatively low, which may limit real-world benefit.
quercetin::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Quercetin is a food-derived compound and generally well-tolerated; high doses may interact with certain medications (especially blood thinners and some cancers drugs) and should be discussed with a physician. Supplement purity and absorption vary significantly—food sources or standardized extracts with enhanced bioavailability (e.g., phytosome forms) are preferable to bulk powder.

reishi::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Reishi (Ganoderma lucidum) is a woody fungus native to East Asia, used in traditional medicine for centuries. It contains bioactive compounds including polysaccharides, triterpenes, and peptidoglycans that are thought to mediate its physiological effects.
reishi::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Reishi appears to work through multiple pathways. Its polysaccharides may enhance immune cell activity by binding to receptors on white blood cells. Triterpenes may influence neurotransmitter systems and stress hormone signaling (cortisol and GABA pathways). The fungus also contains compounds that may reduce oxidative stress and support cardiovascular function through endothelial relaxation and blood pressure regulation. These mechanisms are thought to underlie its traditional use for resilience and balance.

proven_benefits.benefit: cardiovascular health (blood pressure, endothelial function, lipid profile)
proven_benefits.note: Human evidence supports benefits for hypertension, cholesterol, and vascular function across 26 studies.
Human studies show measurable effects on immune markers and infection outcomes, though mechanisms and optimal dosing remain under investigation.
Human evidence supports anxiolytic and stress-reducing effects, though the evidence base is small (3 studies) and larger trials are needed.
Human studies indicate modest benefits for attention, memory, and mental fatigue, supported by 22 studies.

promising_benefits.note: Animal studies and mechanistic research suggest anti-inflammatory potential, but human clinical evidence is lacking; this remains unproven in people.

reishi::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work has explored reishi's effects on sleep quality, gut microbiota composition, and cancer-related fatigue, though human data remain sparse. Some studies suggest synergistic effects when combined with other adaptogens or immune-support compounds. These directions are early and should not be considered established benefits.
reishi::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Reishi is generally well-tolerated, but quality varies widely among commercial products; standardized extracts are preferable. Long-term safety in pregnancy and breastfeeding is not well characterized, and it may interact with immunosuppressive or blood-thinning medications.

resveratrol::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Resveratrol is a polyphenol compound found naturally in red grapes, berries, and peanuts. It functions as a plant antioxidant that crosses the blood–brain barrier and accumulates in several tissues, making it bioavailable for systemic effects.
resveratrol::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Resveratrol activates cellular pathways—particularly sirtuins and AMPK—that regulate stress response, energy metabolism, and inflammatory signaling. By reducing oxidative stress and suppressing pro-inflammatory cytokines, it modulates both immune function and vascular biology. It also influences gut barrier integrity and microbial composition, though the precise mechanisms linking these changes to health outcomes remain incompletely understood.

proven_benefits.note: Robust human evidence (35 studies) shows resveratrol lowers circulating inflammatory markers and dampens immune overactivation.
Human studies (9 trials) demonstrate benefits for vascular function, blood pressure, and lipid profiles in clinical populations.
Human evidence (36 studies) supports anxiolytic effects and improved stress resilience, though effect sizes are modest.

promising_benefits.note: Human studies (30 trials) suggest resveratrol may improve barrier function and shift microbiota composition, but clinical significance and durability are not yet established.

resveratrol::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work explores resveratrol's potential in metabolic health, cognitive aging, and cancer chemoprevention—largely in animal models or mechanistic human studies. Some research suggests synergy with exercise and caloric restriction for longevity pathways, but human lifespan data do not yet exist. These directions are encouraging but require further clinical validation.
resveratrol::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Bioavailability is low (1–5% absorbed orally), requiring high doses or specialized formulations; most clinical doses range 150–1,000 mg daily. Long-term safety in humans is not exhaustively studied, and interactions with anticoagulants or NSAIDs warrant caution. Resveratrol is not a substitute for exercise, diet, or sleep in any longevity protocol.

rhodiola rosea::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Rhodiola rosea is a flowering plant native to arctic and mountainous regions, whose root extract contains active compounds called rosavins and salidroside. It has been used in traditional Scandinavian and Russian medicine for centuries and is classified as an adaptogen—a substance believed to help the body manage stress.
rhodiola rosea::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Rhodiola appears to work by modulating stress hormones (like cortisol) and neurotransmitters involved in mood and cognition, including serotonin, dopamine, and norepinephrine. It also has antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties that may protect brain cells and reduce systemic inflammation. By stabilizing these systems rather than forcing a single effect, it helps the body adapt to physical and mental stressors. The active compounds cross the blood-brain barrier and interact with multiple receptors, which explains its broad effects on mood, energy, and mental clarity.

proven_benefits.note: Evidence from 21 human studies shows Rhodiola supports focus, memory, and mental clarity, particularly under stress or fatigue.
30 human studies document anti-inflammatory effects, suggesting systemic benefit across multiple tissues.
11 human trials show measurable improvements in depressive symptoms and overall mood.
13 human studies confirm Rhodiola reduces perceived stress and anxiety symptoms, though effects are somewhat variable between individuals.

promising_benefits.note: Early animal studies (8 total) suggest potential benefits for gut barrier function and microbial balance, but no human trials exist yet.

rhodiola rosea::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work is exploring Rhodiola's role in gut-brain axis signaling and its effects on the microbiome, though this remains largely in animal models. Some preliminary research also investigates whether Rhodiola may support athletic recovery and endurance, building on its traditional use as an energizer. These areas are too early to claim clinical benefit but represent active frontiers.
rhodiola rosea::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Rhodiola is generally well-tolerated, but quality and potency vary significantly across commercial extracts; standardized products (3% rosavins, 1% salidroside) are preferable. It should not replace medical treatment for depression or anxiety disorders, and may interact with certain medications or cause mild side effects (dizziness, dry mouth) in some users. Long-term safety data in humans remains limited.

saccharomyces boulardii::clarity-engine-.what_it_is: Saccharomyces boulardii is a live, beneficial yeast strain that colonizes the gut microbiome. Unlike bacteria-based probiotics, it's a fungus—specifically a strain of *Saccharomyces cerevisiae*—that survives stomach acid and establishes itself temporarily in the intestinal tract.
saccharomyces boulardii::clarity-engine-.how_it_works: Once in the gut, S. boulardii produces short-chain fatty acids and other metabolites that nourish the intestinal lining and promote a healthy microbial environment. It also produces antimicrobial compounds that inhibit pathogenic bacteria and yeasts, reinforces the gut barrier's tight junctions (reducing 'leaky gut'), and stimulates local immune cells in the intestine. Through these mechanisms, it appears to reduce intestinal inflammation and support both digestive and immune resilience, with emerging evidence suggesting these gut-level changes may influence mood and cognitive function via the gut–brain axis.

proven_benefits.note: 27 human studies show clear benefits for digestive symptoms, diarrhea prevention, and intestinal barrier function.

promising_benefits.note: 35 human studies indicate S. boulardii reduces markers of gut and systemic inflammation, though optimal dosing and individual response vary.
27 human studies suggest it enhances intestinal immune responses and may reduce infection risk, particularly in vulnerable populations.
4 human studies show preliminary links between S. boulardii and reduced anxiety, likely mediated through gut–brain signaling, but evidence remains limited.
7 human studies suggest potential cognitive benefits via gut–brain pathways, though direct cognitive claims require further validation.

saccharomyces boulardii::clarity-engine-.emerging_research: Recent work explores S. boulardii's role in the gut–brain axis, including effects on neurotransmitter production and the vagal signaling pathway that links gut health to mood and mental clarity. Some studies are investigating its use in antibiotic-associated dysbiosis, small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO), and travel-related diarrhea. These directions are still early and mostly small-scale.
saccharomyces boulardii::clarity-engine-.caveats: S. boulardii is generally well-tolerated, but immunocompromised individuals should consult a physician before use, as live microorganisms carry a theoretical risk. Quality varies by manufacturer; choose reputable brands with verified CFU counts and third-party testing. It is not a replacement for antibiotics or medical treatment, and effects are typically temporary—benefits often diminish after discontinuation.

saffron::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Saffron is a spice derived from the dried stigmas (thread-like filaments) of the Crocus sativus flower. It contains bioactive compounds, primarily crocin and safranal, which are responsible for its distinctive color, flavor, and biological effects.
saffron::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Saffron's active ingredients work through multiple pathways in the body. Crocin and safranal act as antioxidants and anti-inflammatory agents, reducing oxidative stress and dampening inflammatory signaling in cells and tissues. In the brain, these compounds appear to modulate neurotransmitter systems—particularly serotonin and dopamine pathways—that regulate mood and stress response. They also support vascular function by improving blood flow and reducing arterial inflammation, which benefits both heart health and cognitive perfusion.

proven_benefits.note: 27 human studies demonstrate significant improvements in depressive symptoms, with efficacy comparable to some conventional antidepressants in clinical trials.
26 human studies confirm saffron's ability to reduce inflammatory markers and systemic inflammation across various conditions.
16 human studies show improvements in blood pressure, endothelial function, and lipid profiles, supporting overall heart and vessel health.
29 human studies indicate meaningful reductions in anxiety and stress-related symptoms, though effect sizes vary by study design.
18 human studies suggest benefits for memory, attention, and cognitive processing, particularly in aging populations.

saffron::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent studies are exploring saffron's potential in neurodegenerative conditions and age-related cognitive decline, with preliminary evidence suggesting protective effects on brain tissue. Researchers are also investigating its role in metabolic health and glucose regulation. These directions remain early and require larger, longer-term human trials to establish clinical significance.
saffron::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Saffron is a culinary herb with a strong safety profile at typical doses (30–100 mg daily of standardized extract), though very high doses may carry risks. Quality varies widely among commercial products; look for standardized extracts with documented crocin and safranal content. Most evidence comes from short-term studies (8–12 weeks); long-term safety and optimal dosing strategies remain less well characterized.

selenium::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Selenium is a trace mineral found in soil, seafood, and plant-based foods that your body needs in small amounts. It's a key component of selenoproteins—specialized proteins that carry out critical functions in cells throughout your body.
selenium::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Selenium is incorporated into selenoproteins, which act as antioxidants and help regulate inflammatory signaling in your immune cells. These proteins are essential for thyroid hormone metabolism, which influences testosterone production and hormonal balance. Selenium also supports the production and function of immune cells that fight infections, and helps manage the stress response by protecting cells from oxidative damage during periods of high demand.

proven_benefits.note: Strong human evidence (37 studies) shows selenium supports healthy testosterone levels and thyroid function, which regulate hormonal balance.
Strong human evidence (23 studies) demonstrates that adequate selenium is critical for mounting and sustaining an effective immune response.
Moderate human evidence (29 studies) suggests selenium supports healthy gut barrier function and digestive enzyme activity.
Moderate human evidence (28 studies) shows selenium helps regulate inflammatory signaling and reduce excessive immune activation.
Moderate human evidence (33 studies) indicates selenium protects cells during stress and supports healthy mood regulation.

selenium::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent studies are exploring whether optimized selenium status may enhance vaccine response and support cognitive health during aging. Some research is also examining its role in mitigating oxidative stress in specific disease states, though these applications remain early and require further confirmation in humans.
selenium::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Selenium is essential in small amounts but toxic in excess; the safe range is narrow, so supplementation should be modest and monitored if you have thyroid disorders or take certain medications. Most people meet selenium needs through diet (Brazil nuts, fish, and eggs are excellent sources); supplementation is most relevant for those with confirmed deficiency or specific health conditions.

semaglutide::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Semaglutide is a glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist—a synthetic peptide that mimics a natural hormone your gut releases after eating. It is administered by injection (weekly) and works by binding to GLP-1 receptors throughout your body to regulate appetite, blood sugar, and metabolic processes.
semaglutide::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: When you eat, your intestines naturally release GLP-1, which signals your brain that you're full and slows stomach emptying. Semaglutide amplifies this signal, making you feel fuller longer and reducing hunger drive. It also directly stimulates your pancreas to release insulin in response to rising blood sugar, improving glucose control. Over time, these combined effects lower calorie intake, reduce appetite, and improve metabolic health.

proven_benefits.note: Robust human evidence (23 studies) shows semaglutide produces significant reductions in body weight and fat mass, with effects seen consistently across diverse populations.
Well-established human evidence (31 studies) demonstrates semaglutide effectively lowers fasting and post-meal blood glucose and HbA1c, making it particularly valuable in type 2 diabetes.
Solid human evidence (25 studies) indicates semaglutide reduces major cardiovascular events, lowers blood pressure, and improves heart disease risk markers in people with obesity or diabetes.

promising_benefits.note: Human evidence (22 studies) suggests semaglutide may lower inflammatory markers, though the clinical significance and mechanisms remain under investigation.
Early human evidence (15 studies) hints at effects on digestion and gut function, but findings are inconsistent and more research is needed to clarify clinical impact.

semaglutide::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent studies are exploring semaglutide's potential effects on liver fat, kidney disease progression, and appetite-independent metabolic benefits. Some preliminary work suggests possible neuroprotective or anti-aging pathways, but these remain speculative and far from clinical application. Most emerging directions require larger, longer-term human trials before firm conclusions can be drawn.
semaglutide::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Semaglutide is a potent injectable peptide; quality, purity, and sterility vary widely outside clinical settings, and counterfeit products are common in unregulated markets. Common side effects include nausea, vomiting, and gastrointestinal upset, particularly at dose initiation; rare but serious risks include pancreatitis and thyroid concerns—medical supervision is essential. Its long-term safety profile beyond 2–3 years, optimal dosing in non-diabetic populations, and sustainability of weight loss after discontinuation remain incompletely characterized.

sermorelin::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Sermorelin is a synthetic 29-amino-acid peptide that mimics growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH), a natural signaling molecule in the brain. It stimulates the pituitary gland to produce and release its own growth hormone, rather than replacing it directly.
sermorelin::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Sermorelin binds to GHRH receptors on pituitary cells, triggering the secretion of endogenous growth hormone in a pulsatile pattern similar to the body's natural rhythm. This differs from exogenous growth hormone injection, which bypasses the pituitary and can suppress its own production. Over time, repeated stimulation may help restore or sustain growth hormone levels, particularly in aging or deficient individuals. The released GH then acts on target tissues throughout the body to influence metabolism, muscle, bone, and immune function.

proven_benefits.note: Human evidence from 9 studies supports an effect on glucose metabolism and insulin sensitivity.
Human evidence from 9 studies indicates potential benefits for immune cell activity and function.

promising_benefits.note: Early human evidence (6 studies) suggests possible effects on testosterone, but findings remain inconclusive and require further confirmation.
Human studies (26 total) show early promise for connective tissue repair, but clinical significance and optimal use remain unclear.
Animal studies (12) suggest anti-inflammatory potential, but no human evidence yet; effects in people are unproven.

sermorelin::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work has explored sermorelin's role in aging-related decline, lean body mass preservation, and metabolic recovery in growth-hormone-deficient populations. Some studies examine its combination with other peptides or agents to enhance tissue repair and recovery. These applications remain early-stage; large, well-controlled human trials are needed to establish clinical utility beyond established uses.
sermorelin::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Sermorelin is a prescription medication in many countries and is sometimes sold as a research chemical of uncertain purity and sterility; use only under medical supervision or from verified pharmaceutical sources. Long-term safety, optimal dosing, and effects on hormone levels in healthy individuals are not fully established; it should not be used without appropriate medical evaluation and monitoring.

sodium bicarbonate::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Sodium bicarbonate is a simple alkaline salt (NaHCO₃), commonly known as baking soda. It acts as a buffer—a chemical substance that neutralizes acids in the body and raises pH.
sodium bicarbonate::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: When ingested, sodium bicarbonate dissolves and releases bicarbonate ions that neutralize stomach acid and circulating hydrogen ions in the blood. This buffering effect reduces acidity in the digestive tract and can modulate blood pH slightly. By reducing local acidity in the gut, it may improve the environment for digestion and nutrient absorption. The same mechanism—buffering excess acid—appears to influence glucose metabolism and insulin response, though the exact pathway remains under study.

proven_benefits.note: Human evidence from 32 studies supports a role in improving digestion and reducing acid-related discomfort.
Human evidence from 26 studies indicates sodium bicarbonate may help support healthy blood glucose levels and insulin sensitivity.

sodium bicarbonate::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work is exploring sodium bicarbonate's potential in athletic performance (via acid buffering during intense exercise) and kidney health in specific populations. These areas remain preliminary and require further human validation before clinical recommendations can be made.
sodium bicarbonate::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Sodium bicarbonate is generally safe at dietary doses, but excessive intake can cause alkalosis (over-alkalinity) and electrolyte imbalance; individuals with kidney disease or on specific medications should consult a healthcare provider. Quality varies by source; pharmaceutical-grade formulations are preferred over unregulated products.

spermidine::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Spermidine is a naturally occurring polyamine—a small organic compound made of linked amino acid building blocks—found in cells throughout the body and in foods like aged cheese, mushrooms, and whole grains. It is one of the body's key molecules for cell division, protein synthesis, and cellular health maintenance.
spermidine::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Spermidine works by stabilizing cell structures, supporting protein folding, and activating autophagy—a cellular 'cleanup' process that removes damaged components and may slow aging-related decline. It also modulates mitochondrial function (the energy factories of cells) and appears to influence signaling pathways linked to inflammation and immune response. As we age, natural spermidine levels drop, which is why supplementation aims to restore youthful cellular housekeeping.

proven_benefits.note: 34 human studies show spermidine can lower inflammatory markers and may support conditions driven by chronic inflammation.
26 human studies indicate potential benefits for memory, processing speed, and neuroinflammation-related cognitive decline.
29 human studies suggest spermidine enhances immune cell activity and adaptive immune responses.

promising_benefits.note: Early human evidence suggests possible benefits for stress resilience and anxiety, but sample sizes remain small and replication is needed.
Preliminary evidence hints at positive effects on gut barrier function and microbiome composition, though mechanisms and clinical significance are still being clarified.

spermidine::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work explores spermidine's potential role in cardiovascular health, metabolic aging, and neurodegenerative disease prevention—largely from animal models and early human studies. Some research suggests synergy with fasting or caloric restriction to enhance autophagy, but this remains investigational in humans. Longevity claims in popular media often exceed current evidence; most human data focus on biomarkers and short-term outcomes rather than lifespan.
spermidine::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Spermidine supplements vary widely in quality and bioavailability; food sources (aged cheese, mushrooms, legumes) may offer more reliable intake. The optimal dose, duration, and long-term safety profile in humans are not yet established, and most studies have been relatively short-term; individuals on certain medications or with specific health conditions should consult a healthcare provider before supplementing.

st. john's wort::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: St. John's Wort is a flowering plant (Hypericum perforatum) native to Europe, now used as a herbal supplement. Its active compounds include hypericin, hyperforin, and flavonoids, which are extracted from the plant's leaves and flowers.
st. john's wort::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: St. John's Wort appears to work by increasing levels of neurotransmitters in the brain—particularly serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine—that regulate mood and stress response. Hyperforin, its primary active ingredient, inhibits the reuptake of these neurotransmitters, meaning they stay active in the brain longer. The herb may also modulate inflammation and oxidative stress in the central nervous system. The exact balance of compounds responsible for its effects remains incompletely understood.

proven_benefits.note: Evidence from 21 human studies supports St. John's Wort as effective for mild-to-moderate depression, with efficacy comparable to some conventional antidepressants in trial settings.
Data from 25 human studies indicate meaningful reduction in anxiety and stress symptoms, though effects are generally more consistent for anxiety than severe panic disorders.
18 human studies show modest improvements in memory, attention, and mental clarity, particularly in older adults or those with age-related cognitive decline.
11 human studies suggest St. John's Wort may support healthy testosterone levels and hormone balance, though mechanisms and clinical significance remain partially unclear.

promising_benefits.note: 29 human studies hint at anti-inflammatory activity, but results are inconsistent and the clinical relevance of these findings in real-world contexts is not yet firmly established.

st. john's wort::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent investigations are exploring St. John's Wort's potential role in neuroinflammation and neuroprotection, as well as its synergistic effects when combined with other botanical compounds. Early work also examines whether specific extraction methods or ratios of active compounds improve consistency and efficacy. These directions remain preliminary and require larger, more rigorous trials.
st. john's wort::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: St. John's Wort is a natural product with variable potency depending on growing conditions and extraction methods; standardization to hypericin or hyperforin content is important. Critically, it interacts with many medications—including birth control, warfarin, certain antidepressants, and immunosuppressants—by inducing cytochrome P450 enzymes, so medical consultation is essential before use. Avoid use in pregnancy or if you have bipolar disorder, as it may trigger mood cycling.

tart cherry::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Tart cherry (Prunus cerasus) is a small, dark red fruit rich in polyphenols, anthocyanins, and melatonin. It is typically consumed as juice, dried fruit, or extract in supplement form.
tart cherry::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Tart cherry's bioactive compounds, particularly anthocyanins and other antioxidants, reduce oxidative stress and inflammatory signaling in the body. The fruit also contains naturally occurring melatonin, which helps regulate circadian rhythm and sleep-wake cycles. These mechanisms work together to lower systemic inflammation, support cardiovascular function, reduce muscle breakdown after exercise, and calm the nervous system—effects that appear to improve sleep quality and reduce perceived stress.

proven_benefits.note: 12 human studies show tart cherry improves sleep onset, duration, and subjective quality, likely via its melatonin and anti-inflammatory content.
23 human studies demonstrate tart cherry reduces perceived stress and anxiety symptoms, probably through antioxidant and nervous-system-calming effects.
29 human studies show tart cherry lowers circulating inflammatory markers and supports recovery, though effects vary by dose and individual.
29 human studies indicate benefits for blood pressure, arterial flexibility, and lipid profiles, supporting overall heart health.
8 human studies show modest benefits for muscle soreness and strength retention after intense exercise, likely via reduced inflammation.

tart cherry::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work is exploring whether tart cherry's anthocyanins may support cognitive function and metabolic health in aging populations, though these areas remain early and require more human data. Some studies are also investigating optimal dosing and timing for athletic performance, but firm recommendations are not yet established.
tart cherry::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Tart cherry is safe for most people; however, quality and potency vary widely among commercial products, and some people report mild digestive upset. The evidence above reflects group averages—individual responses differ, and tart cherry should not replace conventional medical treatment for sleep disorders or anxiety.

taurine::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Taurine is a semi-essential amino acid—a small protein building block—that your body produces naturally but can also obtain from food (especially animal products) and supplements. Unlike most amino acids, taurine is not used to build structural proteins; instead, it circulates freely and concentrates in tissues like muscle, heart, brain, and eyes.
taurine::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Taurine acts as a cellular regulator and protector across multiple systems. It helps stabilize cell membranes, reducing oxidative stress and inflammation at the cellular level. In the cardiovascular system, taurine supports heart muscle function and helps regulate blood pressure. For blood sugar control, it enhances insulin signaling and improves how cells respond to glucose. In the nervous system, it modulates neurotransmitters and may dampen stress responses. It also supports bile acid conjugation in the liver, aiding fat digestion and detoxification.

proven_benefits.note: Robust evidence from 30 human studies shows taurine consistently lowers markers of systemic inflammation and supports immune balance.
29 human studies demonstrate taurine improves insulin sensitivity and helps regulate blood glucose levels, particularly in people with metabolic challenges.
17 human studies indicate taurine benefits heart function, blood pressure regulation, and vascular health, though effects vary by dose and individual.
32 human studies support taurine's role in dampening stress responses and promoting nervous system calm, likely through GABA and neurotransmitter pathways.

promising_benefits.note: 36 human studies show associations with improved digestion and gut barrier function, but mechanisms remain incompletely understood and effects are modest.

taurine::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent studies explore taurine's potential role in cognitive aging, eye health (particularly retinal function), and athletic recovery and muscle endurance. There is also growing interest in taurine for metabolic syndrome and liver health. However, these areas remain early-stage; larger, well-designed trials are needed to establish clinical relevance.
taurine::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Taurine is generally safe at supplemental doses (1–3 g daily); long-term safety data are reassuring but not exhaustive. Quality varies among supplements—source and purity matter. Most human evidence comes from observational studies or small trials; more rigorous randomized controlled trials would strengthen confidence in specific clinical outcomes.

tb-500::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: TB-500 (Thymosin Beta-4) is a naturally occurring peptide of 43 amino acids found in high concentrations in wound-healing cells and immune tissues. It is often synthesized in research settings and sold as an injectable peptide.
tb-500::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: TB-500 appears to promote cell migration and tissue repair by increasing actin dynamics—the structural proteins that allow cells to move and reshape. In the body, it may support wound healing, reduce inflammation, and influence various signaling pathways involved in cell survival and growth. The exact mechanisms in humans remain incompletely understood, but animal studies suggest it acts on multiple cell types, from fibroblasts to immune cells.

promising_benefits.note: 17 human studies suggest potential effects on testosterone or related hormones, but evidence remains preliminary and inconsistent; clinical significance is not yet established.
17 human studies indicate possible metabolic effects on glucose control, but findings are early and mechanisms in humans are not fully characterized.
Only animal studies (1 study) have examined TB-500's effects on digestion and gut function; no human evidence exists.

tb-500::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work has explored TB-500's potential role in tissue repair, immune modulation, and metabolic regulation. However, most clinical data remain early-stage, with small sample sizes and variable protocols. Much of what is known comes from animal models and preliminary human observational studies rather than rigorous controlled trials.
tb-500::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: TB-500 is typically sold as a research chemical or injectable peptide and is not approved by the FDA for human use; quality, purity, and safety profiles vary widely depending on source. Long-term safety data in humans is limited, and the compound's full physiological effects and optimal dosing remain unknown.

thiamine::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Thiamine, also called vitamin B1, is a water-soluble micronutrient essential for energy production and nerve function. Your body cannot synthesize it, so it must come from food or supplementation.
thiamine::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Thiamine is converted into thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), a coenzyme that powers multiple enzyme systems central to carbohydrate metabolism, amino acid breakdown, and nervous system signaling. Without adequate thiamine, cells struggle to generate ATP (energy) efficiently, and inflammatory and oxidative stress pathways can become overactive. It also supports the myelin sheaths that insulate nerve fibers and help regulate neurotransmitter production.

proven_benefits.note: 19 human studies support thiamine's role in lowering inflammatory markers, likely via its role in metabolic efficiency and antioxidant enzyme systems.
17 human studies suggest thiamine helps modulate stress response and reduce anxiety symptoms, possibly through nervous system stabilization and neurotransmitter regulation.
30 human studies indicate thiamine supports heart function, blood vessel health, and may help normalize blood pressure and lipid profiles.
30 human studies show thiamine improves glucose metabolism and insulin sensitivity, particularly in individuals with metabolic dysfunction.

promising_benefits.note: 33 human studies exist, but evidence remains mixed and inconsistent; thiamine likely supports digestive enzyme function and gut barrier integrity, but clinical significance is not yet established.

thiamine::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work explores thiamine's role in chronic neuroinflammation, cognitive decline, and mitochondrial dysfunction in aging and metabolic disease. There is also growing interest in high-dose thiamine for specific conditions like diabetic neuropathy and alcohol-related deficiency syndromes. These directions are promising but remain early and require larger, more rigorous trials.
thiamine::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Thiamine is water-soluble and has a low toxicity ceiling; excess intake is excreted, so overdose is rare. However, quality and bioavailability of supplements vary; deficiency is common in processed-food diets, refined grains (which strip thiamine), and heavy alcohol use, so baseline status matters. Most research reflects correction of inadequacy rather than pharmacological enhancement in replete individuals.

thymosin alpha-1::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Thymosin alpha-1 (Tα1) is a naturally occurring 28-amino-acid peptide originally isolated from the thymus gland, an organ central to immune development. It is typically synthesized for research and clinical use, and is administered by injection.
thymosin alpha-1::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Thymosin alpha-1 acts as an immune modulator, primarily by enhancing the activity and maturation of T cells—the white blood cells that coordinate adaptive immunity. It increases the production of cytokines (signaling proteins) that amplify immune responses and simultaneously dampens excessive inflammation by promoting a more balanced, regulated immune state. In this way, it helps the immune system respond appropriately to threats without overreacting, which is why it shows effects on both immune function and inflammatory control.

proven_benefits.note: Backed by 25 human studies demonstrating enhanced T-cell activity, antibody responses, and infection resistance.
Supported by 28 human studies showing decreased inflammatory markers and improved balance in immune regulation.

promising_benefits.note: Animal studies (6 total) suggest potential effects on hormone levels, but human evidence is currently absent.
Only 2 animal studies exist; no human data yet on effects on digestive function or gut barrier integrity.

thymosin alpha-1::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work has explored thymosin alpha-1's potential in aging-related immune decline and chronic viral infections, with some early signals in respiratory health and vaccine response enhancement. A small number of studies are examining mechanisms in intestinal barrier function and microbiota interactions, though these remain very preliminary and confined to animal models or in vitro work. These directions are promising but require substantial human validation before clinical claims can be made.
thymosin alpha-1::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Thymosin alpha-1 is a peptide and research chemical in most jurisdictions; its manufacture, purity, and sterility are not universally regulated, and users should verify source quality and consult a healthcare provider before use. Long-term safety in humans is not fully characterized, and it should not be self-administered without medical supervision, especially in those with autoimmune conditions or compromised immune states.

tirzepatide::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Tirzepatide is a synthetic peptide that activates two hormone receptors in the body: GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1) and GIP (glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide). It is administered as a weekly injection and was initially developed to treat type 2 diabetes.
tirzepatide::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Tirzepatide works by mimicking two naturally occurring gut hormones that regulate blood sugar and appetite. When you eat, it amplifies insulin release in response to rising glucose, slows stomach emptying to reduce blood sugar spikes, and signals the brain's appetite centers to reduce hunger and food intake. By activating both GLP-1 and GIP pathways simultaneously, it produces stronger effects on weight and metabolic control than single-pathway drugs. The combined action also appears to improve heart and blood vessel function, likely through reduced inflammation and improved metabolic markers.

proven_benefits.benefit: Blood sugar control (glucose reduction in type 2 diabetes)
proven_benefits.note: Consistently lowers fasting and post-meal blood glucose across 26 human studies, with effects comparable to or exceeding existing diabetes medications.
22 human studies show significant reductions in body weight and fat mass, with average losses ranging from 5–20% depending on dose and study duration.
25 human studies demonstrate improvements in heart attack and stroke risk markers, blood pressure, and direct cardiovascular event reduction in high-risk patients.

promising_benefits.note: Only 4 animal studies suggest potential benefits for gut barrier integrity and inflammation; human evidence is absent and effects remain unproven.
Only 4 human studies exist; preliminary data hints at possible effects on sex hormones, but the direction, magnitude, and clinical relevance are not yet established.

tirzepatide::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work is exploring tirzepatide's effects on liver fat, kidney disease progression, and neurodegenerative conditions, though these areas remain very early and largely preclinical. Some research is examining whether tirzepatide's benefits persist after stopping treatment and how it compares to GLP-1–only drugs in real-world settings. These are promising directions but require more human data before firm conclusions.
tirzepatide::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Tirzepatide is an injectable peptide; like all peptides, it is rapidly broken down by stomach acid and must be injected subcutaneously (typically weekly). Quality, purity, and source matter significantly—only pharmaceutical-grade product is appropriate for use. Common side effects include nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea, particularly at higher doses or early in treatment. Long-term safety beyond the studied period (2–3 years) is not yet fully characterized, and it is not approved for weight loss in non-diabetic individuals in all countries.

tongkat ali::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Tongkat Ali (Eurycoma longifolia) is a tropical plant native to Southeast Asia, traditionally used in herbal medicine. Its active compounds include quassinoids and other alkaloids that interact with hormonal and neurological systems.
tongkat ali::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Tongkat Ali appears to work through multiple pathways: it may enhance luteinizing hormone (LH) signaling, which stimulates natural testosterone production in men; it influences neurotransmitter systems involved in mood regulation; and it may support muscle protein synthesis and reduce exercise-induced stress hormones like cortisol. These combined effects on hormones, stress, and neurological function explain its diverse reported benefits.

proven_benefits.note: 31 human studies show Tongkat Ali reliably increases testosterone levels and related hormonal markers in men, with effects typically observed over 4–12 weeks of use.
33 human studies demonstrate consistent improvements in mood, anxiety, and depressive symptoms, likely linked to its effects on cortisol and neurotransmitter balance.
11 human studies indicate modest but measurable gains in strength and lean mass, particularly when combined with resistance training.

promising_benefits.note: Only 3 human studies examined sleep; results are suggestive but too limited to confirm efficacy at this time.

tongkat ali::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work is exploring Tongkat Ali's potential role in sexual function, energy/fatigue, and bone health, but these areas remain early and require larger, well-designed trials. Some studies also investigate whether standardized extracts differ in efficacy, and whether benefits extend to women, though most research has focused on male populations.
tongkat ali::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Tongkat Ali is an herbal extract, so product quality and standardization vary widely between brands; look for verified third-party testing. Long-term safety data beyond 12 months is limited, and it is not recommended during pregnancy or for those on hormone-sensitive medications without medical guidance.

turmeric::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Turmeric is a bright yellow spice derived from the rhizome (underground stem) of Curcuma longa, a plant in the ginger family. Its active compound is curcumin, a polyphenol that gives turmeric its color and most of its biological activity.
turmeric::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Curcumin works primarily by inhibiting inflammatory signaling pathways in the body—particularly NF-κB, a master regulator of pro-inflammatory genes. It also acts as an antioxidant, neutralizing free radicals that damage cells and contribute to aging and disease. In the gut and bloodstream, curcumin modulates immune function and may improve endothelial (blood vessel) health. Curcumin's absorption is poor on its own, which is why turmeric is often combined with black pepper (piperine), which significantly enhances bioavailability.

proven_benefits.note: Supported by 26 human studies; turmeric consistently reduces markers of systemic and localized inflammation.
Supported by 13 human studies; turmeric improves endothelial function, lipid profiles, and blood flow markers.
Supported by 15 human studies; curcumin shows modest anxiolytic and mood-supporting effects in clinical trials.

promising_benefits.note: 27 human studies suggest turmeric may support gut barrier function and healthy microbiota, but the evidence is still developing and mechanisms are not fully clear.
Only 2 animal studies exist; curcumin may support collagen synthesis and tissue repair, but this has not yet been tested in humans.

turmeric::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work explores turmeric's role in brain health and neuroprotection, with early evidence suggesting curcumin may support cognitive function and neuroinflammation reduction. Studies are also investigating its potential in metabolic health and cancer prevention, though these remain largely preclinical or early-stage human research. As with many natural compounds, larger and longer human trials are needed to refine dose recommendations and identify which populations benefit most.
turmeric::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Curcumin has low bioavailability without piperine (black pepper) or fat co-ingestion; standardized extracts are more reliable than whole turmeric powder. High doses may cause mild gastrointestinal upset, and turmeric may interact with blood thinners or certain medications—consult a healthcare provider if on anticoagulants. Most studies use isolated curcumin or standardized extracts; whole turmeric spice provides lower doses and may require supplementation for therapeutic effect.

valerian root::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Valerian root is a dried plant material from Valeriana officinalis, a perennial herb native to Europe and Asia. It contains a complex mixture of volatile oils, alkaloids, and iridoid compounds (valepotriates) that are thought to drive its biological effects.
valerian root::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Valerian's active constituents appear to work through multiple pathways. The main mechanism involves enhancing GABA, a neurotransmitter that calms nervous system activity—similar in concept to how benzodiazepines work, but much more gently. Some compounds in valerian also bind weakly to serotonin and adenosine receptors, which may further promote relaxation. The herb also contains compounds that inhibit the enzyme responsible for breaking down GABA, allowing it to accumulate slightly in the brain. These combined effects make valerian a mild sedative and anxiolytic (anti-anxiety) agent.

proven_benefits.note: Human studies show valerian moderately improves sleep quality and may reduce time to fall asleep, though effects are typically modest and variable between individuals.
Limited but consistent human evidence suggests valerian may reduce subjective anxiety and stress, though the magnitude of effect is moderate.
Human research indicates valerian may support cognitive function, though the specific domains and practical significance require further clarification.
A substantial body of human studies reports valerian is associated with moderate improvements in muscle strength, though mechanisms are not fully understood.

valerian root::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent investigations have explored valerian's potential role in neuroinflammation and neuroprotection, as well as its effects on sleep architecture (REM vs. deep sleep stages) in more granular detail. Some preliminary work suggests valerian may have mild antioxidant properties in brain tissue. These directions remain early and require larger, well-controlled human studies to establish clinical relevance.
