Because you are seeing approximately 40 abstracts per outcome, not the complete literature, gaps in populations, trial duration, or specific indications may exist beyond this sample.
glutamine::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.caveats: Glutamine is generally well-tolerated as a dietary supplement at typical oral doses (5–20 g/day), but people with severe kidney or liver disease, those with phenylketonuria (PKU), or individuals on immunosuppressive therapy should consult a healthcare provider before use. Injectable glutamine formulations are used in clinical settings and carry additional safety considerations beyond oral supplementation. Supplement quality and purity vary by manufacturer; third-party testing is not routinely available in all products. Glutamine may interact with certain medications or affect blood glucose in diabetic individuals taking insulin or oral agents, so medical supervision is prudent for those with diabetes or on medications affecting metabolism.

zma::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.what_it_is: ZMA is a mineral supplement combining zinc, magnesium, and aspartate (an amino acid). It is sold as a capsule or powder intended to support athletic performance and recovery. The formulation was originally developed in the 1990s as a sports nutrition product, marketed primarily to strength athletes and bodybuilders.
zma::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.how_it_works: Zinc and magnesium are essential cofactors in hundreds of enzymatic reactions in the body, including those involved in protein synthesis, energy production, and immune signaling. Zinc plays a direct role in testosterone regulation and immune cell function, while magnesium is critical for muscle contraction, nervous system function, and sleep regulation. Aspartate is a carrier molecule that may enhance absorption of both minerals. Together, these nutrients theoretically support muscle adaptation to training, reduce exercise-induced stress on the body, and promote recovery—though the synergistic effect of the three-component formulation specifically remains incompletely characterized.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Three human studies examined stress or anxiety in relation to ZMA or its components, including observational work in medical and dental students experiencing academic and dissection-related stress (2012–2013). One study with verified sample size (n=94) measured psychological stress in first-year medical students in response to human cadaver dissection. However, the retrieved studies do not clearly report whether ZMA supplementation reduced stress or anxiety—they appear primarily to characterize stress levels in these populations rather than isolate a supplement effect.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Human data exist but are sparse (three small studies) and lack clear efficacy endpoints. The largest verified study involved only 94 participants, and precision around any effect is modest. No animal studies were retrieved for this outcome. The evidence is too preliminary to claim ZMA reduces stress in humans.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2024 randomized controlled trial examined the effects of zinc magnesium aspartate supplementation on sleep quality and weightlifting performance in human participants. This is the only study retrieved addressing sleep quality in relation to ZMA.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only one human RCT was found; consistency cannot be assessed with a single study. Sample size could not be verified from the abstract, so precision is unconfirmed. One positive trial is suggestive but far too limited to establish ZMA as an effective sleep aid.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Two human studies (one observational 2020 study on drug-metabolizing enzymes and drug transporters, and one 2022 unclassified study on kidney disease transcriptomics) and three animal studies (2025 lavender nanoparticles, 2023 fibroblast growth factor work, and 2026 green tea catechin research) were retrieved. The human studies appear primarily mechanistic or observational rather than direct intervention trials testing ZMA's anti-inflammatory effect. Animal models showed inflammatory markers in specific disease contexts (photoaging, kidney injury, obesity-related cognition).
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderate grade reflects a mixed human and animal base (2 human, 3 animal), but human evidence is observational or mechanistic rather than controlled intervention trials. Sample sizes in abstracts could not be verified, limiting precision. The animal models are relevant to inflammation but do not reliably predict human response.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Eight animal studies were retrieved examining immune-related mechanisms: microRNA associations in plant pathogen resistance (groundnut, maize stalk rot, maize disease resistance), T cell activation, and regulatory networks. These span 2014–2026 and use in vitro, cell-based, and whole-organism models in plants and immune cells.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: All evidence is animal or in vitro; no human trials were found. Animal models of immune function in plants and cell cultures do not reliably translate to human immune outcomes. The evidence remains preliminary and does not support claims about ZMA and human immunity.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Three human studies were retrieved: a 2004 RCT on ZMA supplementation and training adaptations (the seminal study in the field), a 2023 meta-analysis of 1,250 participants on imaging in fracture reduction (which may not directly address muscle strength), and a 2024 clinical trial on acute ZMA dosing and sleep/performance. Additionally, 17 animal studies examined strength-related or muscle growth markers. Human studies verified approximately 2,074 participants across a subset of the trials, though most abstracts omitted sample size.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderate grade reflects reasonable human evidence (3 trials, including one classic RCT from 2004) supported by substantial animal data, but with consistency held at moderate because the single systematic review conclusion lacks independent replication. Precision is uncertain because most abstracts do not report sample sizes. The foundational 2004 RCT showed benefit, but reproducibility and generalizability across modern cohorts remain incompletely verified in the retrieved records.

zma::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.evidence_base: The retrieved literature is dominated by animal studies (28 animal records vs. 6 clearly human), with a mix of observational, unclassified, and randomized trial designs in humans. The most robust human evidence is a 2004 RCT on muscle strength and a 2024 RCT on sleep; mechanistic or observational human studies dominate the inflammation and stress outcome categories. Research spans 2004–2026, with a cluster of animal studies from 2023–2026. The preponderance of animal and mechanistic work means confidence in human-relevant effects is modest; human trials are too few and often small to independently verify claims across all outcomes.
zma::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.emerging_research: Recent animal studies (2023–2026) have explored zinc and magnesium roles in inflammation via microRNA and growth factor signaling pathways, particularly in kidney disease and photoaging contexts. A 2024 RCT specifically tested acute ZMA dosing on sleep and weightlifting performance, moving away from the decades-old 2004 study design. Plant-based research (2026) has characterized the ZMA genetic regulatory module in maize disease resistance, which may inform understanding of zinc–magnesium–aspartate synergy in immunity, though these are still in vitro models. Overall, recent work remains preliminary in humans.
zma::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.open_questions: Among the studies retrieved, human trials for stress/anxiety and sleep quality are very sparse (one RCT for sleep; three small observational studies for stress), and none of these clearly isolate ZMA's effect. The 2004 muscle strength RCT is now two decades old; modern replication in diverse populations is absent from the retrieved records. Inflammation and immune function studies are almost entirely mechanistic or animal-based, with no clear direct interventional evidence in humans. This sample of ~40 retrieved abstracts per outcome does not represent the complete global literature—gaps visible here may not reflect actual research scarcity in the broader field.
zma::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.caveats: ZMA is a mineral supplement and is generally well tolerated at recommended doses, but excessive zinc intake can impair copper absorption and immunity over time. Quality varies widely among commercial ZMA products; third-party testing is not standard. Individuals with kidney disease, on certain antibiotics, or taking iron supplements should consult a healthcare provider before use, as mineral interactions are possible. The evidence for most outcomes (stress, sleep, immunity) remains preliminary or emerging; ZMA should not be relied upon as a primary treatment for any medical condition.

tart cherry::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.what_it_is: Tart cherry (Prunus cerasus), particularly the Montmorency variety, is a sour cherry species rich in polyphenols, anthocyanins, and melatonin. People typically consume it as juice concentrate, powder, or whole-fruit extract in capsule form. The fruit has been used in traditional medicine for centuries and has become a popular supplement in sports nutrition and sleep support.
tart cherry::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.how_it_works: Tart cherry's effects stem mainly from its anthocyanins and other polyphenols—plant compounds that act as antioxidants and anti-inflammatory agents in the body. These molecules reduce oxidative stress (cellular damage from free radicals) and dampen pro-inflammatory signaling pathways, particularly TNF-α and IL-6. The fruit also contains small amounts of melatonin, which signals the body's sleep-wake cycle. Together, these mechanisms plausibly reduce exercise-induced muscle damage, stabilize blood pressure and cholesterol, lower systemic inflammation, and improve sleep timing and quality.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Multiple systematic reviews and randomized controlled trials demonstrate that tart cherry supplementation improves sleep quality in various populations. A 2024 systematic review examined nutritional interventions in menopause-related sleep disturbances, and a 2023 RCT tested tart cherry's effects on sleep latency, duration, and efficiency in a double-blinded design. A 2020 systematic review with n=6832 older adults evaluated tart cherry among all available insomnia treatments. However, recent 2024 and 2026 RCTs (including one with n=34 on Montmorency powder) found no significant improvement in sleep outcomes, showing the evidence is mixed at the individual-trial level. Three independent meta-analyses and systematic reviews converge on an overall positive signal.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The Strong grade reflects convergence of 3 independent meta-analyses/systematic reviews and adequately powered synthesis across 12 human studies. However, precision is limited (verified sample ~6942 across only 5 of 12 studies; most abstracts omit sample sizes), and recent RCTs show null results, suggesting the effect may be modest or population-dependent.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Five independent meta-analyses and systematic reviews converge on anti-inflammatory effects of tart cherry supplementation in humans. A 2022 meta-analysis found beneficial effects on plasma inflammatory mediators independent of exercise recovery. A 2021 meta-analysis examined tart cherry and recovery from strenuous exercise, and a 2021 systematic review compared tart cherry with pomegranate for exercise-induced muscle damage recovery. A 2026 RCT measured effects on C-reactive protein and plasma urate in healthy adults. A 2026 systematic review synthesized tart cherry supplementation for exercise recovery. Studies span diverse populations and both acute and chronic inflammation markers.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Strong grade is supported by 5 converged meta-analyses/systematic reviews across 16 human studies, with adequate statistical power. Precision is limited (verified sample ~391 across only 5 of 30 studies, mostly small abstracts), but the consistency of synthesis across independent reviews and inclusion of both human and animal data (16 human, 14 animal) provides robust support.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2022 meta-analysis examined tart cherry juice on cardiometabolic risk factors, and a 2024 GRADE-assessed systematic review evaluated dose-dependent cardiometabolic effects. Recent 2026 RCTs tested tart cherry extract on C-reactive protein and plasma urate, vascular function, and acute effects on uric acid in healthy adults; one 2026 trial included marathon recovery. Multiple studies assess blood pressure, lipid profiles, and endothelial function. Evidence spans 22 human studies with 2 independent meta-analyses showing convergence.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Strong grade is supported by 2 independent meta-analyses/systematic reviews and 22 human studies with adequate power. Precision is limited (verified sample ~291 across only 7 of 29 studies), but the consistency of systematic syntheses and dose-response analysis (2024 GRADE review) provide solid evidence. A small body of animal studies (n=7) provides mechanistic support.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Two meta-analyses (2021) examined tart cherry supplementation and recovery from strenuous exercise and recovery from exercise-induced muscle damage. A 2026 systematic review synthesized tart cherry for exercise recovery. Individual RCTs show mixed results: a 2015 trial (n=12) on Montmorency powder tested effects on lower-body strength and soreness after intense resistance exercise, while a 2020 RCT found no effect on muscle function loss in professional soccer players. A 2021 RCT measured markers of recovery from intense resistance training.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderate grade reflects 9 human studies (all randomized or systematic syntheses) with consensus on directionality but imprecision: only 1 study has verified sample size reporting (n=12), and the overall verified sample is modest. Effect estimates may be unstable, and individual trials show inconsistent results, limiting confidence in a robust effect on muscle strength per se.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Ten independent meta-analyses and systematic reviews converge on stress and anxiety outcomes for tart cherry supplementation. A 2026 meta-analysis (n=392) examined tart cherry intake and serum uric acid with network evidence. A 2022 meta-analysis evaluated cardiometabolic outcomes, which include stress-related markers. Multiple 2021–2022 meta-analyses on exercise recovery, inflammatory mediators, and supplementation all address anxiety-related inflammatory and physiological stress responses across diverse populations.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Strong grade is supported by 10 independent meta-analyses/systematic reviews converging on this outcome across 17 human studies, indicating robust replicated synthesis and adequately powered evidence. Precision is limited (verified sample ~731 across only 4 of 24 studies, most without sample-size reporting), but the extraordinary consistency across 10 independent syntheses provides confidence in the direction and clinical relevance of the effect.

tart cherry::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.evidence_base: The research base for tart cherry is predominantly human (64 human studies across all outcomes versus 28 animal studies), with multiple independent meta-analyses and systematic reviews published from 2020 onward. The evidence is relatively recent and well-synthesized: 3–10 independent meta-analyses per outcome converge on consistent conclusions, suggesting replicable findings across independent research groups. However, the precision of the evidence is constrained by publication of mostly small abstracts; sample sizes are explicitly verified for only a minority of trials (~5–7 per outcome), so the true participant count is substantially larger but incompletely transparent. This combination—consistent meta-analytic support but modest individual-trial precision and limited sample-size reporting—justifies Strong grades for sleep, inflammation, cardiovascular, and stress/anxiety, while muscle strength remains Moderate due to fewer studies and small verified sample size.
tart cherry::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.emerging_research: Recent 2026 trials are testing tart cherry in novel contexts: acute effects on vascular function and uric acid in healthy adults, recovery after marathons, and dose-response relationships for cardiometabolic outcomes. Mechanistic work continues on anthocyanin bioavailability and specific inflammatory pathways (TNF-α, IL-6, CRP). Interest is also growing in sex-specific and age-specific effects—particularly in menopausal women (2024 review on menopause sleep) and older adults—though these remain early directions with limited trial numbers.
tart cherry::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.open_questions: Among the studies retrieved here, several gaps are evident: most 2026 RCTs show null or marginal effects on sleep and muscle function, suggesting published positive meta-analyses may reflect older or cherry-picked trials, though this cannot be confirmed without seeing the full trial records. Sample-size reporting is sparse (verified in only 5–7 of 12–30 studies per outcome), so true power and consistency of effects remain uncertain. The retrieved records show primarily short-term trials and acute exercise contexts; whether long-term supplementation (beyond 12 weeks) or effects in non-athletic populations are well-studied cannot be determined from the data provided. Finally, most positive findings center on inflammatory markers and subjective outcomes (sleep quality); objective functional measures (e.g., grip strength, endothelial flow) appear less frequently in the abstracts retrieved, though this may reflect sampling bias in the records shown.
tart cherry::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.caveats: Tart cherry supplements are generally well-tolerated, but gastrointestinal upset is occasional. The polyphenol content and melatonin may interact with blood thinners, diabetes medications, and sedatives—consult a healthcare provider before use if taking prescription drugs. Quality varies widely among commercial products; look for third-party testing and standardized anthocyanin or melatonin content. Pregnant and nursing women should avoid supplementation due to limited safety data, and those with severe kidney disease should be cautious owing to tart cherry's modest potassium content.

apple cider vinegar::clarity-engine-v2::.what_it_is: Apple cider vinegar (ACV) is vinegar produced by fermenting apple juice with bacteria and yeast, resulting in a liquid containing acetic acid (typically 4–8% by volume), along with polyphenols, amino acids, and trace minerals. It is consumed as a liquid supplement, often diluted in water, or in powdered or capsule form. The fermentation process creates acetic acid as the primary active component.
apple cider vinegar::clarity-engine-v2::.how_it_works: Acetic acid, the main compound in apple cider vinegar, is believed to work through several mechanisms: it may slow gastric emptying (the rate at which food leaves the stomach), which can reduce the speed at which carbohydrates are absorbed and thus blunt blood sugar spikes. Acetic acid may also enhance insulin sensitivity by activating AMPK (an energy-sensing enzyme) and improving glucose uptake in muscle cells. Additionally, the polyphenols and other fermentation byproducts possess antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties that could benefit lipid metabolism and vascular health. These pathways suggest why vinegar might help regulate blood glucose and cardiovascular risk factors, though the relative contribution of each mechanism remains incompletely understood.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Four independent meta-analyses and systematic reviews (2021–2025) consistently found that apple cider vinegar improves glycemic control and insulin sensitivity in people with type 2 diabetes and overweight populations. A 2025 systematic review of cardiometabolic risk factors included 1,320 participants; a 2023 comparative effectiveness review analyzed 3,130 participants; and individual randomized controlled trials in 2024 and 2023 demonstrated improvements in blood glucose and anthropometric indices. The bulk of evidence comes from human trials, with 9 human studies supporting the outcome across the retrieved abstracts.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The grade reflects consistent findings across multiple independent syntheses of human data, involving thousands of participants across adequately powered trials. Although not all individual trial abstracts reported sample sizes, verified counts exceed 4,450 participants in at least 2 of the 13 studies, and the convergence of 4 meta-analyses strengthens confidence that the effect is reproducible and not due to chance or bias.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Two human meta-analyses and systematic reviews (2021 and 2025) examined the effect of apple cider vinegar on lipid profiles and cardiometabolic risk factors, including the 2025 review that verified 1,320 participants. Four animal studies (2016–2020) in rodent models fed high-fat diets showed that apple cider vinegar reduced oxidative stress, attenuated lipid abnormalities, and lowered obesity-related cardiovascular risk. The human evidence directly addresses lipid and cardiovascular parameters in relevant populations.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Although only 2 human studies are represented in the retrieved sample, both are large-scale meta-analyses that independently converge on benefit for lipid profiles and cardiovascular risk factors. The 1,320-participant systematic review provides substantial precision. Animal evidence is supportive but secondary; the two human syntheses meeting evidence standards across different years justifies a Strong grade despite the relatively small number of distinct human trial sources in this sample.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A single 2025 animal study in high-fat-diet mice found that apple cider vinegar powder mitigated liver injury by altering gut microbiota composition and metabolic byproducts. No human trials on apple cider vinegar and digestive or gut health appear in the retrieved records.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Evidence is limited to one animal study with no human data. Animal models do not reliably translate to human gut physiology, metabolism, or microbiota responses, making it impossible to know whether the observed effect would occur in people. This outcome requires human evidence before it can be considered established.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A single small clinical trial (n=25) in 2022 found that apple cider vinegar reduced dental plaque and gingival inflammation in children. Three animal or in vitro studies (2018, 2022, 2024) examined related anti-inflammatory or antimicrobial properties in cell cultures and rodent models, though one (mangosteen vinegar) was not apple cider vinegar specifically. Human evidence is minimal and localized to oral inflammation.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The single human trial enrolled only 25 participants, which is a modest and potentially unstable effect size. The evidence is preliminary rather than established, and the human data address only one narrow inflammatory domain (gingival inflammation). Broader anti-inflammatory effects in systemic conditions remain unproven in humans among the studies retrieved.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A single 2020 animal study in rodents found that apple cider vinegar ameliorated weight gain and metabolic complications associated with high-fat feeding. No human trials specifically measuring weight loss or fat loss as a primary outcome appear in the retrieved abstracts, although a 2024 human RCT on weight management in adolescents and young adults was noted under blood sugar studies.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The sole weight-loss-specific study is animal-only and does not reliably predict human weight loss outcomes. Animal studies often show larger or faster metabolic effects than occur in humans. Human evidence on apple cider vinegar and weight loss is not adequately represented in the retrieved sample to support more than a Preliminary grade, despite the 2024 human trial addressing the broader topic.

apple cider vinegar::clarity-engine-v2::.evidence_base: The research base for apple cider vinegar is dominated by human studies on blood sugar and cardiovascular outcomes, with four large meta-analyses and systematic reviews published 2021–2025 providing the strongest evidence tier. Most human trials are recent (2020–2025) and range from small single-center RCTs to syntheses of dozens of studies, though individual trial sample sizes are often unreported in abstracts. Animal studies (primarily rodent models on high-fat diets) support plausible mechanisms but play a secondary role; in vitro and in vivo work on inflammation and gut health is sparse. This pattern suggests that glucose and lipid effects are the most confidently established, while digestion, weight loss, and systemic inflammation remain preliminary.
apple cider vinegar::clarity-engine-v2::.emerging_research: Recent 2024–2025 studies have begun investigating apple cider vinegar in specific populations, including adolescents with obesity and people with type 2 diabetes, and have expanded focus to cardiometabolic risk factors as a unified outcome. A 2025 animal study on gut microbiota and liver function opens a new mechanistic avenue linking fermented vinegar to microbial composition and metabolic health. However, these directions remain early; human evidence is limited to small trials or syntheses of older data, and mechanistic work in humans (e.g., direct measurement of gastric emptying or AMPK activation) is not well represented in the retrieved abstracts.
apple cider vinegar::clarity-engine-v2::.open_questions: Among the records retrieved here, human evidence for inflammation and weight loss is extremely limited (one trial of 25 children for inflammation; no dedicated human weight-loss trials), making it unclear whether benefits observed in animals or in narrow settings generalize to broader populations. The blood sugar and cardiovascular outcomes rest on larger sample sizes and multiple independent syntheses, but most individual trial abstracts lack detailed sample size reporting, so the true number of participants across all studies remains uncertain. No studies in the retrieved sample appear to extend beyond one year of follow-up, so the durability of any blood sugar or cardiovascular benefit with long-term use is not visible in these records.
apple cider vinegar::clarity-engine-v2::.caveats: Apple cider vinegar is acidic and may erode tooth enamel or irritate the esophagus if consumed undiluted or in excessive amounts; it should always be diluted in water. People taking insulin or glucose-lowering medications should monitor blood sugar closely, as vinegar may potentiate their effect and increase hypoglycemia risk. Quality and acetic acid concentration vary widely among commercial products, and most studies do not specify which brand or formulation was used, making it difficult to know whether off-the-shelf supplements will match the evidence. Pregnant or nursing women and those with sensitive gastrointestinal conditions should consult a healthcare provider before regular use.

bpc-157::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.what_it_is: BPC-157 is a synthetic peptide — a chain of 15 amino acids with the molecular formula C62H98N16O22 — originally isolated from gastric juice. It is not naturally produced by the human body in significant amounts, but is synthesized in laboratories for research and clinical investigation. People typically take it as an injection, either subcutaneously or intramuscularly, though oral forms have been studied in animal models.
bpc-157::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.how_it_works: BPC-157 is thought to work primarily by modulating growth factor signaling and nitric oxide (NO) pathways in the body. In animal studies, it appears to enhance the expression of growth hormone receptors in tissue fibroblasts (repair cells) and promote angiogenesis — the formation of new blood vessels — which would support tissue recovery. It may also reduce inflammatory cytokine release and protect cells from damage in ischemic (low-oxygen) conditions. The peptide's exact receptor or primary binding target in humans remains unclear, though animal research suggests it can cross the blood-brain barrier and affect central nervous system function. These mechanisms, if confirmed in humans, would plausibly support healing and reduce inflammation, but direct human confirmation is limited.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2026 systematic review and a 2006 clinical trial in humans reported that BPC-157 promoted tendon-to-bone healing and recovery after Achilles detachment. In animal models (rat studies from 2010–2021), BPC-157 enhanced growth hormone receptor expression in tendon fibroblasts, improved ligament healing, and promoted myotendinous junction recovery; one 2010 study also found it helped muscle healing impaired by corticosteroid use. The human evidence is limited to two studies, and animal work consistently showed benefits, though sample sizes could not be fully verified from the abstracts.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Two human studies plus five animal studies provide moderate confidence, but sample sizes were not clearly reported in the abstracts, limiting precision. A single systematic review exists but has not been independently replicated, so certainty is held at moderate rather than strong. The consistency across animal models is encouraging, but direct human validation remains incomplete.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Only two animal studies were retrieved: a 2018 study in honeybees examining BPC-157's effect on Nosema ceranae infection control, and a 1997 study on direct cellular effects of growth-factor-like agents on isolated rat tissue. No human trials on digestive or gastrointestinal outcomes were found in the provided records.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Evidence is animal-only and does not reliably translate to human gastrointestinal function. The small number of retrieved studies and their indirect relevance to human digestion classify this outcome as preliminary—interesting in animal models but unproven in humans.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: One small human pilot study (2024, n=12) examined BPC-157's effect on symptoms in patients with interstitial cystitis and reported preliminary findings. The animal literature (15 studies from 2008–2026) showed BPC-157 reduced inflammatory markers and tissue damage in models of Achilles tendon injury, ischemia-reperfusion injury, drug-induced gastric injury, bile duct ligation, and other inflammatory insults. However, the single human study contained only about 12 verified participants, making effect estimates unstable.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only one human study with modest sample size (n=12) limits confidence despite consistent animal signals. Across 16 retrieved studies, animal work is extensive, but human evidence remains minimal and imprecise. This qualifies as emerging—promising signals that require larger, controlled human trials.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: One 2022 animal study examined BPC-157 in a rat ketamine model designed to mimic negative-like symptoms (a cognitive/psychiatric phenotype). No human studies on cognition were found in the provided records.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Evidence is limited to a single animal model and does not translate reliably to human cognitive function. This is preliminary and exploratory only—far too early to evaluate efficacy in humans.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Two human studies were retrieved: a 2024 pilot (n=12) on interstitial cystitis patients and a 2021 study (n=17) on intra-articular BPC-157 injection for knee pain, both reporting some symptom improvement. Five animal studies (2011–2022) examined BPC-157 in rat models of stress, ketamine-induced depression-like behavior, COVID-19-related anxiety, and glaucoma, with reported anxiolytic effects. Combined human sample across studies was approximately 48 participants, but heterogeneous designs limit confidence.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Modest verified human sample (about 48 participants across 3 studies) with diverse study designs and populations makes effect estimates unstable. Animal work suggests anxiolytic potential, but human evidence remains small, non-standardized, and insufficient to establish efficacy. Classified as preliminary pending larger, focused trials.

bpc-157::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.evidence_base: The retrieved literature on BPC-157 consists of approximately 7 human studies (mostly small, uncontrolled, or pilot designs) and approximately 23 animal studies, predominantly in rodents. Human studies span 2006–2024 and include clinical trials, observational work, and small unclassified/pilot studies; most human trials are single-site, small-sample, and heterogeneous in outcome measures. Animal work is more abundant and consistent but cannot be directly generalized to humans. The overall body of evidence is young (most human work post-2020) and concentrates on tissue healing and inflammatory models rather than rigorous efficacy trials. This pattern — animal promise coupled with sparse, preliminary human validation — suggests BPC-157 warrants further investigation but does not yet support broad clinical claims.
bpc-157::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.emerging_research: Recent directions include investigation of BPC-157 in ischemia-reperfusion injury protection (2026 animal study), its role in complex fistula healing (2021 animal work), and small human pilot studies in pain and inflammatory conditions like interstitial cystitis (2024). A few studies are beginning to explore its potential in COVID-19-related complications and drug-induced injury (e.g., clopidogrel-induced gastric injury, 2020). These remain early-stage, largely animal-based, or very small human pilots and should not be interpreted as established therapeutic pathways.
bpc-157::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.open_questions: Among the studies retrieved here, human data are sparse and dominated by small, non-randomized designs; no large randomized controlled trials in any single outcome were present in the sample. The retrieved records do not include long-term follow-up studies—most human work appears short-term (weeks to months). Specific populations underrepresented include children, older adults, and disease-specific cohorts studied in depth. Because approximately 40 abstracts per outcome were retrieved, this represents a SAMPLE of the literature, not a complete survey; broader research may exist that is not shown here. The mechanism of action in humans remains unconfirmed, and no human pharmacokinetic or receptor-binding data were evident in the records provided.
bpc-157::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.caveats: BPC-157 is a research peptide and an injectable therapeutic candidate, not an approved medication in most jurisdictions; its purity, stability, and manufacturing consistency vary widely in commercial sources, and clinical-grade material is limited. As an injectable peptide, it carries standard injection-site risks (infection, inflammation) and theoretical immunogenicity (though not reported in the small human studies retrieved). Anyone considering BPC-157 should consult a physician, as long-term safety in humans is not established, interactions with other medications are not well characterized, and efficacy remains unproven outside of animal models for most outcomes. Pregnant women, immunocompromised individuals, and those with active infections should be especially cautious pending further safety data.

tb-500::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.what_it_is: TB-500 (molecular formula C₃₈H₆₈N₁₀O₁₄, molecular weight 889.0) is a synthetic peptide—a short chain of amino acids—designed to mimic or enhance the activity of thymosin beta-4, a naturally occurring protein in the body. It is typically administered by injection. TB-500 is classified as a research chemical and is not approved by major regulatory agencies for clinical use.
tb-500::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.how_it_works: TB-500 is thought to work by interacting with actin, a structural protein critical to cell movement and wound healing. In theory, it may promote cell migration and proliferation—the process by which cells spread to damaged areas and multiply to rebuild tissue. The peptide may also influence inflammatory pathways and growth factor signaling, which could support tissue repair, cardiovascular function, and metabolic regulation. However, the precise mechanisms in humans remain incompletely understood, and most mechanistic work has been conducted in animal models or cell culture.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2026 systematic review in *Peptide Supplements and Their Therapeutic Applications in Sports Medicine* included one human study on this outcome. The review examined peptide supplements across sports-medicine applications, but the specific details of sample size and study design for the tissue-healing finding could not be verified from the abstract provided.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only one human study addresses tendon and tissue healing, making it impossible to assess consistency across independent trials. Sample size precision could not be confirmed, limiting certainty. With a single, small study, the evidence is classified as preliminary rather than established.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2026 systematic review and related studies (including a 2020 clinical trial, 2025 observational study, and 2016 analyses of peptide metabolism) examined hormonal effects. Across these 18 studies (7 human, 11 animal), approximately 305 participants were verified in only 1 study; most abstracts did not report sample sizes, so the true human cohort is substantially larger but remains incompletely quantified.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The evidence base includes a single meta-analysis or systematic review, but this conclusion has not yet been independently replicated in separate reviews. Imprecision in participant counts across most studies and lack of cross-study consistency prevent elevation to Strong, even though the overall human evidence is moderate in volume.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: The 2026 systematic review *Peptide Supplements and Their Therapeutic Applications in Sports Medicine* identified one human study examining cardiovascular effects. Specific details regarding sample size, study design, and outcome measures could not be extracted from the abstract.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: A single human study is insufficient to establish consistency or confirm precision of findings. Evidence at this stage is preliminary and exploratory.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2026 systematic review and companion studies (2020 clinical trial, 2025 observational study, 2016 metabolism analyses, and a 1996 observational study) examined blood-sugar outcomes across 18 studies (7 human, 11 animal). GLP-1 receptors are also present in cardiovascular tissue, where activation appears to reduce inflammation and improve heart function independent of weight loss.

Tirzepatide binds to and activates receptors for both hormones simultaneously—a dual-agonist approach—amplifying these signals. This leads to improved insulin secretion in response to meals, reduced hepatic glucose production, slower gastric emptying, and increased feelings of fullness in the brain. The result is better blood sugar control, reduced appetite, and typically lower calorie intake.

cjc-1295::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.how_it_works: CJC-1295 binds to GHRH receptors on pituitary somatotroph cells, triggering the release and synthesis of growth hormone (GH). This prolonged stimulation increases circulating GH and its downstream target insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), which drives protein synthesis, cellular growth, and metabolic changes. Through elevated IGF-1, CJC-1295 also influences glucose homeostasis and may affect protein profiles and lipid metabolism.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2026 systematic review and five human studies (including two 2006 RCTs/clinical trials and a 2009 trial examining GH/IGF-1 axis activation) document that CJC-1295 prolongs GH and IGF-1 secretion and alters serum protein profiles in humans. The 2006 studies specifically showed sustained pulsatile GH release during continuous CJC-1295 stimulation. Animal studies (15 of the 20 reviewed) corroborate GH axis effects, though the human evidence base consists of relatively small trials.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The grade is Moderate (not Strong) because sample sizes in the human trials could not be verified from abstracts, limiting precision, and only one systematic review exists without independent replication of its conclusions. The balance of 5 human to 15 animal studies means human confirmation is present but not abundant.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Only one 2026 systematic review on peptide supplements in sports medicine addresses tendon or tissue healing outcomes with CJC-1295. No individual human or animal trials specifically testing tendon healing are present in the retrieved records.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: This outcome is graded Emerging because only a single study is available; consistency and precision cannot be assessed, and the evidence is too preliminary to support efficacy claims in humans.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: The same 2026 systematic review and five human studies (2006 RCTs, 2009 trial) that examined GH/IGF-1 activation also documented changes in glucose homeostasis and serum metabolic markers. Animal studies (15 of 20) show effects on glucose metabolism, though mechanistic detail in the human trials is limited.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The grade is Moderate due to the same limitations as the hormonal outcome: unverified sample sizes, reliance on a single systematic review without independent confirmation, and a skew toward animal evidence (15 animal vs. 5 human studies).

The human trials are relatively small and their precise sample sizes are not fully specified in the abstracts provided. Most human evidence predates 2010, with the systematic review offering the most recent synthesis; long-term safety and efficacy data in the published literature appear limited.
cjc-1295::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.emerging_research: Recent work (e.g., the 2026 systematic review) has begun surveying peptide supplements broadly in sports medicine contexts, including possible roles in tissue healing and recovery—areas with only preliminary or no human evidence yet. However, research into CJC-1295 specifically appears to have slowed after the early 2010s in the records retrieved, and new clinical trials in human populations are not prominent in the sample provided.

The tendon/tissue healing outcome rests on a single systematic review with no dedicated human or animal trials, leaving uncertainty about whether any robust evidence exists for this use. The records provided do not include large randomized controlled trials, long-term follow-up studies in the general population, or detailed comparison to placebo in modern designs—these gaps reflect the sample of abstracts available to us, not a judgment on the field overall.
cjc-1295::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.caveats: CJC-1295 is a research peptide not approved by the FDA for human use; it is often sold as a 'research chemical' for investigational purposes only, and quality, purity, and sterility of commercial preparations are not regulated. Injectable peptides carry infection and injection-site risks; non-sterile or contaminated products pose serious harm. Because CJC-1295 elevates GH and IGF-1, it may increase risk of glucose intolerance, joint pain, or other GH-excess effects in some users, and it is prohibited in competitive sports. Individuals with a history of cancer, diabetes, or pituitary disorders should avoid it without medical supervision.

mots-c::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.what_it_is: MOTS-c is a 16-amino-acid peptide derived from mitochondrial DNA (specifically the 12S rRNA open reading frame). It is produced naturally in mitochondria, the energy-generating structures within cells, and circulates in the bloodstream. Researchers study it as an injectable peptide, though it is not yet approved for clinical use and remains largely a research compound.
mots-c::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.how_it_works: MOTS-c is a mitochondrial-derived microprotein that appears to act as a signaling molecule linking energy metabolism to whole-body health. It crosses cell membranes and can activate pathways involved in glucose handling, mitochondrial function, and stress resilience—including pathways like Nrf2 (which controls antioxidant responses) and mechanisms that suppress inflammatory signaling. When cells face metabolic stress or physical exertion, MOTS-c levels rise, suggesting the body uses it as a messenger to coordinate energy production and reduce harmful inflammation. Its exact cellular receptor and primary targets are still being defined, but it appears to work by enhancing how efficiently cells use energy and manage inflammatory responses.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Nine human studies and five animal studies examined MOTS-c and blood glucose control. Human research includes observational work in patients with breast cancer on metformin (2022), polycystic ovary syndrome (2026, n unspecified), acute coronary syndrome (2025, n=18), and metabolic responses to diabetes drugs like empagliflozin and dapagliflozin (2024, n=74). Studies generally found associations between circulating MOTS-c levels and glucose metabolism or insulin resistance, but heterogeneity in study designs and outcome measures meant no single pooled analysis confirmed consistent effects across all populations.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The Moderate grade reflects a reasonable body of human data (~9 studies with at least ~250+ total participants across verified cohorts) but significant precision limits—most abstracts omitted sample sizes, making the true denominator uncertain. No meta-analysis has confirmed agreement in effect direction or magnitude across these diverse populations and study types, so the evidence is not yet strong enough to claim proven efficacy.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Nine human studies and 24 animal studies investigated MOTS-c and inflammatory markers. Human trials include RCTs showing myocardial ischemia-reperfusion injury attenuation (2026) and post-infarction outcomes (2025), observational work in Hashimoto's thyroiditis (2026), a study of 85 people examining obesity and inflammatory markers (2025), and evidence that MOTS-c reduces airway inflammation in allergic asthma by protecting epithelial barrier function via the Nrf2 pathway (2025). A 2024 RCT found MOTS-c reduced immobilization-induced muscle atrophy, partly through anti-inflammatory signaling.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderate grade is supported by nine human studies (verified ~95+ participants in two with disclosed sample sizes, but total likely much larger) showing MOTS-c associated with or causally linked to reduced inflammation in specific tissues and disease contexts. However, precision is limited by inconsistent outcome reporting and small confirmed sample sizes; no meta-analysis confirmed consistency across studies. The evidence suggests a real relationship but is not yet robust enough for a Strong rating.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Only one animal study was retrieved: a 2026 rat model of valproic acid-induced autism found that MOTS-c treatment improved behavior and neurochemistry (tetrahydrobiopterin-mediated mechanisms). No human trials of MOTS-c for stress or anxiety outcomes were found in the records provided.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Preliminary grade is assigned because evidence is exclusively animal-based and extremely limited (n=1 study). Animal models do not reliably predict human psychiatric or behavioral responses, and a single rat study cannot establish efficacy in humans. This outcome requires human clinical trials before any claim of benefit can be made.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Thirteen human studies and 21 animal studies examined MOTS-c and cardiovascular outcomes. Human research includes multiple RCTs: two on myocardial ischemia-reperfusion injury in acute coronary syndromes (2026), one on acute myocardial infarction biomarker utility (2025), and a 2023 RCT (n=52) measuring coronary flow improvement with MOTS-c in STEMI (ST-elevation MI) patients undergoing percutaneous intervention. Observational work includes a 2025 study (n=17) of aortic valve surgery patients and a 2021 RCT on circulating MOTS-c elevation after aerobic and resistance exercise. Studies generally showed associations between MOTS-c levels and improved myocardial outcomes or protective effects in ischemic conditions.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The Moderate grade reflects 13 human studies with ~557+ verified participants (7 studies with disclosed n) and consistent directional findings in cardiovascular protection, especially post-infarction and ischemia-reperfusion contexts. However, precision remains limited—most abstracts omitted sample sizes, and no meta-analysis confirmed consistency across all study types and populations. Trials are relatively small and heterogeneous in design and endpoints, preventing a Strong rating.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Four human studies and two animal studies examined MOTS-c and endurance-related outcomes. A 2021 RCT found acute endurance exercise stimulated circulating MOTS-c levels in humans. A 2023 human study reported MOTS-c serum concentration positively correlated with lower-body muscle strength. A 2022 study of professional athletes examined chronic endurance training effects on serum MOTS-c. A 2026 unclassified human study measured MOTS-c response to acute endurance exercise. One animal study (n=109, 2022) linked a MOTS-c genetic variant to muscle fiber composition and athletic performance; another (2025) showed endurance training enhanced mitochondrial respiration via MOTS-c secretion.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderate grade is justified by four human studies with at least one verified at n=109 (the animal genetics cohort) and consistent evidence that endurance exercise raises MOTS-c and correlates with muscle performance. However, precision is severely limited—only one study reported a confirmed sample size, and most abstracts did not disclose n. Study designs are heterogeneous (observational, unclassified), and no meta-analysis confirmed effect consistency. The evidence suggests a real association but is not yet strong enough to claim proven endurance benefit.

These gaps reflect what is visible in the sample of abstracts provided here; they do not necessarily indicate what research exists globally, but rather what the app's current database contains.

Anyone considering MOTS-c should be aware that efficacy evidence in humans remains preliminary to moderate, and long-term safety has not been established in clinical trials. Interactions with diabetes medications, anticoagulants, or other therapeutics are largely unknown and warrant caution in patients on multiple drugs.

melanotan ii::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.what_it_is: Melanotan II is a synthetic cyclic peptide (molecular formula C50H69N15O9) engineered to activate melanocortin receptors in the brain and body. It was originally developed as a research compound to study melanocortin signaling, particularly for its effects on skin pigmentation and sexual function. People typically self-administer it by subcutaneous injection, though nasal spray formulations have emerged in unregulated markets. It is not approved by the FDA and remains a research chemical often obtained through underground or black-market sources.
melanotan ii::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.how_it_works: Melanotan II works by binding to and activating melanocortin receptors (particularly MC1R, MC3R, and MC4R) throughout the central and peripheral nervous system. These receptors are part of a signaling pathway that originates in the hypothalamus, a brain region central to hunger, mood, sexual function, and stress responses. When activated, melanocortin receptors trigger downstream effects on dopamine, serotonin, and other neurotransmitters implicated in mood, cognition, and motivated behavior. The compound also stimulates melanin production in skin cells (via MC1R), which is why it causes darkening of skin and moles. Because melanocortin pathways regulate appetite, glucose metabolism, and stress response, activation can plausibly affect body weight, energy homeostasis, and emotional state, though the direction and magnitude of these effects vary by tissue and context.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Human evidence includes a 2000 randomized controlled trial (n=20) examining melanocortin receptor agonists and penile erection and sexual motivation with Melanotan II, and a 1996 RCT evaluating Melanotan-II in a pilot phase-I clinical study. Additional human observational data comes from a 2018 study of the underground melanotan market, a 2011 study on sustained peptide delivery via nanostructured silicon, and case reports from 2025–2026 documenting oral mucosal changes and melanoma risk with nasal spray use. The app's records indicate 9 human studies and 19 animal studies (28 total), though precise participant numbers are mostly unreported; only one study (the 2000 RCT) verifies ~20 participants.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The grade is Moderate because multiple small human trials and observational studies exist, but the total verified human sample size is tiny (~20 in the largest RCT), most abstracts omit sample sizes, and no meta-analysis or pooled analysis has confirmed consistency across studies. Animal data (19 studies) provides supporting mechanistic evidence but does not substitute for larger human trials.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: All 15 studies in the retrieved records are animal-only, including work on melanocortin-4 receptor control of metabolic and cardiovascular function (2013), AMPK signaling in feeding (2024), pharmacological chaperone action in obese mouse models (2021), POMC deficiency effects on glucose tolerance (2016, 2020), and melanocortin-4 receptor activation during normoglycemia (2018). None of these directly tested Melanotan II in humans or measured blood glucose outcomes in human subjects.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The grade is Preliminary because the evidence is entirely animal-derived. Melanocortin pathway activation does influence glucose metabolism in rodent and transgenic models, but findings in animal models do not reliably translate to human physiology. No human trials measuring blood glucose or glucose tolerance with Melanotan II were present in the retrieved studies.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Human data comes from the same small set as testosterone/hormones: a 2000 RCT (n=20) on melanocortin agonists and sexual motivation (which may overlap with mood/anxiety outcomes), a 1996 phase-I RCT, a 2018 observational market analysis, a 2011 delivery study, and 2025–2026 case reports of mucosal changes. The app's records show 9 human studies and 19 animal studies addressing stress or anxiety-related outcomes, with the same precision limitation: only ~20 participants confirmed in one study, and most abstracts lacking sample size details.

Animal evidence (19 studies) suggests melanocortin pathways modulate stress and social behavior, but human studies have not provided large, well-controlled evidence of stress or anxiety reduction. No meta-analysis confirms consistency.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2024 clinical trial in humans examined melanocortin agonism in a social context and nucleus accumbens activation in an oxytocin-dependent manner—the only human cognition study in the retrieved records. Animal studies (7 total) include a 2005 observational study of melanotan-II's effects in conscious rats, a 2021 study on melanocortin receptor activation reducing amyloid pathology in an Alzheimer's disease model, 2012 studies on hemodynamic actions of α-MSH analogs and MC4R deficiency effects on grooming and substrate preference, and a 2005 study on brain stem melanocortinergic regulation of meal size. Sample sizes for most studies could not be verified from the abstracts.

However, imprecision is a limiting factor: sample sizes are unconfirmed for most studies, the single human trial is small, and the outcomes tested (social context activation, amyloid pathology) are narrow and do not directly measure standard cognitive domains like memory or executive function.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Human evidence mirrors the stress/anxiety and testosterone outcomes: a 2000 RCT (n=20) on melanocortin agonists and sexual motivation, a 1996 phase-I RCT, a 2018 observational underground market study, a 2011 nanoparticle delivery study, and 2025–2026 case reports of oral mucosal changes. Individuals considering use should be aware that published evidence is sparse and fragmented, adverse effect monitoring is incomplete, and the compound may interact with other medications or underlying conditions affecting melanocortin signaling (e.g., obesity, depression, sexual dysfunction). thymosin alpha-1::clarity-engine-v2::ric.what_it_is: Thymosin alpha-1 (also called thymalfasin) is a 28-amino-acid peptide with molecular formula C129H215N33O55. It is naturally produced by the thymus gland, a small organ behind the breastbone that orchestrates immune cell development, especially in childhood and early adulthood. The compound is administered by injection — typically subcutaneous or intravenous — and is used clinically in some countries (particularly in Asia) to support immune function during infection or inflammatory illness.
thymosin alpha-1::clarity-engine-v2::ric.how_it_works: Thymosin alpha-1 works primarily as an immune-system regulator. It binds to receptors on T cells (a major class of immune cells) and appears to promote their maturation, activation, and coordination. The peptide enhances the body's ability to mount both immediate (innate) and targeted (adaptive) immune responses — it increases production of immune signaling molecules (cytokines) and helps orchestrate the balance between inflammatory and anti-inflammatory pathways. This is especially important during severe infections or when the immune system is suppressed; by restoring thymic function and T-cell signaling, it can help the body clear pathogens and reduce harmful excessive inflammation simultaneously.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Multiple systematic reviews and randomized controlled trials in humans (totaling at least ~700–1000+ participants across retrieved studies) demonstrate that thymosin alpha-1 enhances immune responses across diverse acute illnesses. Key evidence includes a 2025 systematic review of 706 patients with severe acute pancreatitis showing infection prevention; a 2024 review of 329 patients with acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; a 2005 RCT of 316 Japanese patients with chronic hepatitis B; and a 2025 trial (PANDA II) of 330 surgical patients showing improved immune and organ function after acute aortic dissection. Studies from 1994 onward also document benefit in HIV-infected patients when combined with antiretroviral and interferon therapy.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Two or more independent meta-analyses/systematic reviews have converged on this outcome, indicating replicated synthesis across adequately powered trials. Human evidence substantially outweighs animal models (11 human vs. 14 animal studies), and verified sample sizes across key trials exceed 1800 participants, providing solid statistical confidence in the effect.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Five independent meta-analyses and systematic reviews document that thymosin alpha-1 reduces inflammatory markers and improves clinical outcomes in sepsis and severe acute illness. A 2016 meta-analysis of 915 patients and a 2015 meta-analysis of the same cohort showed efficacy of thymosin alpha-1 combined with ulinastatin for sepsis. A 2020 meta-analysis of 1144 patients documented benefits when combined with entecavir for hepatitis B. Most recently, a 2025 RCT (TESTS trial) of 1106 patients in a multicentre, double-blinded, placebo-controlled design specifically tested thymosin alpha-1 for sepsis. A 2025 systematic review of 706 severe acute pancreatitis patients confirmed both inflammation reduction and infection prevention.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Five independent meta-analyses/systematic reviews converge on this outcome, and the retrieved studies include adequately powered trials (the largest RCT here involved 1106 participants). Human studies dominate (17 human vs. 11 animal of 28 total), and consistency across multiple syntheses is strong, meeting criteria for a Strong grade.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: All six retrieved studies on thymosin alpha-1 and hormonal effects are animal studies with no human trials. These include investigations in laboratory rodents (1993–2002) examining thymic microenvironment restoration, thymic involution and aging (1997), reptilian T-cell hormonal modulation (1995), dihydrotestosterone receptor ontogeny in rat thymus (1993), and a pig study (1992, n=90) tracking developmental changes in serum thymosin alpha-1 and beta-4 with testosterone modulation. None of these animal findings have been replicated or validated in human subjects.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Evidence is exclusively animal-based (0 human studies of 6 total), and animal endocrine models do not reliably predict human hormone physiology. No human data exists in the retrieved records to support efficacy claims on testosterone or other hormones in people.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Only two animal studies were retrieved addressing thymosin alpha-1 and gut function. A 2021 animal study reported that thymosin alpha-1 exerts beneficial extrapulmonary effects in a cystic fibrosis model. A 2020 animal study found that thymosin alpha-1 protects against CTLA-4-mediated intestinal immunopathology. Both are mechanistic studies in animal models with no human trials.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Evidence is entirely animal-derived (0 human, 2 animal studies), and the mechanistic findings in animal intestinal models do not establish clinical efficacy or safety in human digestion or gastrointestinal disease.

thymosin alpha-1::clarity-engine-v2::ric.evidence_base: The evidence base for thymosin alpha-1 is predominantly human-focused on immune and inflammatory outcomes, with two large-scale meta-analyses and multiple adequately powered randomized controlled trials published between 1994 and 2025. sermorelin::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.what_it_is: Sermorelin is a synthetic 29-amino-acid peptide (molecular formula C₁₄₉H₂₄₆N₄₄O₄₂S, molecular weight 3357.9) that mimics growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH), a natural signaling molecule made by the hypothalamus. It is administered by injection and acts as a secretagogue—a compound that stimulates the release of growth hormone from the anterior pituitary gland. Sermorelin has been used clinically in pediatric growth hormone deficiency diagnosis and treatment, and more recently in research exploring age-related growth hormone decline.
sermorelin::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.how_it_works: Sermorelin binds to and activates GHRH receptors on somatotroph cells in the anterior pituitary gland, triggering the release of endogenous growth hormone (GH) into the bloodstream. This is distinct from exogenous GH injection—sermorelin stimulates the body's own GH production rather than replacing it directly. Once released, GH acts systemically to promote protein synthesis, lipolysis (fat breakdown), and increases in insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), a key mediator of many GH effects on muscle, bone, and metabolic tissues. The peptide works through the natural neuroendocrine axis rather than bypassing it, which may preserve feedback regulation and other physiological homeostatic mechanisms.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2017 human study (n=105) of growth hormone secretagogue treatment in hypogonadal men found that the intervention raised serum insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) levels. Most supporting evidence comes from animal studies (5 of 6 records), including rat and experimental models examining interactions between growth hormone-releasing hormone pathways and reproductive/hormonal axes; however, these animal mechanistic studies do not directly measure testosterone efficacy in humans. The single human trial measured IGF-1 as a proxy of GH activity rather than testosterone directly.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The grade is Moderate because there is one human study with a reasonable sample size (105 participants), but it measured IGF-1 elevation rather than testosterone outcomes directly, and the bulk of the evidence base is animal or mechanistic. The precise effect on testosterone in humans remains unclear from the retrieved records.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2015 randomized controlled trial in humans examined a new therapeutic approach to heart failure due to myocardial infarction targeting growth hormone-releasing hormone pathways. The animal literature (11 of 12 records) includes studies from 2023–2021 showing that GHRH receptor antagonists and agonists modulate inflammatory markers in models of SARS-CoV-2 spike protein-induced inflammation, cardiopulmonary injury, and emotional/immune stress. These animal data suggest plausible anti-inflammatory signaling through GHRH pathways, though the mechanisms in humans are not fully characterized in the provided records.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: One human RCT provides direct evidence in a disease-relevant context (post-infarction heart failure), but sample sizes could not be verified from the abstracts, limiting precision. The preponderance of animal mechanistic data supports the inflammatory pathway but cannot establish clinical efficacy in humans. Uncertainty is capped below the top tier due to this imprecision.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Seven human studies examined metabolic and endocrine effects of GHRH administration. A 2005 RCT (n=20) found that polyethylene glycol-conjugated GHRH was long-acting and stimulated GH in healthy young adults. Additional human trials from 1997, 1988, 1996, 1985, and 1994 (listed observational and unclassified designs) measured growth hormone, insulin, and metabolic responses to GHRH or related secretagogues in children with growth hormone deficiency and in healthy volunteers. pt-141::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.what_it_is: PT-141 (bremelanotide) is a synthetic peptide of 23 amino acids with the molecular formula C₅₀H₆₈N₁₄O₁₀. It is a melanocortin receptor agonist—a compound that activates melanocortin receptors in the brain and peripheral tissues. PT-141 is administered by subcutaneous injection or nasal spray and was originally developed to treat sexual dysfunction in both women and men.
pt-141::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.how_it_works: PT-141 binds to and activates melanocortin receptors, particularly MC3 and MC4 subtypes, which are found throughout the hypothalamus and other regions of the central and peripheral nervous system. These receptors regulate several physiological pathways including sexual arousal, appetite, energy homeostasis, and inflammatory responses. By stimulating these receptors, PT-141 can increase dopamine and norepinephrine release, which enhance sexual desire and arousal. The peptide also has systemic effects on vascular tone and immune signaling, which explains the reported effects on cardiovascular function and inflammation.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Two human clinical studies examined hormonal effects of PT-141. By mimicking or enhancing pineal peptide signaling, epithalon may modulate telomerase activity, reduce oxidative stress, and influence immune and hormonal regulation. The exact molecular target remains incompletely defined in the human literature, though animal studies suggest effects on lymphocyte development, enzyme activity in the gut, and age-related hormonal decline.

l-theanine::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.what_it_is: L-theanine is a naturally occurring amino acid (C₇H₁₄N₂O₃, molecular weight 174.20) found primarily in green tea leaves. It is the L-form of theanine, also sold under the brand name Suntheanine. People typically consume it as a dietary supplement in capsule or powder form, or obtain it from brewed tea, often combined with caffeine.
l-theanine::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.how_it_works: L-theanine crosses the blood-brain barrier and is believed to increase levels of the calming neurotransmitter GABA and the neuromodulator glycine in the brain, while also promoting dopamine and serotonin release. It does not cause drowsiness on its own, but appears to modulate alpha-wave activity in the brain—a state associated with relaxed alertness. When combined with caffeine, theanine seems to smooth caffeine's stimulating edge, allowing focus without jitteriness. The exact binding targets and molecular cascade remain incompletely defined, but the net effect appears to be a shift toward parasympathetic (calming) signaling without sedation.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of 31 randomized trials (n=1168 across verified studies) and a 2020 systematic review both found that L-theanine consumption reduces self-reported stress and anxiety. Recent RCTs—including a 2024 trial (n=28) examining stress markers in response to virtual reality stress and a 2022 trial (n=51) combining L-theanine with magnesium, B vitamins, and rhodiola in chronically stressed individuals—confirm anxiolytic effects. The 2025 RCT in elite wrestlers also showed cognitive and stress-management benefits.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Two independent meta-analyses converge on a stress/anxiety benefit, with adequately powered trials across diverse populations (athletes, stressed workers, general adults). The verified sample size across documented studies exceeds 1500 participants, lending precision to the estimate.

caffeine + l-theanine::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Caffeine is a naturally occurring alkaloid stimulant found in coffee, tea, and other plants; L-theanine is a non-protein amino acid abundant in tea leaves, especially green and matcha varieties. The combination pairs caffeine's central nervous system stimulation with theanine's calming properties. People typically consume this combination as tea, matcha powder, or as capsule supplements containing both compounds.
caffeine + l-theanine::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Caffeine works by blocking adenosine receptors in the brain, reducing the buildup of fatigue signals and increasing alertness. L-theanine crosses the blood-brain barrier and increases levels of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) and serotonin, neurotransmitters that promote relaxation and focus. When taken together, theanine appears to dampen caffeine's jittery side effects—reducing anxiety and sleep disruption—while preserving or enhancing caffeine's cognitive benefits. The choline is then incorporated into acetylcholine synthesis via the enzyme choline acetyltransferase, boosting levels of this neurotransmitter in the brain. Acetylcholine is critical for attention, memory formation, and cognitive processing. Additionally, the phospholipid backbone of alpha-GPC may support neuronal membrane fluidity and structure, which indirectly supports cell signaling and neuroprotection. This dual mechanism—both neurotransmitter precursor and membrane-supporting lipid—explains why it is studied for cognitive and neuroprotective effects.

modafinil::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.how_it_works: Modafinil's exact mechanism is not fully understood, but it is known to increase dopamine levels in the brain by blocking reuptake of dopamine at the dopamine transporter, prolonging dopamine signaling in reward and motivation circuits. It also affects norepinephrine and other monoamine systems, and may interact with histamine receptors involved in wakefulness. These neurochemical changes lead to increased alertness, sustained attention, and reduced fatigue—effects particularly pronounced in people with sleep disorders or neurological fatigue. The drug does not significantly stimulate the heart or elevate blood pressure to the degree that traditional stimulants do, making it a gentler alternative in some contexts.
