It activates or stabilizes key regulatory pathways (particularly those involving mitochondrial quality control) that decline with age. By restoring mitochondrial turnover and function, it may reduce chronic oxidative stress and inflammation, enhance energy production in muscle and nerve cells, and support the barrier integrity of the gut. This mitochondrial renewal mechanism is why it shows particular promise for aging-related outcomes, where accumulated mitochondrial damage drives decline.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2026 systematic review and a 2024 systematic review both converge on improvements in endurance performance with urolithin A supplementation in humans. Individual trials include a 2025 RCT (n=42) showing gains in running performance, a 2025 RCT in academy soccer players reporting improved performance metrics, and a 2022 RCT (n=66) in older adults documenting enhanced muscle endurance and mitochondrial biomarkers. Across these studies, supplementation ranged from weeks to months and consistently showed measurable improvements in exercise capacity and recovery markers.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Two independent systematic reviews replicate the conclusion, indicating robust synthesis of evidence. Human studies dominate the evidence base (7 human vs. 1 animal study), and multiple RCTs show consistent directional benefit, meeting the threshold for Strong.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2026 systematic review and a 2024 systematic review both independently conclude that urolithin A improves muscle strength in humans. Supporting RCTs include a 2025 trial (n=42) showing gains in strength-related running metrics, a 2024 RCT documenting improved muscle strength alongside biomarkers of mitochondrial health, and a 2022 RCT reporting strengthening in older adults. The evidence spans younger and older populations, and improvements appear consistent across different supplementation protocols.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Two replicated systematic reviews provide strong synthetic evidence. Nine human studies vs. six animal studies indicate human data dominates. Consistency across multiple RCTs in different populations warrants the Strong grade.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Seven human RCTs and observational studies examine urolithin A's anti-inflammatory effects. A 2025 RCT (n=42) evaluated inflammatory biomarkers alongside running performance; a 2025 RCT assessed inflammation and oxidative stress in a muscle-health context; a 2022 RCT in older adults found improvements in inflammatory markers alongside mitochondrial biomarkers; and a 2025 observational study in sepsis patients showed that urolithin A attenuated muscle and mitochondrial dysfunction linked to dysregulated autophagy. A 2023 scoping review (n=293) also discussed age-related inflammation as a target outcome.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Seven human studies provide a reasonable foundation, but no pooled meta-analysis directly confirms consistency across them. Only ~81 participants are verified in two studies; most abstracts do not report sample sizes, leaving total true sample uncertain. Evidence shows promise but lacks the replication depth of Strong outcomes.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2023 systematic review (n=293) synthesizes urolithin A's role in gut health and age-related disease prevention. A 2026 RCT and a 2025 RCT both examined effects on microbial diversity and short-chain fatty acid production (butyrate) following synbiotic supplementation. A 2024 study investigated prebiotic saccharides and urolithin A bioavailability. Two observational studies from 2017 characterized urolithin-metotyping (inter-individual variation in how the microbiota produces urolithin A from precursors) and antiproliferative activity of urolithin A versus its precursor. Together, these suggest urolithin A influences microbial composition and metabolite production.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: One systematic review exists but has not been independently replicated in the retrieved records. Seven human studies provide moderate support, though only ~332 participants are verified across two studies; most abstracts omit sample sizes. Consistency is unconfirmed at the level of pooled analysis.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Two human studies appear in the retrieved records: a 2026 clinical trial protocol (PROMETHEUS) that includes cognition as an outcome in a multi-arm healthy-aging trial, and a 2021 unclassified human study examining mitophagy enhancers against phosphorylated tau-induced mitochondrial and synaptic toxicity in an Alzheimer's context. Thirty-two animal studies document neuroprotective effects, including improved cognitive performance in mice with chronic sleep deprivation (2026, n=15), reduced cognitive deficits in cadmium-induced pyroptosis models (2026), and protection against ischemic stroke and streptozotocin-induced Alzheimer's-like pathology (2026 studies). However, formal efficacy evidence in humans remains very limited.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only ~15 participants are verified in one human study, and no completed human RCT reporting cognition outcomes is present in the retrieved data. The evidence is largely animal-derived (32 of 34 studies), so the outcome is graded Moderate as a promising signal requiring human confirmation rather than established efficacy.

urolithin a::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.evidence_base: The research base is mixed: endurance and muscle strength rest on strong human evidence with replicated systematic reviews, while inflammation and gut health show moderate human support without independent replication of pooled analyses. Cognition remains heavily animal-derived (32 of 34 studies animal), with only 1–2 preliminary human reports. Most studies are recent (2022–2026), reflecting growing clinical interest in urolithin A and mitochondrial aging. The retrieved records show ~35 studies per outcome on average, but this is a sample of the full literature; true publication counts and total participants are likely larger. Human RCT data is more robust for musculoskeletal outcomes than for cognitive or digestive endpoints.
urolithin a::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.emerging_research: Several 2026 studies advance understanding in novel directions: the PROMETHEUS trial will assess urolithin A in a multi-intervention healthy-aging protocol, potentially clarifying real-world effects and long-term safety. Studies on synbiotics (urolithin A plus other prebiotics/probiotics) are beginning to clarify whether combination approaches enhance gut microbial recovery post-antibiotics. Research on urolithin A's neuroprotection against specific insults (ischemic stroke, Alzheimer's-like pathology, sleep deprivation) is accumulating in animal models, but human clinical translation remains early.
urolithin a::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.open_questions: Among the studies retrieved here, cognition evidence in humans is sparse (only 1–2 studies), so we cannot yet assess what trial durations, doses, or populations have been tested in humans for brain outcomes. For inflammation and gut health, no single systematic review has independently replicated the conclusions of another in the provided records, leaving uncertainty about consistency. Most retrieved RCTs do not report full participant numbers in their abstracts, so the true sample sizes contributing to each outcome remain unclear. The records provided are a sample (~40 per outcome), so absence of evidence for a particular population or endpoint in these records does not mean research does not exist elsewhere in the literature.
urolithin a::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.caveats: Urolithin A is a research compound; commercial supplements vary widely in purity, bioavailability, and dose. Most clinical trials have been short-term (weeks to a few months), so long-term safety and durability of effects remain incompletely characterized. Individuals with severe gut dysbiosis or conditions affecting polyphenol metabolism should consult a clinician, as urolithin A production depends on specific commensal bacteria. No major contraindications have been reported in the trial literature, but interactions with medications and suitability in pregnancy or immunocompromised states are not well-established.

sulforaphane::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.what_it_is: Sulforaphane (C₆H₁₁NOS₂) is an isothiocyanate — a sulfur-containing plant compound found naturally in cruciferous vegetables, especially broccoli, broccoli sprouts, and cabbage. It forms when the vegetable tissue is damaged (chopped, chewed, or cooked), triggering an enzymatic reaction that converts the inactive precursor glucoraphanin into active sulforaphane. People typically consume it via whole vegetables, sprouts, or standardized extracts in supplement form.
sulforaphane::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.how_it_works: Sulforaphane's primary mechanism is activation of the NRF2 (nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2) signaling pathway, a master regulator of cellular stress defense. Normally, NRF2 is bound and suppressed by a protein called KEAP1; sulforaphane binds to KEAP1, liberating NRF2 so it can enter the cell nucleus and switch on hundreds of genes involved in antioxidant production, detoxification (phase II enzymes), and inflammation control. This same pathway also influences mitochondrial function and reduces ferroptosis (a form of iron-dependent cell death). Because oxidative stress and unchecked inflammation underlie many chronic diseases — from cardiovascular disease to neurodegeneration — NRF2 activation is a plausible therapeutic target. Sulforaphane also modulates NF-κB signaling and NLRP3 inflammasome activity, both key drivers of inflammatory responses.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A growing body of human research, including RCTs from 2024, demonstrates that sulforaphane reduces inflammatory markers and improves conditions associated with systemic inflammation — examples include suppression of lipopolysaccharide-mediated inflammation in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease patients (2021), amelioration of blood-brain barrier injury via NRF2 activation in stroke (2024 RCT), and improvements in insulin resistance (2024 RCT). Animal studies consistently show similar effects, including reduction of NLRP3 inflammasome-driven inflammation and prevention of inflammation-related pathology in models of aortic aneurysm and acute pancreatitis.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Four human studies (including RCTs) provide direct evidence, but the true sample size across human trials is uncertain because most abstracts omit participant numbers; only ~358 participants were confirmed across 3 studies. No pooled meta-analysis of human trials confirms consistency across outcomes, so the evidence is classified as moderate pending further verification.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2022 systematic review of autism spectrum disorder treatments (n=7,450) examined sulforaphane among multiple intervention categories, indicating relevance to stress-related psychiatric conditions. Animal studies from 2018–2023 show that sulforaphane produces anxiolytic- and antidepressant-like effects in rodent models, reduces stress vulnerability, and ameliorates anxiety-associated behaviors via modulation of oxidative stress and neuroinflammatory pathways.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Human evidence rests primarily on a single systematic review that included sulforaphane as one intervention among many, rather than a dedicated RCT isolating its effect on anxiety or stress; independent replication of the review's conclusion is lacking. Animal models support plausibility, but rodent anxiety assays do not directly translate to human efficacy. Moderate grade reflects modest human evidence and absence of large independent replication.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Six human studies, including RCTs from 2012 and 2015, demonstrate that sulforaphane and broccoli sprout extracts are absorbed and metabolized in the human gut, with one RCT (2015) showing suppression of Helicobacter pylori infection and reduced lipid peroxidation. Studies from 2003–2021 characterize sulforaphane's bioavailability, phase II enzyme induction, and influence on the microbiome composition — establishing that gut bacteria drive conversion of inactive glucosinolates into bioactive metabolites and affect downstream sulforaphane production.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Sample sizes for human trials could not be verified from the available abstracts, limiting precision assessment; no meta-analysis confirms consistency across human studies. Evidence is sufficient to establish that sulforaphane is absorbed and bioactive in the human gut and can modulate local inflammation, but the clinical significance for broader digestive health remains incompletely characterized.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Three human studies (2021 RCT on NLRP3 and ischemia–reperfusion injury, 2025 observational work on NRF2–KEAP1–BACH1 in autism, 2024 cross-sectional study on superoxide dismutase and CRP in schizophrenia) show associations between sulforaphane exposure, immune markers (SOD, CRP), and clinical outcomes. Animal studies (2017–2025) consistently demonstrate that sulforaphane enhances immune cell function (macrophage polarization, efferocytosis), suppresses NLRP3-driven inflammation, and improves wound healing and infection outcomes.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Human sample sizes are extremely small (~81 confirmed across 1 study); most human studies are observational or cross-sectional rather than randomized. No meta-analysis confirms agreement across human trials. The NRF2-driven antioxidant mechanism is well-established, but direct human evidence for improved immune outcomes at clinically relevant scales is limited.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Seven human studies, including RCTs and a 2021 meta-analysis of rodent lipid profile data, suggest sulforaphane improves cardiovascular risk factors. A 2024 RCT (n=30) in hemodialysis patients showed no modulation of NRF2 and NF-κB mRNA, indicating inconsistent effects depending on disease context; a 2024 RCT demonstrated blood-brain barrier protection in stroke via NRF2-dependent ferroptosis inhibition; case evidence (2025) suggests therapeutic potential in myeloproliferative disorders. Animal studies (20 total) show benefits for lipid profiles, vascular dysfunction, and atherosclerosis-related pathology.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Human evidence for cardiovascular benefit exists but is fragmented across small trials, mixed outcomes (e.g., the n=30 hemodialysis trial showed no gene expression changes), and derives from a single meta-analysis that has not been independently replicated. Sample sizes are very small (~30 confirmed); direct cardiovascular event outcomes (MI, stroke, death) are not present in the retrieved studies. Moderate grade reflects plausibility from mechanism and animal data, but limited and inconsistent human efficacy data.

sulforaphane::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.evidence_base: The research base is dominated by animal studies (~83 of 124 retrieved records), with humans represented in 21 studies across all outcomes — mostly small RCTs, observational trials, and a few systematic reviews. Human sample sizes are often unreported or very small (confirmed totals range from ~7,450 for the autism review to ~30 for the hemodialysis trial), limiting statistical precision. Recent work (2021–2026) predominates, reflecting growing interest in NRF2 and isothiocyanate therapeutics. The mechanism — NRF2 activation and antioxidant/anti-inflammatory gene induction — is biochemically sound and consistently demonstrated in cellular and animal models, which supports plausibility; however, human clinical translation remains incomplete, with few large RCTs and no meta-analyses pooling human trial data for any single outcome.
sulforaphane::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.emerging_research: Recent directions include NRF2-targeted formulations for specific disease contexts: SFX-01 (a sulforaphane derivative) is under investigation for myeloproliferative disorders (2025); sulforaphane is being examined for COVID-19-related lung injury and macrophage-driven immune dysregulation (2025); and bioavailability optimization via nanoencapsulation and microbiome-informed dosing is advancing (2021–2025). Autism spectrum disorder and schizophrenia have emerged as test cases for sulforaphane's neuroinflammatory effects, though human evidence remains sparse.
sulforaphane::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.open_questions: Among the retrieved studies, no human trials exceed 12 weeks in duration — the long-term safety and efficacy of sulforaphane supplementation over months to years is not documented in these records. Sample sizes in human RCTs are consistently small (the largest confirmed is n=7,450 but primarily from a systematic review rather than a dedicated efficacy trial), and most trials omit complete demographic and baseline characteristic reporting, making it difficult to assess generalizability to diverse populations. Notably, the retrieved studies do not appear to include large, adequately powered trials in otherwise healthy populations; most focus on disease models (stroke, COPD, hemodialysis, autism) or animal systems. Because you are viewing only a sample of ~40 abstracts per outcome, you cannot determine whether larger or longer trials exist in the published literature outside this retrieval.
sulforaphane::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.caveats: Sulforaphane from whole vegetables is recognized as safe, but commercial supplements vary widely in potency, stability, and whether they contain the active form or the inactive precursor glucoraphanin (which requires enzymatic conversion). Injectable or highly concentrated formulations have not been extensively tested in humans; if considering research-grade or pharmaceutical-grade sulforaphane (e.g., SFX-01), medical supervision is prudent. Sulforaphane may interact with medications that rely on phase I cytochrome P450 metabolism or blood coagulation (via vitamin K effects in cruciferous vegetables), and persons taking anticoagulants or with estrogen-sensitive cancers should consult a clinician before high-dose supplementation.

astaxanthin::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.what_it_is: Astaxanthin (C₄₀H₅₂O₄, molecular weight 596.8) is a naturally occurring carotenoid pigment—a fat-soluble organic compound responsible for the red color in salmon, shrimp, and algae. It is produced primarily by the microalga *Haematococcus pluvialis* and accumulates in aquatic animals through the food chain. People typically consume it as a supplement derived from algal extracts or aquaculture byproducts, usually in capsule or powder form.
astaxanthin::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.how_it_works: Astaxanthin is a potent antioxidant that crosses cell membranes and the blood–brain barrier due to its lipophilic (fat-soluble) structure. It scavenges free radicals and reactive oxygen species (ROS)—unstable molecules that damage cells—by donating electrons to stabilize them. It also modulates inflammatory pathways, including regulation of microRNAs and immune signaling proteins, and can influence antioxidant enzyme systems like superoxide dismutase. This oxidative stress reduction and anti-inflammatory action underpin its proposed benefits for cardiovascular, immune, and cognitive health.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2022 meta-analysis of 380 participants showed astaxanthin supplementation mildly reduced oxidative stress and inflammation biomarkers. Multiple recent randomized controlled trials (2024–2025) in type 2 diabetes, poor ovarian responders, and firefighters found astaxanthin improved inflammatory markers and clinical outcomes. A 2021 systematic review on skin aging also supported anti-inflammatory effects. Across the retrieved studies, 10 human trials converged on reduced inflammation, supported by 20 animal studies showing mechanistic pathways via oxidative stress reduction and miRNA regulation.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Two independent meta-analyses/systematic reviews in the literature converged on this outcome, meeting the consistency threshold for Strong. Verified sample sizes across identified trials exceeded 425 participants, and multiple recent adequately powered randomized controlled trials demonstrated reproducible effects on biomarkers and clinical measures.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: All nine retrieved studies on stress and anxiety are animal-only, spanning rats and rodent models of neurobehavioral disorders. A 2025 study in spontaneously hypertensive rats suggested astaxanthin mitigated ADHD-like symptoms via dopaminergic modulation. A 2011 rat study proposed anxiolytic effects via oxidative stress reduction in the forebrain. Other animal studies examined effects under prenatal stress, neurotoxic exposure, and spatial memory tasks. No human trials directly tested anxiety or stress outcomes.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Evidence is limited entirely to animal models with no human data. Animal findings do not reliably translate to human anxiety or stress disorders, making claims about efficacy in people premature and speculative.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis identified effects on cardiovascular risk factors. Recent randomized controlled trials (2025, 2024, 2023) in participants with heart failure (n=80), firefighters, and individuals with elevated cholesterol (n=34) showed astaxanthin reduced oxidative markers, uric acid, adipokine levels, and cardiovascular risk biomarkers. A 2023 trial (n=12) combined astaxanthin with high-intensity training and found decreased adipokines and improved cardiovascular parameters. Five human trials and nine animal studies were retrieved, though verified sample sizes spanned only ~174 participants across four studies.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: A single meta-analysis exists without independent replication of its conclusion, and most abstracts omit sample sizes, limiting precision of the overall effect estimate. The human evidence is modest and weighted toward biomarker outcomes; larger or longer trials may be needed to confirm clinical significance.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2024 meta-analysis of 11 participants examined effects on fatigue, motor function, and cognition in randomized trials. A 2020 systematic review and a 2024 open-label trial assessed cognitive improvement in healthy adults. A 2020 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial found cognitive benefits with astaxanthin and tocotrienol intake. Animal studies (n=20 of 24 retrieved) showed preventive effects on memory deficits under high-fat diet and anxiolytic/antidepressant effects in rat models. Four human trials and 20 animal studies were retrieved, but human evidence is sparse.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Human evidence is modest—only 11 participants verified in the sole meta-analysis, and most trials are small or combine astaxanthin with other compounds, making it difficult to isolate its specific cognitive effect. Animal studies show promise but do not establish efficacy in humans.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2026 systematic review examined astaxanthin as an antioxidant and anti-inflammatory agent in human health. A 2026 randomized controlled trial in fish (Plectropomidae species, n=504) studied immune response and antioxidant capacity. A 2021 trial in laying hens reported astaxanthin enriched immunological responses. A 2012 observational study in rats examined combined fish oil and astaxanthin effects on lymphocyte function. Animal studies (n=24 of 28) addressed autoimmune hepatitis, antiviral responses, and immune modulation. Four human or human-relevant trials and 24 animal studies were retrieved.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only one study with a verified large sample (n=504) exists, and it was conducted in fish, not humans. A single human systematic review is available but not independently replicated. Most evidence is animal-based or observational, limiting confidence in human immune outcomes.

astaxanthin::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.evidence_base: The retrieved literature comprises 10 human trials, 1 human systematic review, and 82 animal studies across all outcomes—a mix that is weighted toward mechanistic animal work and smaller human observational or short-term randomized trials. Meta-analyses and systematic reviews exist for inflammation (2 independent), cardiovascular health (1), cognition (1), and immune function (1), providing some degree of evidence synthesis. Most studies are recent (2020–2026), reflecting growing interest in astaxanthin. However, verified participant counts are often modest, and many abstracts omit sample sizes, so the true human sample across the field is likely substantially larger than what can be confirmed from the provided records. The evidence is strongest for inflammation (with replicated meta-analyses) and moderate for cardiovascular, cognition, and immune outcomes (single meta-analyses or small trials).
astaxanthin::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.emerging_research: Recent 2025–2026 studies are exploring astaxanthin's role in specific disease contexts: type 2 diabetes via microRNA regulation, poor ovarian responder fertility outcomes, and heart failure biomarkers. A 2025 study in spontaneously hypertensive rats proposed dopaminergic mechanisms for ADHD-like symptom mitigation. Animal research continues to focus on molecular pathways—including STING carbonylation in antiviral responses and CD8⁺ T-cell modulation in autoimmune conditions. These directions are promising but remain preliminary in humans, and clinical translation is not yet established.
astaxanthin::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.open_questions: Among the studies retrieved here, human evidence for stress/anxiety is entirely absent—all nine studies are animal-only, limiting any claim about human applicability. For cognition, the single meta-analysis included only 11 participants, raising questions about effect stability in larger or longer-duration trials. Most human trials are short-term (weeks to a few months) and do not address long-term safety or sustained benefit. The retrieved records do not show trials comparing astaxanthin dose–response relationships, nor do they clearly distinguish effects when astaxanthin is combined with other supplements versus given alone. You are seeing only a sample (~40 abstracts per outcome); global literature may include additional studies not represented here.
astaxanthin::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.caveats: Astaxanthin is a lipid-soluble compound and is generally well tolerated at supplemental doses (4–12 mg/day in trials reviewed); however, quality and purity vary widely among commercial products. It may interact with blood-thinning medications or increase bleeding risk if combined with anticoagulants. Pregnant and nursing women, and people with severe cardiovascular disease, should consult a healthcare provider before supplementing. As an injectable or intravenous form is not standard for astaxanthin, typical safety concerns apply to oral supplements—primarily gastrointestinal tolerance and potential allergic reaction in sensitive individuals.

dhea::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.what_it_is: DHEA (dehydroepiandrosterone) is a steroid hormone naturally produced by the adrenal glands, sitting upstream of both testosterone and estrogen in the body's hormone synthesis pathway. It is also known by its IUPAC designation (3S,8R,9S,10R,13S,14S)-3-hydroxy-10,13-dimethyl-1,2,3,4,7,8,9,11,12,14,15,16-dodecahydrocyclopenta[a]phenanthren-17-one, with molecular formula C₁₉H₂₈O₂. DHEA levels peak in early adulthood and decline steadily with age. People typically supplement with oral DHEA tablets or, in some clinical contexts, vaginal formulations; the compound is available over-the-counter in the United States but is prescription-regulated in many other countries.
dhea::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.how_it_works: DHEA acts as a prohormone—a precursor molecule that the body converts into active sex hormones (testosterone and estrogen) via enzyme-catalyzed pathways in peripheral tissues. It also exerts direct effects on cells bearing DHEA receptors and may modulate the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis, the body's central stress-response system. Because DHEA levels correlate inversely with cortisol (the primary stress hormone), supplementation is thought to shift this balance, potentially dampening chronic stress signaling and supporting anabolic processes like muscle protein synthesis and bone formation. Additionally, DHEA may enhance neuroplasticity and anti-inflammatory signaling in the brain, though the full scope of its receptor interactions remains incompletely mapped.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Multiple randomized controlled trials and meta-analyses consistently demonstrate that DHEA supplementation elevates serum testosterone in adult men. A 2013 RCT found acute DHEA administration increased free testosterone in middle-aged and young men following high-intensity exercise; a 1999 RCT (n=19) showed oral DHEA raised serum testosterone and enhanced adaptations to resistance training. A 2016 RCT (n=32) documented effects on systemic lipolysis linked to testosterone changes. A 2018 RCT examined systemic and local hormonal effects of vaginal DHEA in women (NCCTG N10C1). Two independent meta-analyses and systematic reviews, including a 2020 review on DHEA in bone and osteoporosis, converged on this outcome across approximately 2,022 verified participants.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The Strong grade reflects 28 human studies with robust consensus across 2 independent meta-analyses, adequate sample sizes, and consistent directionality. Most abstracts do not report sample numbers, so the true participant count is substantially larger than 2,022 verified here, strengthening confidence in the finding.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2018 meta-analysis of DHEA for depression and a 2014 systematic review both synthesized evidence from multiple RCTs showing DHEA supplementation is associated with improvements in depressive symptoms and overall mood in various populations. A 2024 RCT (n=206) in refugees examined associations between hair cortisol and DHEA with posttraumatic stress disorder symptoms, finding correlations consistent with DHEA's putative mood-protective role. Systematic reviews from 2023 (in postmenopausal women), 2008 (antiglucocorticoid treatments), and 2000 all reported DHEA-related benefits for mood and well-being. Five independent meta-analyses and systematic reviews converge on this outcome.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The Strong grade is justified by 25 human studies, no animal evidence for this outcome, and convergence across 5 independent meta-analyses and systematic reviews. Although only ~483 participants could be verified from abstract data (indicating most studies omit sample sizes in their abstracts), the replicated synthesis and sample adequacy support a strong overall rating.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2023 meta-analysis of biological and emotional responses to the Trier Social Stress Test (a standardized stressor) examined DHEA's role in acute stress reactivity. Recent RCTs (2025, n=30; 2024, n=54) investigated DHEA's associations with stress and anxiety outcomes in chronic pain and posttraumatic contexts. A 2019 RCT examined pharmacological actions of ashwagandha alongside stress hormones; a 2013 systematic review on burnout addressed occupational stress; and 2020 RCT data explored anxiety as a confounder in stress-related conditions. The 2023 meta-analysis and 2013 systematic review represent 2 independent syntheses converging on stress/anxiety reduction linked to DHEA.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The Strong grade reflects 30 human studies and 1 animal study, with 2 independent meta-analyses/systematic reviews converging on the outcome. Approximately 1,756 participants were verified across 12 studies; most abstracts omit full sample sizes, indicating a substantially larger true cohort. Consistency and adequacy of power support the strong rating despite sparse replication numbers.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2020 systematic review examined DHEA and DHEAS in Alzheimer's disease, and a 2000 systematic review addressed DHEA supplementation for cognition and well-being broadly. A 2025 systematic review explored adrenarche and social cognition in relation to autism spectrum traits. Recent RCTs (2025, n=30; 2024, n=206) measured cortisol and DHEA associations with spatial memory consolidation and posttraumatic stress (cognitive dimensions). A 2015 RCT investigated DHEA and DHEAS in emotional processing and cognitive-behavioral tasks. Three independent meta-analyses and systematic reviews converge on cognitive benefit.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The Strong grade is supported by 18 human studies and 2 animal studies, with 3 independent meta-analyses and systematic reviews converging on the outcome. Approximately 1,115 participants were verified across 7 studies; most abstracts lack complete sample reporting. The convergence across three syntheses and consistent directionality in cognitive domains justify the strong rating.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2019 meta-analysis of endogenous DHEA/DHEAS and coronary heart disease examined associations across multiple cohorts; a 2023 observational study (n=1,287) of elderly men found serum DHEA inversely associated with coronary artery calcification; a 2022 observational study investigated DHEAS levels and cardiovascular outcomes in chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy. A 2020 study of plasma DHEAS in older adults (n=8,143) assessed cardiovascular disease risk. A 2022 study (n=40) examined the cortisol/DHEA ratio before and after bariatric surgery in relation to metabolic parameters, and a 2000 RCT explored DHEA's broader aging and cardiovascular effects.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The Moderate grade reflects 8 human and 4 animal studies with only a single meta-analysis/systematic review identified in the retrieved records; this single synthesis has not been independently replicated or verified, preventing a strong rating. Although approximately 9,496 participants were verified across 4 studies (indicating substantially larger total cohorts), the absence of consistent independent replication of the synthesis limits confidence to moderate.

dhea::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.evidence_base: The evidence base for DHEA is predominantly human-derived: 81 human studies versus 9 animal studies across the four major outcomes. The literature is dominated by randomized controlled trials, observational cohorts, and meta-analyses/systematic reviews, with study dates ranging from 1999 to 2025, indicating sustained and recent research interest. Multiple independent meta-analyses converge on mood, stress/anxiety, and cognition; single meta-analyses exist for testosterone and cardiovascular outcomes. The verified sample sizes range from tens (single RCTs) to thousands (large epidemiologic cohorts), though most abstracts omit sample numbers, suggesting the true participant count is substantially larger than reported here.
dhea::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.emerging_research: Recent 2024–2025 studies are exploring DHEA's role in posttraumatic stress disorder symptomology (hair cortisol correlates), spatial memory consolidation under stress, and social cognition in autism spectrum development. A 2025 systematic review connected adrenarche to social-cognitive traits, opening new developmental avenues. Bariatric surgery research (2022) is examining how the cortisol/DHEA ratio shifts after metabolic intervention. These directions suggest interest in DHEA's neuroprotective and stress-resilience mechanisms, though all remain early and require replication before clinical recommendations can be drawn.
dhea::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.open_questions: Among the studies retrieved here, sample sizes are frequently omitted from abstracts, making precise participant counts difficult; the true cohorts are substantially larger than the verified totals. Trial durations and long-term follow-up windows are not evident from the abstracts provided, raising questions about whether benefits persist beyond the study period. No clear demographic breakdown is visible in the records given—it is unclear from these abstracts alone which age groups, sex distributions, or disease populations dominate each outcome, or whether certain groups (e.g., younger vs. older adults, pre- vs. postmenopausal women) show different response patterns. These gaps reflect limitations in the retrieved abstract data, not necessarily in the literature overall.
dhea::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.caveats: DHEA is a hormone and should be used cautiously; excessive supplementation can elevate testosterone and estrogen above physiological norms, potentially increasing risks of hormone-sensitive cancers, cardiovascular events, or liver strain in susceptible individuals. Quality varies widely among over-the-counter formulations, and purity is not federally regulated in the United States. DHEA may interact with hormone replacement therapies, antidiabetic agents, and immunosuppressants. Pregnant and nursing women should avoid DHEA, and individuals with a personal or family history of hormone-sensitive cancer or uncontrolled hypertension should consult a physician before use.

pregnenolone::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.what_it_is: Pregnenolone (C₂₁H₃₂O₂, molecular weight 316.5) is a naturally occurring steroid hormone synthesized primarily in the adrenal glands and gonads from cholesterol. It serves as a precursor to many other steroid hormones, including DHEA, progesterone, and cortisol, making it a key branch point in steroid biochemistry. People typically take it as an oral supplement, though it is also studied in clinical research settings; the compound is available over-the-counter in some countries but remains a prescription medication or research agent in others.
pregnenolone::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.how_it_works: Pregnenolone is produced in mitochondria via the enzyme P450scc (side-chain cleavage enzyme), which converts cholesterol into pregnenolone in the first committed step of steroid hormone synthesis. Once formed, it is metabolized into multiple downstream hormones—each with distinct receptor targets and physiological roles—or can itself exert effects via intracellular pathways and possibly membrane receptors. In the nervous system, pregnenolone and its metabolites act as neuroactive steroids, modulating GABA and NMDA receptors and potentially influencing neuroinflammation, mitochondrial function, and synaptic plasticity. Because it sits at the top of the steroid cascade, pregnenolone's effects are partly direct and partly mediated through its conversion into other hormones; this dual action makes it relevant to mood, cognition, and hormonal balance.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Multiple randomized controlled trials and systematic reviews converge on cognitive benefit in psychiatric populations. A 2009 proof-of-concept RCT (n=21) in schizophrenia showed improvement in cognitive and negative symptoms; a 2010 RCT (n=44) in schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder found adjunctive pregnenolone benefit; another 2010 RCT (n=70) in dual diagnosis patients reported gains in both cognition and mood. Three independent systematic reviews (2015 meta-analysis on sex hormones in schizophrenia, 2024 review of non-dopaminergic treatments, and 2018 review of HPA axis and sex steroids in mood disorders) all synthesized evidence supporting this outcome.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The outcome rests on 9 human studies (including multiple RCTs) and 12 animal studies, with convergent systematic reviews providing independent replication at the synthesis level. Although most individual abstracts omitted sample sizes, at least 1,149 participants were verified across synthesized trials, and the consistency across three independent meta-analyses substantially reduces the risk of single-study bias.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2014 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (n=80) specifically tested pregnenolone for bipolar depression and found benefit. A 2017 RCT (n=11) in bipolar depression showed effects on microtubule-associated protein 2, a biomarker of neuronal integrity. The 2010 dual diagnosis RCT (n=70) also measured mood improvement. A 2023 RCT examined estrogen, progesterone, and neuroactive steroids (including pregnenolone-related pathways) in suicidal patients. Two independent systematic reviews (2016 on non-conventional agents for bipolar disorder, and 2018 on HPA axis and sex steroids in major mood disorders) synthesized evidence supporting mood and depression outcomes.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The outcome is supported by 18 human studies (including multiple RCTs and systematic reviews) and 10 animal studies. Two independent meta-analyses or systematic reviews converge on this outcome, and at least 386 participants were verified across 9 trials with available sample sizes. The convergence of reviews and adequately powered individual RCTs justifies the Strong grade.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Studies examining pregnenolone's relationship to testosterone and other hormones include a 1976 clinical trial measuring pregnenolone, 17-OH-pregnenolone, and testosterone in congenital adrenal hyperplasia; a 1985 observational study of testosterone and its precursor steroids in response to anabolic steroids; a 1989 observational study on gonadotropins and steroid cofactors; a 2022 observational study (n=29) of androgen concentrations in PCOS; a 2024 RCT (n=56) comparing hormone levels under different ovarian stimulation protocols; and a 2023 observational study of pregnenolone and testosterone in male shift workers.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: While 16 human and 17 animal studies exist, the human evidence base is predominantly observational or uncontrolled, and no pooled analysis confirms agreement across studies on magnitude or clinical direction of effect. At least 488 participants were verified across 4 trials, but the inconsistency in study design and lack of meta-analytic synthesis keep this at Moderate rather than Strong.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Only 5 human studies directly examine pregnenolone and inflammation outcomes. A 2026 observational study (n=500) identified pregnenolone in plasma metabolomic profiles of vascular and inflammatory signatures in hospitalized patients. A 2023 biomolecular study (n=225) mapped albumin in acute liver failure. A 2021 unclassified study (n=30) measured pregnenolone sulfate and related steroids in women with a specific condition. A 2019 metabolomic study (n=955) in type 2 diabetes included pregnenolone in metabolic signatures. A 2018 study examined pregnenolone changes after MDMA administration. Animal studies (22) provide mechanistic support.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Human evidence is sparse (5 of 27 studies) and mostly observational or metabolomic in nature—none are randomized trials designed to test anti-inflammatory efficacy. These studies document pregnenolone's presence in inflammatory states but do not establish causal benefit. The Moderate grade reflects reasonable animal-based mechanistic plausibility combined with limited direct human clinical evidence.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2020 systematic review (n=508) identified pregnenolone in circulating metabolite profiles that differentiate acute ischemic stroke from stroke mimics. A 2025 RCT (n=21) measured pregnenolone effects on parasympathetic response to stress and alcohol cue provocation in treatment-seeking individuals. A 2018 RCT examined add-on pregnenolone with L-theanine to antipsychotics for anxiety symptoms, which may have cardiovascular relevance. A 2026 observational study (n=500) profiled pregnenolone in vascular and inflammatory metabolomic signatures. A 2018 observational study reviewed daily testosterone management for testosterone deficiency. A 2025 unclassified metabolome study examined pregnenolone in sleep-related phenotypes relevant to cardiovascular health.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Eleven human studies exist (mostly observational or small RCTs) and 15 animal studies provide mechanistic plausibility. However, only a single meta-analysis or systematic review synthesizes the human cardiovascular evidence, and its conclusions lack independent replication. The evidence base is moderate in quantity but limited by design heterogeneity and sparse direct cardiovascular outcome trials.

pregnenolone::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.evidence_base: The research base includes 45 human studies (predominantly in psychiatric populations and metabolomic profiling) and 76 animal studies, with substantial weight on RCTs and systematic reviews for cognition and mood but predominantly observational or metabolomic designs for hormonal, inflammatory, and cardiovascular outcomes. Human trials range from small proof-of-concept studies (n=11–21) to meta-analyses synthesizing dozens of reports, with most published between 2010 and 2026. The convergence of three independent systematic reviews on cognition and two on mood indicates that the evidence for psychiatric applications is both recent and subject to independent synthesis and replication, while the hormonal and cardiovascular evidence rests more heavily on biomarker and observational data. This heterogeneity across outcomes explains the gradient from Strong (cognition, mood) to Moderate (hormones, inflammation, cardiovascular).
pregnenolone::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.emerging_research: Recent work has expanded pregnenolone research into metabolomic profiling, with large observational studies (n=500, 2026) mapping pregnenolone as a biomarker in vascular and inflammatory disease states, and investigations into its role in shift work-related hormonal dysregulation (2023). A 2025 RCT examined pregnenolone's effects on parasympathetic tone and alcohol cue reactivity in addiction treatment, suggesting potential applications in stress-related disorders beyond schizophrenia and bipolar depression. Animal studies continue to explore neuroactive steroid mechanisms in neuroinflammation and neuroprotection. These directions are early and mostly smaller or observational in design.
pregnenolone::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.open_questions: Among the retrieved studies, cognition and mood evidence concentrates in schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, and bipolar depression; RCTs in other psychiatric or neurodegenerative conditions are not evident in the sample provided. For hormonal effects, the retrieved records show observational and reproductive-focused studies but lack large randomized trials directly testing pregnenolone as a hormone replacement or optimization agent. Inflammation and cardiovascular outcomes rely primarily on metabolomic or observational data rather than prospective clinical trials; among the records provided, none appear to follow participants for more than a few weeks to months, limiting understanding of long-term tolerability or sustained benefit. Because these data represent approximately 40 abstracts per outcome (not a complete literature search), gaps in these records may not reflect gaps in the field at large—broader literature may contain additional populations, durations, or mechanistic insights not visible here.
pregnenolone::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.caveats: Pregnenolone is a hormonal agent and carries the general caution that modifying steroid hormone levels—even by upstream supplementation—can have systemic effects and potential drug interactions; it may affect other steroid hormone metabolism or interact with hormonal medications or contraceptives. Because most clinical trials have been small and short-term, long-term safety data in general populations are limited. Individuals with hormone-sensitive conditions (certain cancers, endometriosis), those pregnant or nursing, and those on other hormonal or psychiatric medications should consult a healthcare provider before use; the compound's status varies by jurisdiction (over-the-counter supplement in some places, prescription in others, research-only in others).

vitamin d::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.what_it_is: Vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol, C₂₇H₄₄O) is a steroid hormone precursor synthesized in the skin upon sun exposure and obtained from foods like fatty fish and fortified dairy. It is inactive until metabolized in the liver and kidneys into its active hormonal forms, calcitriol and calcifediol. People obtain it through sun exposure, dietary intake, or oral supplementation (pills, oils, or injections in clinical settings).
vitamin d::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.how_it_works: Vitamin D circulates as a steroid hormone that binds to vitamin D receptors (VDR) in cells throughout the body—in the immune system, pancreas, blood vessels, bone, and others. Once bound, it acts as a transcription factor, switching hundreds of genes on and off. This controls calcium absorption (critical for bone), regulates immune cell maturation and activation, modulates insulin secretion and sensitivity, and dampens inflammatory pathways by reducing pro-inflammatory cytokine production. Because vitamin D is hormonal rather than merely nutritional, its effects ripple across multiple body systems.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Eight independent meta-analyses and systematic reviews in humans consistently show associations between vitamin D status and improved blood sugar control and reduced diabetes risk. A 2020 meta-analysis of 3,094 participants found vitamin D supplementation was linked to lower prediabetes prevalence; a 2024 systematic review of 2,982 participants examining type 2 diabetes found vitamin D supplementation improved glycemic control. The body of evidence includes meta-analyses on polycystic ovary syndrome (n=3,182) and cardiovascular risk in obesity (n=1,179), all converging on benefit.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Strong grade reflects 28 human studies with 8 independent meta-analyses showing consistent, replicated findings across large pooled populations. The convergence of multiple systematic reviews on the same outcome provides high confidence despite some abstracts omitting exact sample sizes.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Five independent meta-analyses and systematic reviews in humans—totaling 30 human studies—document associations between vitamin D status and testosterone levels in adult men and women. A 2021 meta-analysis of 9,892 participants directly examined the relationship between vitamin D and testosterone, finding positive correlation; a 2026 systematic review focused on vitamin D supplementation and total testosterone in adult men; a 2023 systematic review investigated vitamin D, testosterone, and depression in middle-aged and elderly men; and a 2025 RCT (n=253) in breast cancer survivors measured testosterone response to vitamin D supplementation.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Strong grade reflects 30 human studies with 5 independent meta-analyses converging on hormone modulation. Replication across multiple systematic reviews and adequately powered pooled analyses—including one of nearly 10,000 participants—provides robust evidence.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Four independent meta-analyses and systematic reviews in humans consistently show vitamin D supplementation and higher vitamin D status are associated with lower inflammatory markers. A 2024 meta-analysis (n=58) in asthma patients linked vitamin D to reduced inflammation-related biomarkers; a 2020 meta-analysis (n=579) in chronic kidney disease found vitamin D supplementation reduced vascular inflammation; a 2025 systematic review examined vitamin D's effects on fasting glucose, insulin sensitivity, and inflammation in type 2 diabetes; and observational and cross-sectional studies (n=65–70) documented associations between vitamin D insufficiency and elevated inflammatory cytokines in metabolic and cognitive conditions.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Strong grade reflects 6 human studies in the retrieved sample with 4 independent meta-analyses showing consistent direction. Although ~772 participants are explicitly verified, the true total is larger because most abstracts do not report sample sizes; multiple replicated syntheses provide confidence despite precision limitations.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2019 meta-analysis (n=454) examined vitamin D supplementation and mortality in cardiovascular contexts; 2021–2024 clinical trials and observational studies in humans investigated vitamin D's relationship to cardiovascular structure and function, with particular focus on chronic kidney disease patients and kidney transplant recipients. The studies examined epimeric vitamin D metabolites and cardiovascular outcomes in advanced chronic kidney disease (n=165, 2024) and cardiovascular disease risk in chronic kidney disease (CRIC Study, 2023).
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderate grade reflects only 4 human studies (not yet meeting the consistency threshold of independent replicated meta-analyses) and a single meta-analysis whose conclusion has not yet been independently verified. While 2 studies report sample sizes (n=454, n=165), most abstracts omit this detail, limiting precision assessment.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Two human studies examined vitamin D's role in immune function: a 2019 RCT tested whether vitamin D and phenylbutyrate supplementation modulate gut-derived immune activation in HIV-1; a 2020 observational case-control study compared immune function and serum vitamin D levels in shelter dogs. Two animal studies demonstrated vitamin D's role in neutrophil generation and function in zebrafish (2022) and in macrophage immune response regulation via microRNA networks (2022).
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderate grade reflects only 2 human studies without independent meta-analyses to replicate findings, paired with unclear sample sizes from abstracts, capping precision confirmation. The small human sample base and lack of replicated systematic reviews prevent a higher grade despite plausible mechanisms shown in animal models.

vitamin d::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.evidence_base: The retrieved literature for vitamin D is predominantly human (66 human studies vs. 19 animal/in vitro studies across all outcomes). Evidence is dominated by meta-analyses and systematic reviews—particularly for blood sugar, hormones, and inflammation—demonstrating multiple independent syntheses converging on the same outcomes. Studies span 2015–2026, with a strong cluster from 2020–2025, reflecting active recent investigation. The convergence of 8 meta-analyses on blood sugar and 5 on hormones provides substantial confidence in those domains, whereas immune function rests on fewer human studies and no replicated syntheses. Overall, the evidence base supports vitamin D as a hormone with broad systemic effects backed by repeated synthesis-level findings, though confidence varies by outcome.
vitamin d::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.emerging_research: Recent work (2023–2025) is expanding investigation into vitamin D's role in specific populations: vitamin D and testosterone in cancer survivors (2025 RCT), the triglyceride-glucose index and vitamin D status (2024 systematic review), and vitamin D's impact on insulin sensitivity and inflammation in type 2 diabetes (2025 systematic review). Mechanistic studies are revealing how vitamin D regulates immune function through microRNA networks in macrophages (2022) and enhances neutrophil generation (2022 zebrafish model). These directions suggest growing interest in precision outcomes (specific cytokines, epimeric metabolite forms, and metabolic phenotypes) rather than broad health claims.
vitamin d::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.open_questions: Among the studies retrieved here, most do not report participant sample sizes in their abstracts, so the true total population studied cannot be verified—we can confirm only ~2,300 participants explicitly stated across all outcomes, though the actual number is substantially larger. The cardiovascular outcome rests on a single meta-analysis not yet independently replicated; it is unclear from these records whether additional independent cardiovascular syntheses exist in the wider literature. For immune function, both human studies identified come from non-typical populations (HIV-infected individuals and shelter dogs), raising questions about generalizability to healthy people—though this limitation is specific only to what the retrieved records show, not the field overall. Trial durations and long-term follow-up are not apparent from the abstracts provided.
vitamin d::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.caveats: Vitamin D is fat-soluble and can accumulate with excessive supplementation; sustained intakes above 4,000 IU/day in adults warrant monitoring of serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels to avoid hypercalcemia and related toxicity. People with granulomatous diseases (sarcoidosis, tuberculosis), hyperparathyroidism, or certain kidney conditions should consult a clinician before supplementing, as vitamin D metabolism is altered. Vitamin D interacts with medications affecting calcium metabolism (thiazide diuretics, some anticonvulsants) and bisphosphonates; concurrent use requires medical oversight.

progesterone::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.what_it_is: Progesterone (C₂₁H₃₀O₂) is a steroid hormone naturally produced primarily by the ovaries after ovulation, and later by the placenta during pregnancy. It is also synthesized in smaller amounts by the adrenal glands and brain. People take it as a supplement in micronized oral form, transdermal patches, creams, or injections, often to manage menopausal symptoms, support fertility, or regulate menstrual cycle symptoms.
progesterone::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.how_it_works: Progesterone acts by binding to progesterone receptors found throughout the body—in the uterus, brain, immune cells, and other tissues—triggering changes in gene expression and cellular function. In the brain, it modulates neurotransmitter systems and can reduce excitability, which is thought to underpin effects on mood and seizure risk. In immune tissue, progesterone shifts the balance of inflammatory responses and influences how immune cells recognize and react to pathogens and allergens. It also interacts with other hormonal pathways, including those involving estrogen and cortisol, creating complex effects on metabolism, mood regulation, and inflammation. These widespread receptor actions explain why progesterone is implicated in multiple physiological systems beyond reproduction.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2024 meta-analysis and five observational studies (spanning 1976–2025) examined sex hormone profiles in varied populations, including women with torsades de pointes arrhythmias, trigeminal neuralgia, and COVID-19 recovery. Studies also tracked hormonal changes related to ovulation, luteal function, and tumor cell responses. While verified sample sizes across five studies total approximately 6,877 participants, most study abstracts omit detailed participant numbers, so the true sample is likely larger. The research documents associations between progesterone and other sex hormones (testosterone, estradiol, LH) but does not establish strong causal or dose–response relationships.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Evidence is graded Moderate because human and animal studies are roughly balanced (14 each of 28), yet only a single meta-analysis exists and its conclusions lack independent replication. Study designs are mostly observational, which limits causal inference. Precision is further reduced because most abstracts omit sample sizes, obscuring the true evidence base.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Fifteen human randomized controlled trials and observational studies (2015–2026) examined progesterone's role in mood and depression, particularly in the context of premenstrual dysphoric disorder, menopausal depression, and suicidality. Key trials include a 2018 RCT (n=172) on transdermal estradiol and micronized progesterone for depression prevention, a 2015 RCT (n=727) on hormone therapy effects on mood in postmenopausal women, and a 2026 clinical trial (n=920) on transdermal therapy for menopausal mood symptoms. A 2023 RCT examined progesterone's effects on neuroactive steroids and cytokines in suicidal patients. Studies document associations between progesterone and mood outcomes but show variable results.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Grade is Moderate because all 15 studies are human-based (no animal data), but no pooled meta-analysis confirms the findings agree; studies report mixed outcomes without independent replication of a single synthesis. Designs are largely RCTs (stronger than observational), which supports this grade, but inconsistency across trials prevents a Strong rating.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Six human studies (2015–2025) and twenty animal studies examined progesterone's immunomodulatory effects. Human trials include a 2020 RCT on post-ischemic stroke inflammation and a 2016 RCT on progesterone-induced changes in serum injury markers. Observational and unclassified human studies tracked progesterone in settings of ovarian inflammation (n=45, 2015), alveolar bone resorption (2025), postpartum inflammation (n=163, 2021), and myometrial inflammation (2020). Verified human participants across three studies total approximately 277, though true numbers are likely higher due to unreported sample sizes in abstracts.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Grade is Moderate due to low human precision (only ~277 verified participants across 3 of 26 studies) and heavy reliance on animal models (20 of 26 studies). No pooled human meta-analysis exists, and the few human studies show inconsistent outcomes without independent replication. This limits confidence that animal findings translate to clinical efficacy in humans.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Four human studies (1997–2012) and twenty-four animal studies examined progesterone's effects on immune function. Human studies include a 1997 RCT in sheep on uterine immune regulation during the estrous cycle, a 2012 observational study (n=13) comparing mucosal immunity in amenorrheic versus eumenorrheic runners, an unclassified 2006 study (n=270) on hormone allergy, and a 1998 unclassified study on immune changes in intrahepatic cholestasis. A 2024 animal study found progesterone amplified allergic inflammation and airway pathology; a 2022 animal study examined progesterone's modulation of innate immune responses to viruses including SARS-CoV-2.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Grade is Moderate because human evidence is sparse (only 4 of 28 studies, ~283 verified participants across 2 studies) and lacks independent replication via meta-analysis. The field relies heavily on animal models (24 of 28), which cannot yet confirm human immune effects. Study designs vary and sample sizes are small, limiting precision and generalizability.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Nineteen human studies (2005–2023) and five animal studies examined progesterone's cognitive effects. Six independent meta-analyses and systematic reviews converged on this outcome: a 2017 meta-analysis (n=637) on long-term hormone therapy in perimenopausal and postmenopausal women, a 2005 meta-analysis (n=108) on estrogen for schizophrenia, a 2023 systematic review (n=457) on progesterone for catamenial epilepsy, a 2023 systematic review on progesterone and progestin actions in the brain, a 2014 systematic review on emotional and cognitive imaging of hormone effects, and a 2012 systematic review of progesterone use by midlife and menopausal women. Verified participants across eight studies total approximately 3,037.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Grade is Strong because six independent meta-analyses and systematic reviews convergently synthesize human evidence, demonstrating replicated findings and adequate statistical power. Human evidence (19 of 24 studies) substantially outweighs animal models. Sample sizes are larger and more consistently reported than other outcomes, yielding greater precision. The existence of multiple independent syntheses reaching similar conclusions is the hallmark of Strong evidence.

progesterone::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.evidence_base: The literature on progesterone is predominantly human-based (58 of 121 total studies), with a mix of randomized controlled trials, observational studies, and systematic reviews/meta-analyses. Cognition has the strongest evidence foundation, with six independent meta-analyses providing convergent synthesis; other outcomes rely on fewer pooled analyses and show inconsistency. Research spans from 1976 to 2026, with recent work (2023–2026) focusing on menopausal and reproductive applications. A substantial portion of abstracts omit sample sizes, limiting precision across all outcomes; verified participant counts range from 13 to 6,877 depending on the outcome. This pattern suggests the true evidence base is larger than directly quantifiable from the records provided.
progesterone::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.emerging_research: Recent studies (2024–2026) are exploring progesterone's role in post-COVID immune recovery (antibody titers and DHEA/cortisol correlation), alveolar bone resorption in inflammatory states, and the interaction between progesterone and the kynurenine pathway in postpartum inflammation. A 2024 animal study suggests progesterone may amplify allergic airway responses via type 2 innate lymphoid cells, a finding that contradicts simpler anti-inflammatory models and highlights context-dependent effects. These emerging directions indicate renewed interest in progesterone's immunomodulation beyond classical reproductive roles, though findings remain preliminary in humans.
progesterone::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.open_questions: Among the study records retrieved here, cognition has the broadest human evidence base with multiple independent meta-analyses, while immune function and inflammation rely heavily on animal models (24 and 20 of 28 studies, respectively) and very few human participants (~277–283 across small studies). Mood and depression research is entirely human-based but lacks a pooled synthesis confirming agreement. Notable gaps in the retrieved records include: no long-term follow-up studies extending beyond 12 weeks are described in most abstracts; diverse populations (younger women, athletic amenorrhea, intrahepatic cholestasis) appear in limited studies, raising questions about generalizability; and dose–response relationships are not evident in the abstracts provided. These limitations describe only what is or is not visible in the ~40 abstracts per outcome supplied here; the global literature may contain additional evidence not represented in this sample.
progesterone::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.caveats: Progesterone is a prescription hormone in most jurisdictions and should be prescribed and monitored by a healthcare provider, especially in users with a history of breast cancer, thromboembolic disease, or liver dysfunction, as hormone therapy carries established cardiovascular and malignancy risks. Bioavailability and efficacy vary substantially depending on route (oral, transdermal, intramuscular) and formulation (micronized, synthetic progestins); the studies provided do not systematically compare these variations, so clinical guidance on optimal dosing or form is limited. Progesterone interacts with cytochrome P450 enzymes and may alter metabolism of other medications; concurrent use of anticonvulsants, corticosteroids, or anticoagulants should be reviewed with a clinician.

omega-3::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.what_it_is: Omega-3 refers to a family of polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs), most notably eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA), a 20-carbon chain with five double bonds (C20H30O2, molecular weight 302.5). These are essential fats the human body cannot synthesize and must obtain from food — primarily fatty fish, fish oil supplements, and certain plant sources like flaxseed and algae. People typically consume omega-3s as part of their diet or as isolated supplements in capsule, liquid, or powder form.
omega-3::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.how_it_works: Omega-3 fatty acids integrate into cell membranes throughout the body, where they influence membrane fluidity, flexibility, and the function of embedded proteins. They are substrates for specialized signaling molecules called lipid mediators (resolvins, protectins, and others) that actively suppress inflammatory cascades and promote tissue repair—this is why omega-3s are potent anti-inflammatory agents. In blood vessels, omega-3s improve endothelial function (the health of the inner lining), reduce platelet aggregation, and help regulate blood pressure and lipid profiles. In the brain, they support neuronal membrane health, synaptic signaling, and are particularly enriched in gray matter; they also dampen neuroinflammation, a driver of cognitive decline. These same mechanisms—reduced inflammation, improved cellular signaling, and tissue protection—underlie their effects on muscle maintenance, gut barrier function, and general cardiovascular resilience.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Multiple meta-analyses and systematic reviews, including a 2024 GRADE-assessed review of 2,385 participants, consistently demonstrate that omega-3 supplementation improves endothelial function, reduces aortic valve calcification, and modifies the relationship between systemic inflammation and cardiovascular outcomes. A 2021 meta-analysis (n=267) examined dose-response effects on cardiovascular outcomes, and observational cohorts (e.g., Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis, n=862) show associations between omega-3 levels and reduced vascular calcification. Four independent meta-analyses and systematic reviews converge on benefit.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Strong grade reflects 8 human studies with 4 pooled meta-analyses showing consistent, replicated conclusions across adequately powered samples. The evidence base is substantial and convergent, with verified sample sizes totaling over 10,000 across the full set of studies.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2025 meta-analysis (n=881) of omega-3 and cognitive decline in adults with mild cognitive impairment or non-dementia, and a 2023 meta-analysis (n=1,135) examining omega-3 fatty acids in relation to dementia and cognitive decline, both support protective effects. A 2020 meta-analysis (n=4,247) found domain-specific improvements in cognitive test performance in youths. Earlier systematic reviews (2015) and a 2025 dose-response analysis further corroborate benefit. Twelve independent meta-analyses and systematic reviews converge on this outcome.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Strong grade reflects 22 human studies with 12 independent pooled analyses showing replicated, consistent conclusions. The preponderance of human evidence, large aggregate sample sizes, and multiple meta-analyses across different populations (youths, older adults, at-risk groups) establish robust support.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2024 meta-analysis (n=853) demonstrates that omega-3 supplementation reduces markers of inflammation and improves endothelial function in patients with inflammatory conditions. A 2021 meta-analysis (n=751) found long-term omega-3 supplementation beneficial in inflammatory bowel disease. A 2020 meta-analysis showed effects on oxidative stress and inflammation, and a 2024 systematic review (n=215) documented anti-inflammatory benefit in endometriosis. A 2026 meta-analysis evaluated omega-3 in sports inflammation and recovery. Seven independent meta-analyses and systematic reviews converge on anti-inflammatory effect.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Strong grade reflects 14 human studies with 7 pooled meta-analyses showing consistent, replicated conclusions. Verified sample sizes exceed 5,000, and multiple meta-analyses across different disease contexts (IBD, endometriosis, sports, general inflammation) provide robust and convergent support.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2025 RCT (n=30) found that a multifunctional dietary approach including omega-3 reduced intestinal inflammation in relation to changes in gut microbiota. A 2021 RCT (n=11) examined bioavailability of oral omega-3 PUFAs in the distal small intestine. A 2014 RCT assessed omega-3 combined with probiotics on lipid profile and inflammatory markers related to gut function. A 2005 RCT (n=40) showed preoperative omega-3 supplementation beneficially altered phospholipid fatty acid composition. However, studies remain heterogeneous in design and outcome measurement, and no pooled meta-analysis has confirmed consistency across trials.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderate grade reflects 6 human studies with promising but non-pooled findings. Sample sizes are small and inconsistently reported (only 3 of 16 studies provide verified n, ~81 participants total), and no independent systematic review has confirmed agreement across studies, preventing upgrade to Strong.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2021 meta-analysis examined omega-3 supplementation on muscle maintenance and quality of life. RCTs from 2026, 2022, and 2019 show benefits of omega-3 supplementation in the context of exercise and resistance training, attenuating disuse atrophy and supporting muscle quality. Two RCTs (2020, n=210 each) evaluated early posthatch omega-3 and vitamin E on skeletal muscle outcomes. However, the evidence rests primarily on a single meta-analysis whose conclusion has not been independently replicated.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderate grade reflects 10 human studies with only one meta-analysis synthesizing results; no independent replication of pooled conclusions exists. Verified sample sizes total ~470 participants across 4 studies, and heterogeneity in study design (ages, exercise protocols, outcome measures) limits confidence despite promising individual RCTs.

omega-3::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.evidence_base: The evidence base for omega-3 is predominantly human, with 52 human studies and 33 animal studies across all outcomes. Meta-analyses and systematic reviews dominate the literature for cardiovascular, cognition, and inflammation outcomes (4, 12, and 7 pooled analyses respectively), reflecting high confidence in those areas. Recent studies span 2014–2026, with most high-quality evidence published 2019 onward. The convergence of multiple independent meta-analyses on cardiovascular, cognitive, and inflammatory benefits provides unusually strong synthesis-level support.
omega-3::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.emerging_research: A 2026 scoping review examined omega-3 and adipose tissue inflammation specifically, suggesting refinement of understanding about peripheral versus central inflammatory effects. Recent work (2025–2026) increasingly explores dose-response relationships and domain-specific cognitive effects, as well as omega-3's role in exercise recovery and sports performance. Early evidence also explores interaction of omega-3 with other dietary components (e.g., resveratrol, probiotics) and with specific exercise protocols. These directions suggest the field is moving toward personalization and combination strategies, though the evidence remains preliminary.
omega-3::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.open_questions: Among the studies retrieved here, gut/digestion evidence remains sparse and non-pooled (6 human studies, smallest verified samples of ~81 total participants), and muscle growth evidence rests on a single meta-analysis without independent replication. Most abstracts do not report sample sizes, making true participant totals uncertain beyond verified counts. The retrieved studies are predominantly recent (2014–2026); whether longer-term effects (beyond 12 weeks in many trials) are sustained is not evident from the abstracts provided. Geographic and demographic representation in the retrieved studies—e.g., whether certain age groups, ethnic populations, or disease contexts are underrepresented—cannot be fully assessed from the data given.
omega-3::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.caveats: Omega-3 supplements vary widely in EPA/DHA content and purity; pharmaceutical-grade formulations (e.g., prescription icosapentaenoic acid) differ from dietary supplements in regulation and standardization. Omega-3 supplements can increase bleeding risk, particularly at high doses or in combination with anticoagulants; people on warfarin, aspirin, or other antiplatelet agents should consult a clinician before supplementing. Vegetarian and vegan omega-3 sources (alpha-linolenic acid from flax or chia) have lower bioavailability and require much larger doses to achieve equivalent EPA/DHA levels compared to fish oil or algae-derived products.

fish oil::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.what_it_is: Fish oil is a natural fat extracted from fatty fish tissues, rich in long-chain omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs), primarily eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA, C20H32O2) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA). It is available as liquid supplements, capsules, or as part of food-based formulations. Fish oil has been used for decades in both clinical and consumer health contexts.
fish oil::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.how_it_works: Fish oil's main bioactive components—EPA and DHA—integrate into cell membranes and influence multiple signaling pathways. They reduce production of pro-inflammatory molecules (particularly arachidonic acid–derived eicosanoids and cytokines like TNF-α and IL-6) by competing with arachidonic acid as a substrate and activating specialized pro-resolving mediators. EPA and DHA also modulate the vagus nerve and HPA (hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal) axis, which regulate stress and mood; activate G-protein–coupled receptors (GPR120) involved in immune tolerance; and support gut barrier integrity and microbial diversity. These mechanisms explain why fish oil has been studied across inflammatory, cardiovascular, mental health, and digestive domains.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Multiple independent meta-analyses and systematic reviews—including a 2022 meta-analysis on hemodialysis patients, a 2020 systematic review of 18 randomized trials in psoriasis, a 2023 network meta-analysis of parenteral omega-3 nutrition, and a 2021 review of multiple sclerosis—all converge on a consistent anti-inflammatory effect. A 2025 RCT in healthy volunteers found acute fish oil supplementation reduced muscle soreness and inflammation markers after eccentric exercise; a 2024 RCT showed combined fish oil and probiotics lowered serum inflammatory markers in adults with low-grade inflammation.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The evidence is graded Strong because four independent meta-analyses or systematic reviews all reach similar conclusions (strong consistency), and the evidence base includes 14 human studies alongside 14 animal studies. Although sample sizes are omitted from most abstracts, verified data across confirmed studies spans well over 247 participants, with adequately powered trials reported.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2019 systematic review on high-DHA fish oil health effects and a 2020 RCT examining fish oil combined with curcumin both assessed vascular and endothelial outcomes in older adults. A 2019 RCT in China found fish oil protective against cardiovascular stress from air pollution; a 2013 RCT (n=34) showed improved neurovascular reactivity to mental stress; and a 2007 RCT (n=26) in healthy volunteers demonstrated improved cardiovascular and endothelial function. A 2026 RCT examined fish oil effects on vascular biomarkers in middle-aged and older adults.
