taurine::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.open_questions: Among the studies retrieved here, the gut/digestion evidence rests almost entirely on observational associations with taurine-conjugated bile acids rather than supplementation trials, leaving a gap in direct intervention evidence for digestive outcomes. The cardiovascular outcome is notably under-represented in human trials (only 3 human studies) relative to animal work. For stress/anxiety, trial durations and populations are not consistently reported in the abstracts provided, making it unclear whether acute effects (e.g., energy drinks) versus chronic supplementation benefits are being measured. The retrieved records span mostly 2014–2026, so longer-term safety and efficacy data beyond a few years remain limited in this sample, though this is a snapshot of available abstracts only and does not characterize the full literature.
taurine::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.caveats: Taurine is generally well tolerated, but some individuals report gastrointestinal upset or headache with high oral doses (>3 g/day); those with kidney disease or on certain medications should consult a healthcare provider. Oral taurine bioavailability varies widely between individuals, and absorption may be reduced by concurrent medications or in older age. Injectable forms marketed as 'research peptides' lack FDA oversight and quality assurance; such products should be avoided outside clinical or regulated research settings.

algae oil::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.what_it_is: Algae oil is a plant-based source of omega-3 fatty acids, particularly docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), extracted from microalgae species. Unlike fish oil, which comes from fish that have accumulated DHA by consuming algae, algae oil provides DHA directly from the original source. It is typically sold as a liquid supplement or in capsule form and is commonly used by vegans, vegetarians, and those seeking sustainable alternatives to fish-derived omega-3s.
algae oil::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.how_it_works: Algae oil's primary active compound, docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), is a long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acid that integrates into cell membranes, particularly in the brain and cardiovascular system, where it influences membrane fluidity and cell signaling. DHA and other omega-3s are precursors to specialized lipid mediators (resolvins, protectins, and other eicosanoids) that help regulate inflammatory pathways and immune responses. In the cardiovascular system, DHA appears to reduce triglyceride levels and may support healthy HDL cholesterol by modulating how the liver processes lipids. Because DHA is incorporated into cell membranes throughout the body, it can affect signaling pathways involved in inflammation, oxidative stress, and cellular stress responses—mechanisms that would theoretically influence both cardiovascular and neurological health.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2012 meta-analysis of algal oil studies found that docosahexaenoic acid from algae reduces serum triglycerides and increases HDL cholesterol. More recent work includes a 2021 clinical trial examining docosahexaenoic acid as a nanoencapsulated therapy for atherosclerosis regression, and a 2026 secondary analysis of omega-3 supplementation in older adults that assessed lipid changes and inflammatory markers. Several animal studies also showed cardiovascular benefits from algae-based supplements mixed with other oils, though these cannot be directly translated to human outcomes.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The evidence rests on a small number of human trials (4 of 15 studies) and a single meta-analysis that has not yet been independently replicated. Sample sizes in most studies could not be verified from available abstracts, limiting confidence in the precision of the estimates. The consistency of findings across studies is plausible but not yet confirmed by independent replication.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2022 systematic review of 3,581 participants found that functional foods including algae oil modulate inflammation in chronic disease contexts. Human studies include a 2026 RCT on omega-3 supplementation that measured lipid mediators and inflammatory markers in older adults, a 2021 trial of docosahexaenoic acid-rich algae oil in breastfeeding mothers, and a 2016 study on docosahexaenoic acid supplementation and inflammation markers after eccentric exercise. The majority of the retrieved studies (18 of 25) were animal models, which showed promising anti-inflammatory effects but do not directly confirm human outcomes.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Human evidence is limited to 6 studies, with only 2 providing verified sample sizes (totaling ~3,581 participants in the systematic review). A single meta-analysis or systematic review exists but has not been independently replicated or verified in the literature provided. Most individual studies lack reported sample sizes in their abstracts, making it impossible to assess overall precision.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: All three retrieved studies on gut and digestion were conducted in animal models (fish and poultry), including a 2023 study on alternative ingredients in aquaculture feeds, a 2025 study on seaweed potential, and a 2024 study on fish oil replacement with alternative oils in poultry. None of these studies have been translated to human populations.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The evidence is entirely animal-based with no human studies identified in the retrieved records. Animal models do not reliably predict human gastrointestinal or digestive outcomes, so this evidence cannot support claims about human gut health or digestion.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2022 systematic review including 3,581 participants listed functional foods and algae oil in the context of modulating metabolism and stress-related outcomes in chronic disease. The human evidence base is extremely sparse—only one human study was identified in the retrieved records. The remaining 25 studies were animal models examining algae oil or related compounds in the context of cellular stress, neurological pathways, and oxidative stress (including studies from 2020, 2019, and 2018 examining algae oil's effects on retinal cells, folliculogenesis, and microbiota composition).
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The grade reflects a single human systematic review of 3,581 participants versus 25 animal studies, an imbalance that prevents firm conclusions about human stress and anxiety. There is no independent replication of human findings, and the single verified human study does not isolate algae oil's effect on stress or anxiety specifically. Animal studies, while numerous, do not translate reliably to human psychological outcomes.

algae oil::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.evidence_base: The evidence for algae oil is heavily weighted toward animal studies (37 of 59 total studies), with human evidence concentrated in a small number of trials and systematic reviews, most published in the last decade (2012–2026). The human studies focus primarily on cardiovascular lipid changes and inflammatory markers, with pregnancy/breastfeeding and exercise contexts represented. Most human abstracts lack complete sample size information, making it difficult to assess the true scale of the participant base beyond the ~3,581 verified in systematic reviews. This mixed evidence base—combined with inconsistency in replication—supports a 'Moderate' overall assessment but does not constitute strong or conclusive proof for any outcome.
algae oil::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.emerging_research: Recent work (2025–2026) has begun exploring novel delivery mechanisms for algae oil, including nanoencapsulation for targeted atherosclerosis therapy and emulsion-based formulations to improve bioavailability of DHA. A 2026 animal study examined algae oil-based emulsions in cancer models, and a 2020 study explored algae oil's effects on retinal ganglion cells via ERK signaling pathways, suggesting potential neuroprotective applications. These directions remain early-stage and are not yet established in human populations.
algae oil::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.open_questions: Among the studies retrieved here, human evidence is sparse for stress/anxiety (only 1 human study versus 25 animal studies) and absent entirely for gut and digestion outcomes (all 3 studies animal-only). The cardiovascular and inflammation evidence rests heavily on lipid and inflammatory marker measurements, but the retrieved records do not show longer-term trials (beyond 12 weeks in most cases) assessing hard clinical outcomes such as cardiovascular events or disease progression. Notably, the retrieved studies do not clearly show whether algae oil's effects differ meaningfully from fish oil or other omega-3 sources in human populations—a comparison that would strengthen claims about its unique value. This sample of ~40 abstracts per outcome does not represent the complete global literature; claims about what is or is not known overall in the field cannot be made from these records alone.
algae oil::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.caveats: Algae oil is generally well-tolerated, but high-dose omega-3 supplementation can increase bleeding risk in individuals on anticoagulant medications (e.g., warfarin) or antiplatelet agents; consult a healthcare provider before use if taking these drugs. Quality and DHA content vary significantly between commercial products—look for third-party testing (e.g., NSF, USP) to verify purity and label accuracy. Pregnant and breastfeeding women should consult their physician before supplementing, as the long-term safety profile at high doses in these populations is not fully established in the retrieved evidence.

selank::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.what_it_is: Selank is a synthetic heptapeptide (seven amino acids: Thr-Lys-Pro-Arg-Pro-Gly-Pro) with molecular formula C₃₃H₅₇N₁₁O₉ and molecular weight 751.9 Da. It is a synthetic analog of tuftsin, a naturally occurring immunomodulatory peptide fragment. Selank is administered by injection and is often encountered in research or clinical settings outside mainstream pharmaceutical markets.
selank::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.how_it_works: Selank is believed to act as an immunomodulator and neuromodulator, though its precise mechanism in humans is not fully established. Animal studies suggest it may influence neurotransmitter systems—particularly monoamines (dopamine, serotonin, norepinephrine) and opioid pathways—potentially via effects on brain catecholamine systems. It also appears to modulate cytokine expression and immune cell activity, consistent with its tuftsin-like structure. Why this might matter: if these pathways are involved in anxiety, cognition, mood, or immune response, then shifting their activity could theoretically affect those outcomes. However, animal findings do not reliably predict human effects, and direct evidence for a specific molecular target in humans is limited in the records provided.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Seven animal studies (2002–2017) show that selank reduced anxiety-like behaviors in rodent models of chronic mild stress and other stressors, and enhanced the effect of the anxiolytic diazepam in one 2017 study. These include behavioral measures in mice and rats, as well as investigations of opioid and monoamine systems. No human trials for anxiety are present in the records retrieved.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: All evidence is from animal models, which do not reliably translate to human anxiolytic effect. The studies are small and mechanistic, but offer no data on actual clinical anxiety in people. Therefore, selank's anxiety benefit remains unproven in humans.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: One human study (2025, n=168) in postoperative gastroduodenal perforation patients examined alanyl-glutamine and omega-3 PUFAs alongside other interventions, but selank's isolated contribution to inflammatory markers cannot be determined from the abstract alone. Four animal studies (2011–2021) found selank modulated expression of inflammation-related genes and cytokine levels under stress conditions in mouse spleen and other tissues.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The single human record does not isolate selank's effect, and most study abstracts did not report sample sizes, so precision is unconfirmed. Animal data support an inflammatory pathway, but human efficacy is not yet established.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Two human studies (2011, 2017) recorded EEG measures—long-distance gamma coherence and affective picture processing—but neither directly assessed cognitive performance, and selank's role is unclear from the abstracts. Four animal studies (1998–2019) found selank protected against cognitive impairment in rodent models of ethanol exposure, antenatal hypoxia, and catecholamine system damage; mechanisms included BDNF upregulation.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Sample sizes for human studies could not be verified, and the human data do not clearly measure cognition per se. Animal mechanistic findings are promising but do not establish that selank improves cognition in humans.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: One animal study (2008) examined selank in a genetic and induced depression model in rodents, finding effects on depression-like behavior. No human studies of selank and mood or depression appear in the records retrieved.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Evidence is limited to a single animal study with no human data. Animal models of depression do not reliably predict antidepressant efficacy in humans, so mood/depression benefit remains unproven in people.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: One human observational study (2008) in patients with anxiety-asthenic disorders reported immunomodulatory effects of selank, suggesting immune-enhancing properties in a clinical context. One animal study (2014) examined a related tripeptide fragment (Pro-Gly-Pro) on brain transcriptome in focal ischemia, providing mechanistic support for immune and neuroprotective pathways. The human record is limited and observational, without quantified sample size verification.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: A single human observational study provides real-world clinical data, elevating confidence above 'Preliminary,' but sample size could not be verified from the abstract, and no randomized or blinded trials are present. The grade reflects genuine human evidence with meaningful limitations in precision and study design.

selank::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.evidence_base: The evidence base is dominated by animal studies (12 of 15 records are animal or of unclear design), with only three human records across all outcomes combined. Most animal work is from the 2000s–2010s, with a few recent studies (2019–2025). The human evidence includes one observational clinical study (immune function), one EEG study (cognition), and one surgical intervention trial (inflammation) in which selank's isolated role is unclear. This imbalance—heavily weighted toward animals with sparse, non-interventional human data—means confidence in clinical benefit remains low; selank's properties in humans are largely inferred from mechanistic animal findings rather than demonstrated in controlled trials.
selank::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.emerging_research: Recent animal work (2019–2021) has focused on molecular mechanisms, including BDNF regulation in alcohol-induced cognitive damage and cytokine dynamics under psychosocial stress. A 2025 human study examined combined nutrient supplementation in a surgical population, suggesting emerging interest in multi-modal immune support postoperatively. However, these remain preliminary in humans; no large, recent clinical trials of selank monotherapy for any outcome are evident in the retrieved records.
selank::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.open_questions: Among the studies provided here, no human randomized controlled trials for anxiety, cognition, mood, or depression appear—all efficacy claims in those domains rest entirely on animal models. The single human immune function study is observational and lacks verified sample size details. None of the retrieved human studies explicitly report adverse effects, drug interactions, or longer-term safety data. It is important to note that these observations reflect only the ~40 abstracts per outcome retrieved for this review; they do not characterize the full scope of research on selank globally, and other human trials or safety data may exist in the literature not captured here.
selank::clarity-engine-v2::rich4.caveats: Selank is a research peptide and is not approved by major regulatory agencies (FDA, EMA) for clinical use in most countries; availability and purity vary, and it is often obtained through research-supply or international channels where quality control may be uncertain. As an injectable peptide, it carries risks of infection, allergic reaction, and injection-site complications. The human evidence base is too limited to establish safety in general populations, and interactions with medications (particularly psychotropic or immune-modulating drugs) are not documented in the records provided. Anyone considering use should consult a physician familiar with peptide therapeutics and recognize that efficacy claims remain largely unproven in humans.

mots-c::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::103122.what_it_is: MOTS-c is a 16-amino-acid peptide (molecular formula C₁₀₁H₁₅₂N₂₈O₂₂S₂, MW 2174.6) encoded by mitochondrial DNA and naturally produced within mitochondria—the energy-generating compartments of cells. It circulates in the bloodstream and can be administered as an injectable peptide. MOTS-c belongs to a family of 'mitokines'—signaling molecules released by mitochondria that affect cellular and systemic function.
mots-c::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::103122.how_it_works: MOTS-c acts as a mitochondrial-to-cell communication signal, activating the transcription factor Nrf2 (nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2), which controls cellular stress-defense and antioxidant gene programs. When mitochondria are stressed or dysfunctional—by aging, injury, or metabolic disease—MOTS-c levels may drop; exogenous MOTS-c restores this signaling, triggering the cell's protective machinery. This pathway is thought to reduce cellular apoptosis (programmed death), suppress inflammasome activation (a key driver of inflammatory signals), and enhance mitochondrial bioenergetics. In principle, restoring this mitochondrial crosstalk could benefit tissues with high energy demand or inflammatory burden, but human evidence is currently absent.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Three animal studies (2019–2024) in diabetic rats and D-galactose-treated mice showed that MOTS-c improved glucose-related measures and reduced inflammasome activation in pancreatic and systemic tissues. One 2026 study in a streptozotocin-induced diabetic rat model found MOTS-c suppressed systemic and cardiac inflammasome markers. However, no human trials have yet been conducted to determine whether these effects translate to people with diabetes or prediabetes.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: All evidence comes from animal models (rodents), which do not reliably predict human efficacy. The mechanism (Nrf2-mediated stress protection) is plausible but unproven in human glucose homeostasis.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2025 human study (unclassified design and sample size) examined MOTS-c in allergic asthma and found it attenuated airway barrier dysfunction by inhibiting epithelial apoptosis via Nrf2 activation. Additionally, 23 animal studies (mostly 2026, in rats and mice) demonstrated MOTS-c reduced inflammatory markers in diverse tissue injury models—including radiation-induced lung injury, cardiac ischemia-reperfusion, myocardial infarction, and brain injury. Study designs ranged from acute injury models to chronic inflammatory conditions.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only one human study is included in the retrieved records, with unverified sample size and design details limiting precision. The bulk of evidence is animal-based, and human data remain too sparse to establish efficacy in people.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A single 2026 animal study in a valproic acid-induced autism model in rats reported that MOTS-c showed therapeutic effects, with a putative mechanism involving tetrahydrobiopterin (a neurotransmitter cofactor) metabolism. No human trials on stress or anxiety have been published.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Evidence is limited to one animal model of neurodevelopmental stress; human translational data do not exist, making any claim about efficacy in human anxiety or stress speculative.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Nineteen animal studies (predominantly 2025–2026, in rats and mice) demonstrated MOTS-c protective effects in acute and chronic cardiovascular injury models: myocardial ischemia-reperfusion, cardiac ischemia, neonatal cardiac hyperoxia injury, and lung ischemia-reperfusion. Mechanisms involved mitochondrial bioenergetics preservation, inflammasome suppression, and Nrf2/KEAP1 pathway activation. All studies were conducted in rodent disease models; no human cardiovascular trials have been reported.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The entire body of evidence is animal-derived. While the mechanism is biochemically rational and consistent across models, animal ischemia-reperfusion and injury models have historically shown poor predictive value for human heart disease outcomes.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A single 2022 animal study (n=109, presumed mice or rats based on typical muscle-genetics designs) examined a K14Q polymorphism in the MOTS-c mitochondrial DNA sequence and found it was associated with differences in muscle fiber composition and muscular performance. This is an observational association study, not an intervention trial. No human endurance or exercise performance trials have been conducted.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only one animal association study exists in the retrieved records; it does not constitute proof of efficacy, and no human exercise intervention data are available.

mots-c::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::103122.evidence_base: The research on MOTS-c is dominated by very recent animal studies (predominantly 2025–2026), with only one human study retrieved (2025, in allergic asthma, with unverified sample details). Across outcomes, rodent models of acute injury (ischemia-reperfusion, radiation, hyperoxia) and chronic disease (diabetes, autism-like phenotype) predominate. The biochemical rationale—Nrf2-mediated mitochondrial signaling—is consistent across studies, but the field remains at the proof-of-concept stage in animals. No human efficacy or safety data of meaningful scale currently exist for any indication.
mots-c::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::103122.emerging_research: The most recent work (2025–2026) focuses on engineered variants (e.g., R13A-MOTS-c with enhanced cellular uptake via LAT1 transporters) and mechanism refinement, particularly the Nrf2/KEAP1 and MYH9 pathways in tissue-specific injury contexts. A handful of studies are beginning to examine MOTS-c in complex disease models (diabetes, autism spectrum phenotypes, neonatal lung disease) rather than simple acute injury. However, no human clinical trials have yet been registered or completed for any indication.
mots-c::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::103122.open_questions: Among the study records retrieved here, only one human study is present, making it impossible to characterize dose-response, safety, or efficacy in any human population. None of the retrieved animal studies appear to examine long-term dosing, tolerance, or systemic toxicity in detail. The single human study provides no information on optimal dose, treatment duration, or patient populations most likely to benefit. Because only ~40 abstracts per outcome were retrieved, I cannot state whether longer-term human trials exist elsewhere in the literature—only that they are not present in this sample.
mots-c::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::103122.caveats: MOTS-c is a research peptide and is not approved by the FDA or other regulatory bodies for human use; it is sold only as a research chemical. Because it is injectable and acts on fundamental cellular processes (mitochondrial signaling, inflammasome, Nrf2), safety must be carefully characterized in humans before any use—particularly regarding off-target immune effects, dose-limiting toxicity, and potential interactions with medications affecting mitochondrial function. Quality and purity of synthetic MOTS-c from commercial sources is unverified; contamination or misidentification could pose unknown risks.

creatine monohydrate::clarity-engine-v2:.what_it_is: Creatine monohydrate is a naturally occurring compound (C₄H₁₁N₃O₂·H₂O) synthesized in the body from amino acids and also found in meat and fish. It is the most common and studied form of supplemental creatine, taken orally as a powder or capsule. The body stores creatine mainly in muscle tissue, where it plays a central role in energy production during intense physical activity.
creatine monohydrate::clarity-engine-v2:.how_it_works: Creatine works by donating a high-energy phosphate group to adenosine diphosphate (ADP), rapidly regenerating adenosine triphosphate (ATP)—the cell's primary energy currency. This process is especially important during short bursts of intense effort, when ATP demand exceeds the speed at which normal aerobic metabolism can produce it. In the brain, creatine similarly supports ATP availability during periods of high cognitive demand, which is why supplementation may influence both muscle performance and mental function. The body maintains a creatine pool in muscle and other tissues; supplementation increases this pool, enhancing the capacity to rapidly regenerate ATP during repeated contractions or sustained mental effort.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Multiple randomized controlled trials and a 2019 systematic review demonstrate that creatine monohydrate supplementation increases muscle strength gains during resistance training. Studies include an 8-week progressive resistance training trial (2019) showing strength increases, a 2012 trial (n=12) measuring one-repetition maximum strength, and a 2010 trial (n=33) in ambulatory Duchenne muscular dystrophy patients. A 2022 randomized open-label study examined jump ability and strength combined with training, and a 2023 RCT measured strength alongside oxidative stress markers.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Ten human randomized trials and systematic reviews provide consistent evidence that creatine enhances strength during resistance training. However, only one meta-analysis/systematic review exists in the retrieved records and has not yet been independently replicated, which keeps the grade at Moderate rather than Strong.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Two recent systematic reviews (2024, n=492; 2026, n=1542) synthesize evidence on creatine and cognitive function in adults and older adults. Individual randomized trials include a 2025 study on creatine loading and cognitive function, a 2016 trial (n=52) measuring brain metabolic outcomes in women with depression, and a 2015 RCT examining cognitive performance during oxygen deprivation. Across studies, supplementation shows associations with improved cognition, though effect sizes and specific domains vary.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Ten human studies and one animal study were retrieved, including pooled analyses covering approximately 2,126 verified participants across five trials, but most abstracts omit sample sizes, making the true total larger but imprecise. Only 4 primary human randomized trials are clearly identified in the retrieved records, below the threshold for the highest tier. This inconsistency and limited number of foundational trials support a Moderate grade.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A single 2017 randomized controlled trial (n=18) examined creatine monohydrate as adjunctive therapy in patients with bipolar depression and found cognitive improvements. This is the only study addressing mood or depression in the retrieved records.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only one human study addresses this outcome with a small sample (~18 participants), and no independent replication exists. The lack of consistency and imprecision make this Emerging—promising but far from established in humans.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A single 2023 randomized controlled trial examined creatine monohydrate supplementation in female collegiate athletes and reported changes in body water and lean mass; stress or anxiety outcomes may have been measured but are not detailed in the retrieved abstract.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only one study addresses this outcome and sample sizes could not be verified from the abstract. There is no independent evidence or consistency, and minimal human data, placing this in the Emerging category.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A single 2009 randomized controlled trial (n=20) in college-aged males found that three weeks of creatine monohydrate supplementation affected the dihydrotestosterone-to-testosterone ratio. This is the only study on hormonal effects in the retrieved records.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only one small human trial (n=20) addresses hormonal outcomes, with no replication or consistency. The limited and preliminary nature of this evidence places it squarely in the Emerging tier.

creatine monohydrate::clarity-engine-v2:.evidence_base: The research base is dominated by human randomized controlled trials, particularly for muscle strength, where ten human studies form the foundation. Cognition is supported by two recent systematic reviews (2024, 2026) and multiple individual trials totaling over 1,500 verified participants across five studies, though most abstracts lack sample-size details. Studies on mood, stress/anxiety, and hormones rest on single trials with small samples and no replication. The literature is relatively recent (2009–2026), with most cognition and strength studies published in the last 5–10 years. This mix of robust evidence for strength and moderate evidence for cognition, but minimal data for other outcomes, reflects creatine's strongest use case in performance and emerging but unproven roles in mental health.
creatine monohydrate::clarity-engine-v2:.emerging_research: Recent trials (2024–2026) are expanding the study of creatine in aging and cognitive decline, with systematic reviews specifically examining older adults. A 2025 trial investigated creatine loading on sleep metrics alongside cognitive and physical outcomes, suggesting research interest in recovery and sleep quality. Additionally, mechanistic studies such as the 2016 trial using brain metabolic imaging (fMRI) are beginning to clarify how creatine affects neural function. These directions are early and have not yet established clinical utility beyond strength training, but they signal growing exploration of creatine's role in cognitive aging and sleep.
creatine monohydrate::clarity-engine-v2:.open_questions: Among the studies retrieved here, none of the cognition trials appear to extend beyond 12–24 weeks, leaving long-term effects on brain function unknown in the provided records. The mood, stress/anxiety, and hormone outcomes rest on single small trials with no apparent follow-up; we cannot assess whether these are isolated findings or represent reproducible effects. The retrieved strength studies focus primarily on younger and middle-aged populations during resistance training; the 2010 trial in Duchenne dystrophy is an exception, but broader evidence in elderly, sedentary, or disease populations is not visible in these records. Because you are seeing only a sample of the literature (~40 abstracts per outcome), you cannot conclude that these gaps represent the full state of the field—only that they are gaps in the studies provided here.
creatine monohydrate::clarity-engine-v2:.caveats: Creatine monohydrate is generally well tolerated, but users should ensure adequate hydration, as creatine increases intramuscular water retention. Individuals with kidney disease or on medications affecting renal function should consult a healthcare provider before use. Quality and purity vary by manufacturer; sourcing from third-party tested suppliers reduces risk of contaminants. Creatine is not an injectable peptide and requires no special medical administration, but consistent daily dosing (typically 3–5 g) is necessary to build tissue stores and see effects.

ginkgo biloba::clarity-engine-v2::rich4:.what_it_is: Ginkgo biloba is a tree native to China whose fan-shaped leaves contain a complex mixture of flavonoids, terpenoids (including ginkgolides and bilobalide), and organic acids. The extract is standardized to contain defined levels of these active constituents and is typically taken as a capsule, tablet, or liquid supplement. It is one of the oldest and most widely studied herbal medicines in clinical use.
ginkgo biloba::clarity-engine-v2::rich4:.how_it_works: Ginkgo's active compounds work through multiple overlapping mechanisms. The flavonoids and terpenoids are potent antioxidants that scavenge free radicals and reduce oxidative stress in tissues including the brain and blood vessels. Ginkgolides inhibit platelet-activating factor (PAF), a signaling molecule involved in inflammation, clotting, and immune responses. The extract also enhances blood flow by relaxing blood vessel walls and improving oxygen delivery to tissues. These combined effects—antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and vasodilatory—create the theoretical basis for benefits in cognitive, cardiovascular, and mood-related outcomes.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2015 meta-analysis (n=561) and a 2010 meta-analysis (n=2,372) of ginkgo biloba in cognitive impairment and dementia reported a pooled difference of approximately −2.86 points on cognitive scales (95% CI −3.18 to −2.54), suggesting modest improvement. However, these were systematic reviews and meta-analyses rather than primary trials, and the retrieved human evidence consisted only of 3 pooled analyses. Animal studies from 2024 and 2025 in rats showed positive effects on spatial memory and cognitive function in an Alzheimer's disease model.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The evidence is graded Moderate rather than Strong because the human evidence base rests entirely on meta-analyses (no primary human trials were retrieved), and the number of underlying primary studies was below the threshold for top-tier confidence. The pooled effect size is modest in magnitude, and human studies are substantially outnumbered by animal research.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2022 meta-analysis (n=104 verified participants) in humans found beneficial effects of ginkgo biloba leaf extract on inflammatory markers. The human evidence is limited to this single meta-analysis. Animal studies from 2022–2024 consistently demonstrated reductions in oxidative stress and inflammatory markers in models of hepatotoxicity, testicular toxicity, and vascular dysfunction.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Evidence is Moderate because human data consist of a single meta-analysis with modest verified sample size (~104 participants), and this finding has not been independently replicated or verified in the retrieved records. The conclusion cannot be rated higher without consistency across multiple independent human studies. Animal evidence is more abundant but does not replace human confirmation.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Two animal studies (2026 and 2015) examined ginkgo biloba extract in rats with behavioral stress or aging. The 2026 study reported mitigation of behavioral deficits, oxidative stress, and hippocampal remodeling in a stress model. The 2015 study found effects on cognitive function related to oxidative stress in aged female rats.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: This outcome is graded Preliminary because all evidence is animal-only; no human studies on stress or anxiety with ginkgo biloba were retrieved. Animal findings do not reliably predict human outcomes, and direct evidence in human subjects is needed before efficacy can be established.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2025 clinical trial examined ginkgo biloba extract's effect on macula and peripapillary perfusion using optical coherence tomography angiography, suggesting vascular effects on blood flow to the eye. Two animal studies (2025, 2019) reported antithrombotic effects and alleviation of viral myocarditis through mechanisms including S100A4 and MMP-3 suppression.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Evidence is Moderate because human evidence is limited to a single clinical trial with unverified sample size, preventing confident assessment of precision. The mechanism (vascular perfusion) is plausible and supported by animal data, but the small human evidence base and lack of clarity on sample size preclude a higher grade.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Three human studies—a pilot RCT (2006, multiple sclerosis), an RCT (2003, healthy elderly, n=34), and a clinical trial (2001, major depression with tricyclic antidepressant augmentation, n=16)—examined ginkgo biloba's effects on mood or mood-related measures. A 2012 animal study investigated bilobalide (a ginkgo constituent) on anxiety and hippocampal glucocorticoid receptors in rats.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Evidence is Moderate due to imprecision: fewer than 50 participants were verified across human trials, and sample sizes for 2 of 4 studies could not be confirmed. The effect estimates from small, heterogeneous trials (different populations: elderly, depressed, multiple sclerosis) are unstable and may not generalize broadly. More adequately powered and focused trials are needed.

ginkgo biloba::clarity-engine-v2::rich4:.evidence_base: The retrieved literature for ginkgo biloba is predominantly animal research (13 animal studies vs. 8 human studies overall), with human evidence concentrated in meta-analyses and small pilot or clinical trials rather than large randomized controlled trials. Studies are recent, spanning 2001–2026, with a cluster of publications from 2022 onward. The human evidence base is modest in size and often lacks fully reported sample sizes, limiting precision estimates. This mix of older small trials, recent animal work, and meta-analytic reviews suggests moderate confidence for some outcomes but highlights the need for larger, contemporary human trials.
ginkgo biloba::clarity-engine-v2::rich4:.emerging_research: Recent work (2024–2026) has focused on mechanistic studies in animal models, examining ginkgo's effects on specific pathways implicated in aging and neurodegeneration (e.g., oxidative stress markers, hippocampal remodeling, vascular dysfunction). A 2025 clinical trial on vascular perfusion and a 2026 stress study in rats suggest continued interest in refining how ginkgo affects blood flow and stress resilience. However, these emerging studies remain preliminary in humans and require replication.
ginkgo biloba::clarity-engine-v2::rich4:.open_questions: Among the studies retrieved here, no human trials followed participants beyond 12 weeks, leaving long-term safety and efficacy unclear. Human evidence for stress/anxiety is entirely absent from the retrieved records, while cardiovascular and depression studies include only small, heterogeneous trials with different patient populations (elderly, depressed, those with multiple sclerosis), making it difficult to assess generalizability. The retrieved meta-analyses do not consistently report individual trial characteristics or effect heterogeneity, limiting visibility into which subgroups or dosing regimens drive benefits. Since this represents a sample of ~40 abstracts per outcome, important trials may exist in the broader literature that are not represented here.
ginkgo biloba::clarity-engine-v2::rich4:.caveats: Ginkgo biloba is widely available but quality and standardization vary considerably across commercial products; look for extracts standardized to 24% ginkgo flavones and 6% terpene lactones. The herb can increase bleeding risk, especially when combined with anticoagulants (warfarin) or antiplatelet drugs (aspirin, clopidogrel); consult a physician if taking these medications. People with known ginkgo allergies or those undergoing surgery should avoid use or discuss with their healthcare provider. Ginkgo is not a substitute for proven treatments of cognitive decline, cardiovascular disease, or depression.

creatine monohydrate::clarity-engine-v2:.what_it_is: Creatine monohydrate (C₄H₁₁N₃O₃) is a naturally occurring compound found mainly in muscle tissue and synthesized in the liver and kidneys from three amino acids. It is sold as a white crystalline powder that mixes in water, and is one of the most researched and widely used supplements in sports nutrition and cognitive health. The body uses creatine to rapidly regenerate ATP (adenosine triphosphate), the primary energy currency of cells, particularly during intense or repeated muscle contractions and high mental demand.
creatine monohydrate::clarity-engine-v2:.how_it_works: Creatine enters muscle and brain cells and is phosphorylated to form creatine phosphate (PCr), which donates a high-energy phosphate group to regenerate ATP during the first ~10 seconds of intense activity or cognitive effort. This process is particularly important in tissues with high, rapid energy demand—skeletal muscle during resistance training and the brain during sustained mental work. By expanding the muscle and brain's ATP buffer, creatine supplementation allows muscles to sustain force longer and neurons to maintain performance under fatigue or stress. Creatine also appears to enhance water retention in muscle cells, which may promote protein synthesis and lean tissue growth, and has been shown to influence energy metabolism in mitochondria and modulate neurotransmitter and antioxidant systems in the brain. The mechanisms underlying its cognitive effects are not yet fully mapped but likely involve improved cellular energy availability and possible neuroprotective pathways.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Multiple systematic reviews and randomized controlled trials (2019–2025) show that creatine monohydrate supplementation enhances muscle strength and lean mass gains, particularly when combined with resistance training. A 2020 systematic review examined additive effects in aging populations, while a 2025 RCT specifically found short-term creatine supplementation enhanced strength and accelerated recovery in resistance training. Studies have also evaluated creatine combined with HMB and in postmenopausal women, indicating benefit across diverse populations.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Twenty-two human studies and no animal studies support this outcome. However, most abstracts omit sample size, meaning the true total participant count is larger than the ~133 verified across just 5 studies. Multiple independent systematic reviews exist but no formal pooled meta-analysis confirms they agree, so the grade reflects adequate human evidence with some inconsistency in reporting.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Five independent systematic reviews and meta-analyses (2020–2026) converge on cognitive benefit from creatine supplementation. A 2023 meta-analysis examined memory in healthy individuals; a 2026 systematic review analyzed cognition in older adults (n=1542); and a 2024 systematic review assessed cognitive function in adults generally (n=492). A 2026 RCT found that even a single dose of creatine reduced cognitive deterioration induced by sleep deprivation, demonstrating acute effects. The evidence base includes ~2213 verified participants across 8 of 22 studies, with 21 human and only 1 animal study.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: This outcome earned Strong because five independent meta-analyses or systematic reviews converge on the finding, indicating replicated synthesis and consistency across multiple research groups. The verified sample is substantial (~2213 participants), and the weight of human evidence is overwhelming. The evidence is recent (2020–2026) and represents adequately powered synthesis of the literature.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: One small randomized controlled trial (2017, n=18) in patients with bipolar depression found cognitive effects of creatine as adjunctive therapy. Two animal studies (2010, 2012) in rodents reported sex-specific antidepressant-like effects of dietary creatine, with and without fluoxetine co-administration.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only one human study with a very small sample (~18 participants) directly addressed mood/depression, making precision imprecise and unstable. Two animal models exist but do not translate directly to human psychiatric benefit. This outcome lacks the human evidence base needed for higher certainty and remains preliminary.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A single 2023 randomized controlled trial examined creatine monohydrate supplementation in female collegiate athletes, reporting changes in total body water and DXA lean mass estimates. The study's abstract did not clearly delineate stress or anxiety as a primary outcome measure.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only one human study addresses this outcome, precluding any assessment of consistency or replication. Sample size could not be verified from the available abstract. Evidence is too sparse and unconfirmed to support any claim of efficacy for stress or anxiety.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Six randomized controlled trials spanning 2001–2025 examined hormonal effects of creatine supplementation. A 2009 RCT (n=20) found effects on the dihydrotestosterone-to-testosterone ratio in college-aged participants; a 2004 RCT (n=17) assessed hormonal response to short-term supplementation and resistance training; a 2003 study (n=28) examined health indices with HMB/creatine combinations; and a 2001 RCT found short-term creatine did not alter the hormonal response to resistance training. A 2025 trial investigated whether creatine causes hair loss (a concern related to DHT).
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Six human studies provide a modest evidence base, but verified sample size is small (~75 participants across 4 studies), making effect estimates potentially unstable. Results are mixed—some studies show changes in DHT/testosterone ratios, while others show no hormonal effect—and no meta-analysis has been provided to synthesize these findings. The grade reflects adequate human research with uncertainty about true magnitude of effect.

creatine monohydrate::clarity-engine-v2:.evidence_base: The research on creatine monohydrate is predominantly human-based and extensive, with 21–22 human studies per outcome and minimal animal work. The literature is recent (2001–2026), dominated by randomized controlled trials and systematic reviews/meta-analyses, particularly for cognition (5 independent meta-analyses converge) and muscle strength (multiple systematic reviews). Verified participant counts are substantial for cognition (~2213) but more modest for other outcomes. The consistency and recency of evidence, especially multiple converging meta-analyses for cognition, provide high confidence for that outcome; muscle strength has good human support but less formal synthesis; and mood, anxiety, and hormones rest on fewer and smaller trials.
creatine monohydrate::clarity-engine-v2:.emerging_research: Recent 2025–2026 studies have begun examining creatine in specific populations (postmenopausal women, older adults, female athletes) and contexts (sleep deprivation, hair loss concerns, combination therapies with HMB). A 2026 systematic review explicitly synthesized creatine and cognition in aging, and acute-dose studies (e.g., single-dose cognition trial) suggest creatine may work rapidly, not only through chronic loading. These directions are early but reflect growing interest in creatine beyond bodybuilding contexts.
creatine monohydrate::clarity-engine-v2:.open_questions: Among the retrieved studies, cognition is well-powered with multiple large trials and meta-analyses, but most other outcomes rely on smaller, fewer trials—particularly mood/depression (1 human trial, n=18) and stress/anxiety (1 trial, sample unconfirmed). Sample sizes are omitted from most abstracts, so true participant totals are likely larger than verified but remain unknown. Notably, the records provided do not indicate whether long-term (>12 weeks) safety or efficacy studies exist for any outcome, nor do they clarify whether results generalize across young, middle-aged, and older populations—these gaps reflect what is absent from the sample of abstracts retrieved here, not necessarily what is absent from the full literature.
creatine monohydrate::clarity-engine-v2:.caveats: Creatine monohydrate is generally well-tolerated and has no established serious toxicity at standard doses (~3–5 g/day), but it causes weight gain through water retention in muscle and may elevate creatinine levels (a standard kidney-function marker) without indicating kidney damage. People with pre-existing kidney disease should consult a healthcare provider before supplementing. Quality varies; pharmaceutical-grade creatine (e.g., Creapure) is more consistent than generic powder. The 2017 mood trial reporting adjunctive benefit in bipolar depression was small (n=18); replication in larger cohorts is needed before clinical recommendation.

beta-alanine::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::.what_it_is: Beta-alanine is a non-essential amino acid with the chemical formula C₃H₇NO₂ (3-aminopropanoic acid). It is naturally produced in the body and also found in foods like poultry and beef. Most people use it as an oral supplement in powder or capsule form, typically taken in divided doses throughout the day.
beta-alanine::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::.how_it_works: Beta-alanine works primarily by serving as a precursor to carnosine, a dipeptide (two-amino-acid compound) found in muscle tissue. When you supplement beta-alanine, your body combines it with the amino acid histidine to synthesize carnosine. Carnosine acts as a buffer, helping neutralize lactic acid and hydrogen ions that accumulate during intense exercise, which can otherwise cause muscle fatigue and the 'burn' sensation. This buffering capacity may support sustained high-intensity work and influence metabolic processes related to blood sugar regulation, though the exact mechanisms in these contexts remain incompletely understood.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2025 systematic review synthesizing data from 377 participants found that beta-alanine (or carnosine) supplementation showed a benefit for blood sugar control in individuals with prediabetes or type 2 diabetes mellitus. This conclusion is supported by at least two randomized controlled trials: a 2015 study (n=11) examining 28 days of supplementation alongside high-intensity cycling, and a 2013 trial (n=16) in rowers, both of which measured blood sugar or related markers alongside performance measures.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The evidence is graded Moderate because only a single meta-analysis/systematic review exists and its conclusion has not yet been independently replicated or verified in other published meta-analyses. While the 2025 review synthesizes multiple human trials, the limited replication of this overall finding means confidence remains moderate rather than strong.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Two animal studies were retrieved: a 2025 study examining serum metabolomic shifts in response to altitude exposure, and a 1986 study investigating the effects of carnosine and beta-alanine on wound healing. Neither study provided human evidence, and the mechanisms by which beta-alanine might influence inflammation in people remain unestablished in the records provided.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: This outcome is graded Preliminary because all available evidence is from animal models, which do not reliably translate to human physiology and disease. No human studies of beta-alanine and inflammation were found in the retrieved records, making any claim of human efficacy unwarranted at this stage.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Three human randomized controlled trials were retrieved: a 2025 study showing that beta-alanine improved time to exhaustion but not aerobic capacity in competitive middle-distance runners; a 2025 study examining effects on intraocular and ocular perfusion pressure; and a 2010 trial (n=19) investigating six weeks of high-intensity interval training with and without beta-alanine supplementation for cardiovascular improvements. The animal studies (2025, 2010, 2008) examined metabolic markers, mitochondrial function, and oxidative stress in cardiac tissue, but did not establish clear cardiovascular benefit.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Despite seven studies (three human, four animal) addressing cardiovascular outcomes, the evidence as a whole does not support a clear benefit. The human evidence is limited by modest sample size in one key trial (n=19), and the findings are inconsistent or show improvements in performance metrics (time to exhaustion) without corresponding gains in aerobic capacity or clear heart-health markers. This pattern—well-studied but without clear clinical benefit—earns the 'no clear benefit' designation.

beta-alanine::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::.evidence_base: The research on beta-alanine is predominantly human-based for the outcomes with any evidence at all (blood sugar and cardiovascular), though sample sizes in individual trials tend to be small (ranging from 11 to 19 participants in the RCTs retrieved). Most studies are fairly recent (2010–2025), reflecting growing interest in the supplement's metabolic effects. The inflammation outcome relies entirely on animal models from 1986 and 2025, which cannot be assumed to translate to human physiology. Overall, the evidence base is modest in scope: you are seeing only a sample of the full literature (~40 abstracts per outcome), so these records do not represent a complete picture of all research on beta-alanine globally.
beta-alanine::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::.emerging_research: Recent 2025 studies are beginning to investigate beta-alanine's effects in new contexts—including its impact on intraocular pressure, metabolic responses to altitude exposure, and its combination with other supplements like caffeine. A 2025 systematic review on carnosine/beta-alanine and diabetes control suggests growing clinical interest in the compound's potential role in glycemic management, though the field is still working to establish and replicate such claims independently. These directions are early and require further human trials to clarify efficacy.
beta-alanine::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::.open_questions: Among the studies retrieved here, the blood sugar evidence consists of relatively small trials (11–16 participants in individual RCTs) and relies on a single meta-analysis; longer-term and larger trials would strengthen confidence in this outcome. The cardiovascular research includes one trial with notably modest sample size (n=19), limiting the precision of its effect estimates. The inflammation outcome has no human studies in the records provided, making it impossible to assess whether animal findings translate to humans. Because these are only a sample of available literature, I cannot comment on what research may exist elsewhere in the broader field, but within these retrieved records, human evidence is limited and often short-term.
beta-alanine::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::.caveats: Beta-alanine is generally well tolerated, but some people experience transient paresthesia (tingling in the skin), particularly at higher doses—this is harmless but noticeable. Quality and purity of supplements can vary; third-party testing is advisable. While beta-alanine has no major drug interactions, individuals with kidney disease should consult a healthcare provider before supplementing, as the kidneys help eliminate metabolic byproducts. The evidence for blood sugar control is moderate and not yet independently verified, so it should not be relied upon as a primary treatment for diabetes or prediabetes.

caffeine::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::c368.what_it_is: Caffeine (1,3,7-trimethylpurine-2,6-dione; molecular formula C8H10N4O2) is a naturally occurring alkaloid found in coffee beans, tea leaves, cacao, and guarana. It is a methylxanthine—a small molecule that crosses the blood-brain barrier easily. Most people consume it orally as a beverage, tablet, or capsule, and it reaches peak blood levels within 30–60 minutes.
caffeine::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::c368.how_it_works: Caffeine works primarily by blocking adenosine receptors in the brain and body. Adenosine is a neurotransmitter that accumulates during waking hours and signals fatigue; by occupying adenosine receptors, caffeine prevents this 'sleep signal' from being received, creating the sensation of alertness and reduced tiredness. It also increases the release of dopamine and noradrenaline, neurotransmitters involved in attention, motivation, and arousal. Additionally, caffeine enhances calcium release in muscle cells, which can improve muscle contraction force and endurance during exercise. These effects on the central and peripheral nervous systems explain why caffeine influences cognition, mood, physical performance, and cardiovascular function.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2021 meta-analysis and systematic review of caffeine and cognitive functions in sports summarized findings across multiple trials. Several randomized controlled trials—including a 2010 study (n=44) and a 2008 study (n=27)—demonstrated that caffeine, particularly when combined with L-theanine, improved cognitive performance and subjective alertness. A 2025 RCT examined caffeine combined with taurine in a hypoxic setting, and a 1995 RCT looked at caffeine effects on cognition and mood without abstinence periods. A 2022 study showed that expectation of having consumed caffeine also modified cognitive outcomes in college students.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The evidence is graded Moderate rather than Strong because although 10 human trials exist, they rest on a single meta-analysis whose conclusions have not yet been independently replicated or verified in a separate pooled analysis. This consistency limitation prevents a higher grade despite reasonable sample sizes in individual RCTs.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Multiple meta-analyses spanning 2010 to 2024 examined caffeine's effects on muscle strength and endurance. A 2024 meta-analysis reviewed acute caffeine capsule ingestion on muscle strength and endurance; a 2021 meta-analysis synthesized effects on muscle endurance, maximum strength, and perceived exertion in adults; a 2020 umbrella review covered 21 publications on caffeine supplementation and exercise performance. A 2010 meta-analysis (n=27 studies) specifically analyzed caffeine ingestion on muscular strength and endurance. A 2026 RCT indicated that caffeine increased muscle strength but not endurance, and suggested that expectation also plays a role.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Although 15 human studies exist across multiple meta-analyses, the evidence is held at Moderate due to inconsistency: several meta-analyses have been published, but their conclusions have not been pooled into a single agreed-upon systematic review. This inconsistency across reviews, pending full reconciliation, prevents upgrading to Strong despite a large body of human research.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2025 systematic review (n=597) examined energy drinks (which contain caffeine) on the cardiovascular system. A 2021 RCT (n=30) found that caffeine slowed heart rate autonomic recovery following strength exercise in healthy subjects. Historical studies including a 2003 RCT examined caffeine and noradrenaline effects on cardiovascular function; a 1993 RCT (n=10) studied the cardiovascular interaction between caffeine and nicotine. A 2022 observational study (n=84) looked at caffeine and caffeine cessation on cerebrovascular reactivity in migraine patients. A 2007 RCT investigated maternal caffeine consumption and risk of cardiovascular malformations.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: This outcome is graded 'Well studied—no clear benefit' rather than 'Moderate benefit' because the retrieved records do not show consistent beneficial cardiovascular effects. While 9 human and 3 animal studies exist, sample sizes are often unreported in abstracts (~721 participants confirmed across 4 of 12 studies), and a single meta-analysis conclusion lacks independent replication. The pattern suggests cardiovascular function is affected (heart rate changes, autonomic effects), but no clear harm or benefit emerges across trials.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2011 RCT (n=88) found that expectation of having consumed caffeine improved mood and performance. A 2019 RCT addressed the timing of caffeine intake, noting that resetting late sleep timing had positive mental health impacts. A 2000 clinical trial examined nicotine and caffeine separately and combined on mood and EEG measures. Observational studies including a 2023 cross-sectional analysis examined the association between caffeine intake and depression in a national sample, and a 2021 observational study (n=206) looked at caffeine consumption and behavioral symptoms in nursing home residents. A 2025 unclassified study found caffeine intake mediated the relationship between problematic overstudying and psychological distress.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Evidence is Moderate because 13 human trials exist but rest on a single meta-analysis or systematic review conclusion that has not been independently replicated. Sample sizes are documented for only 5 of 17 studies (~858 participants), and the broader population represented remains incomplete. Mood effects appear real but moderate in magnitude, and individual differences (e.g., expectation effects) influence outcomes substantially.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2022 RCT (n=100) examined stress, caffeine, and psychosis-like experiences in a double-blind, placebo-controlled design. A 2025 RCT (n=20) studied caffeine and CBD co-administration on THC subjective effects. A 2025 RCT examined caffeine and L-theanine's performance-enhancing effects in Iranian elite wrestlers, including cognitive and anxiety measures. Cross-sectional studies including a 2026 unclassified study (n=38) and a 2023 unclassified study examined associations between caffeine consumption and anxiety/stress levels in student populations. A 2025 unclassified study found caffeine intake mediated stress and psychological distress outcomes.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Evidence is Moderate rather than Strong: 10 human trials exist, but they rely on a single meta-analysis or systematic review conclusion without independent replication. Sample sizes are documented for only 5 of 16 studies (~443 participants), and most are short-term designs. Caffeine's effects on stress and anxiety appear dose- and individual-dependent (some show increases, some decreases), making a consistent benefit claim difficult.

caffeine::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::c368.evidence_base: The research on caffeine is predominantly human-based, with 10–15 human trials per outcome and 1–6 animal studies. Meta-analyses and systematic reviews dominate the higher-quality evidence for cognition, muscle strength, and cardiovascular outcomes (spanning 2007–2025), while mood and anxiety evidence includes a mix of RCTs, observational studies, and unclassified designs. Across outcomes, sample sizes in individual trials range from small (n=10–27) to moderate (n=88–206), though many abstracts omit sample size, obscuring the true sample. The research is recent (heavy emphasis 2019–2026), indicating active investigation, but single meta-analyses without independent replication limit confidence in several domains.
caffeine::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::c368.emerging_research: Recent trials (2025–2026) explore caffeine combined with other compounds—L-theanine for cognition and anxiety, taurine for cognitive resilience in hypoxia, and CBD for modulating THC effects—suggesting a shift toward synergistic formulations rather than caffeine alone. Expectation and timing effects are receiving new attention: studies document that belief about caffeine consumption and circadian timing of intake both modify outcomes, hinting at stronger placebo and chronobiology angles than older literature emphasized. A 2026 RCT distinguishing caffeine's effect on strength versus endurance adds mechanistic nuance to performance claims.
caffeine::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::c368.open_questions: Among the studies retrieved here, cardiovascular and mood/anxiety outcomes show relatively sparse sample-size reporting (only ~4–5 of 12–17 studies provided n values), making it unclear whether apparent effects are supported by adequate participant numbers. No studies among those provided followed participants beyond 12 weeks of regular caffeine use, so long-term tolerability, dependence, or efficacy erosion is not addressed in these records. Most cognition and muscle-strength trials employed acute caffeine dosing or short interventions; the retrieved records do not include robust chronic-use designs. Specific populations (e.g., children, pregnant individuals, those with anxiety disorders) appear sporadically; the breadth of applicability across demographics is not fully visible here.
caffeine::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::c368.caveats: Caffeine is a central nervous system stimulant; excessive intake can trigger anxiety, sleep disruption, and dependence. Individuals with panic disorder, uncontrolled hypertension, arrhythmias, or caffeine sensitivity should be cautious and consult a healthcare provider. Caffeine interacts with certain medications (e.g., some antidepressants, fluvoxamine) and pregnancy guidelines recommend limitation, given observational data on cardiovascular developmental risks. Quality varies by source: commercial supplements may contain variable caffeine amounts or contaminants, so standardized, third-party-tested products are preferable.

whey protein::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::.what_it_is: Whey protein is a complete protein derived from milk during cheese production, containing all nine essential amino acids. It is typically sold as a powder (concentrate, isolate, or hydrolysate form) mixed into beverages or food. Whey makes up about 20% of milk protein; the remainder is casein. People consume it primarily as a supplement to support muscle recovery and body composition.
whey protein::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::.how_it_works: Whey protein is rapidly absorbed in the small intestine and delivers amino acids—especially branched-chain amino acids (leucine, isoleucine, valine)—that stimulate muscle protein synthesis, the process by which the body builds and repairs muscle fibers. Leucine in particular activates mTOR, a key signaling pathway that drives muscle growth when combined with resistance exercise. Whey also contains bioactive compounds including lactoferrin and immunoglobulins that may support immune function and gut health. High protein intake increases satiety (fullness signals) and thermogenesis (calories burned during digestion), which can support weight loss when combined with calorie restriction or exercise.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Four meta-analyses and systematic reviews (2014–2026), involving hundreds of randomized controlled trials in overweight and obese adults, consistently show that whey protein supplementation combined with resistance exercise or energy-restricted diets reduces body fat and improves body composition. A 2014 meta-analysis of 626 participants and a 2022 review of postmenopausal women both found significant improvements in fat loss and lean mass retention. Recent 2026 systematic reviews confirm efficacy in weight loss interventions and in patients with metabolic disease.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Strong grade reflects convergence across four independent meta-analyses or systematic reviews with adequate sample sizes (hundreds to thousands of participants across pooled trials) and human-only evidence. The consistency across multiple syntheses and real-world populations (obese, postmenopausal, metabolic disease) provides robust confidence in the effect.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2024 meta-analysis of 1,154 participants in randomized controlled trials found whey protein effective for improving sarcopenia (age-related muscle loss) in older adults. A 2024 systematic review of 424 adults with type 2 diabetes showed positive effects on muscle mass. Recent RCTs (2025–2026) in healthy older adults, pre-menopausal women, and other populations demonstrate improvements in muscle strength and body composition, though one 2020 RCT found no significant difference between whey and soy protein.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderate reflects 13 human studies (8 primary trials plus 2 pooled analyses), which is below the threshold for the top tier, though the meta-analyses show consistent benefit. Sample sizes were verifiable for only some trials, leaving some imprecision in overall effect estimates. The evidence is solid but not yet at the density or consistency of the weight loss outcome.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2022 meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials found whey protein supplementation improves postprandial blood glucose (blood sugar after meals) in people with type 2 diabetes. Individual RCTs (2014–2021) with sample sizes ranging from 24 to 73 participants show whey protein lowers blood glucose spikes, improves insulin sensitivity, and modulates hormones involved in glucose control (GLP-1, GIP, glucagon). Effects are most evident when whey is consumed with meals or after exercise.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderate grade is assigned because only one meta-analysis / systematic review exists, and its conclusion has not been independently replicated in the study records retrieved. Although 15 human studies are present, most abstracts omitted sample sizes, so true precision across the body of evidence is uncertain. The 179 participants verified across 6 studies show measurable effects, but the evidence base is not yet as deeply synthesized as for weight loss.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Two randomized controlled trials in humans (2026, 2018) with verified sample sizes totaling approximately 57 participants found that whey protein supplementation improves glutathione levels (a key antioxidant), enhances immune markers, and supports pulmonary immune response in cancer patients and other populations. Animal studies (2016, 2020) similarly showed enhanced lymphocyte function and immunomodulatory effects in mice and other models.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderate grade reflects modest sample sizes (57 participants across 2 verified human studies), which create imprecision and may lead to unstable effect estimates. Although the direction of effect is consistent across human trials, the small sample sizes and limited number of independent human studies prevent a higher tier. Animal evidence supports plausibility but cannot confirm efficacy in humans.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A single 2026 human study examined effects of whey protein isolate on gut microbiota and intestinal function in older adults. Four animal studies (1996–2025) explored whey protein's effects on gut bacteria, antioxidant capacity, and microencapsulation strategies with fructooligosaccharides or anthocyanins. In vitro digestion studies (2022) modeled how whey protein behaves during gastrointestinal processing.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Preliminary grade is assigned because only one human study is available, and sample sizes could not be verified from abstracts, leaving certainty unconfirmed. The bulk of evidence comes from animal models or in vitro systems, which cannot directly establish effects in humans. This outcome requires further human research to move beyond preliminary status.

whey protein::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::.evidence_base: The evidence base for whey protein is predominantly human and dominated by randomized controlled trials and meta-analyses, especially for weight loss and muscle growth—outcomes studied since the 2010s with increasing rigor. Over 40 human studies span 1996–2026, with major meta-analyses published 2014–2026 showing convergence on weight/fat loss and muscle outcomes. Blood sugar and immune function rest on smaller human samples but are supported by animal and mechanistic work. Gut/digestion evidence is thin in humans (1 trial) but has animal backing. Overall, confidence is high for weight loss, solid for muscle growth and blood sugar, moderate for immune function, and preliminary for gut health.
whey protein::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::.emerging_research: Recent work (2025–2026) is exploring whey protein's role in preventing sarcopenia in older adults and in metabolic disease (type 2 diabetes, metabolic-associated fatty liver disease), with promising results in RCTs. Novel formulations—such as whey-inulin conjugates and microencapsulated versions with polyphenols—are being tested for enhanced antioxidant and prebiotic effects in animal models. Mechanistic studies are examining whey's effects on hormones (IGF-1, GLP-1) and mitochondrial function in muscle, suggesting avenues for optimizing dosing and timing.
whey protein::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::.open_questions: Among the studies retrieved here, gut/digestion evidence rests on only one human trial, making it impossible to draw firm conclusions about efficacy in diverse populations. For muscle growth and blood sugar, most retrieved trials are relatively short-term (weeks to a few months); studies following participants beyond 12 weeks are sparse in the provided records, so durability of benefits is unclear. Additionally, the retrieved muscle growth studies do not clearly distinguish effects in very young, very old, or disease-specific populations—populations that may respond differently. Note: this assessment reflects only the ~40 abstracts per outcome provided to this analysis; broader gaps in the global literature cannot be inferred from these records alone.
whey protein::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::.caveats: Whey protein is generally well-tolerated, but people with lactose intolerance or milk allergy should avoid it or use lactose-free isolates. Quality varies by manufacturer; third-party testing for contaminants and label accuracy is advisable. Whey may interact with certain medications (e.g., bisphosphonates for bone health); individuals on medications should consult a healthcare provider. Efficacy for muscle growth and weight loss depends on adequate total protein intake, resistance exercise, and calorie management—whey alone is not a substitute for these lifestyle factors.

citrulline malate::clarity-engine-v2::ri.what_it_is: Citrulline malate (C₁₀H₁₉N₃O₈) is a compound combining the amino acid L-citrulline with malic acid (malate). L-citrulline is a non-essential amino acid found naturally in watermelons and synthesized in the body; the malate salt form is marketed as a supplement, often under the brand name Stimol. It is typically taken orally in powder or capsule form, usually 6–8 grams per dose before or around workouts.
citrulline malate::clarity-engine-v2::ri.how_it_works: Citrulline is a precursor in the nitric oxide (NO) synthesis pathway. Once ingested, it is converted to arginine in the kidneys and other tissues, which then serves as substrate for nitric oxide synthase to produce NO — a signaling molecule that relaxes blood vessel walls and improves vascular blood flow. Better blood flow can theoretically enhance oxygen and nutrient delivery to muscles during exercise, reduce fatigue-inducing metabolic byproducts like lactate, and support recovery. Malate, a component of the citric acid cycle (energy metabolism), may also play a minor role in energy production during high-intensity effort.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Fifteen human randomized trials and systematic reviews have examined citrulline malate's effect on strength performance in resistance-trained and recreational populations, including a 2021 meta-analysis pooling 137 verified participants and a 2025 RCT measuring changes over six weeks. Studies tested both acute and chronic dosing protocols, measuring outcomes such as repetition performance and total work in weightlifting tasks. Overall, the published record shows inconsistent results — some trials report small improvements in volume or work capacity, while others report no significant benefit.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Despite 15 human studies, the evidence is graded 'no clear benefit' because meta-analyses have not confirmed consistent agreement across trials, and the body of literature shows mixed outcomes. Most abstracts lack reported sample sizes, so the true total sample is substantially larger than the 137 verified, but this imprecision and inconsistency across studies prevent a higher grade.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Five human RCTs, spanning 2010 to 2024, tested citrulline malate on cardiovascular outcomes including blood pressure, blood flow, and performance in CrossFit and resistance exercise. Two studies verified approximately 40 total participants. Trials examined acute and chronic supplementation effects on vascular function and exercise-induced cardiovascular responses.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Although five human studies exist, they represent a modest and imprecise evidence base (only ~40 participants verified across 2 studies), and results do not show consistent cardiovascular benefit. The small and unstable effect estimates prevent confidence in a clear clinical benefit.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Nine human studies — including two meta-analyses and six primary trials — evaluated citrulline malate on endurance outcomes such as aerobic cycling performance and submaximal weightlifting capacity. Three studies verified approximately 158 participants; others lacked reported sample sizes. A 2021 meta-analysis pooled 137 participants, while more recent systematic reviews (2026) summarized the acute and chronic effects. Results show mixed findings: some trials report improvements in lower-limb function and exercise repetitions, while others (e.g., 2021 aerobic cycling trial) found no effect during aerobic tasks.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The grade 'Moderate' reflects that nine human studies exist with some supportive findings in submaximal and resistance-endurance tasks, but the evidence base falls short of top-tier confidence due to limited primary evidence (6 primary trials and 2 analyses retrieved), modest precision (~158 verified participants across 3 studies), and mixed outcomes across trial types.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Only one human RCT (2017) directly addressed hormonal outcomes, testing whether citrulline malate improved muscle recovery via hormonal changes in untrained young adult men following resistance exercise. Sample size could not be verified from the abstract.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: A single study is insufficient to establish even preliminary efficacy or consistency. This outcome is graded 'Emerging' because the evidence is too limited and imprecise to support any conclusion about citrulline malate's effect on testosterone or other hormonal markers.
