A 2026 meta-analysis (n=2,551) focused on obesity-related disease showed benefit; a 2022 meta-analysis found efficient improvements in endothelial health; a 2020 meta-analysis (n=388) showed favorable impacts on blood pressure and renal function markers. A 2019 meta-analysis confirmed effects on endothelial function and blood pressure in metabolic syndrome patients. A 2013 meta-analysis (n=282) demonstrated effects on plasma lipids. Evidence comes primarily from randomized controlled trials in patients with metabolic syndrome, hypertension, and related conditions.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Twenty human studies with eight converging systematic reviews provide robust evidence. At least 3,575 participants are documented across nine studies with disclosed sizes; the actual total is larger. High consistency across multiple independent meta-analyses and diverse cardiovascular endpoints (endothelial function, blood pressure, lipids) supports Strong classification.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Meta-analyses (2023, 2021, 2020) including 216 participants in one 2021 analysis demonstrate resveratrol's effects on liver enzymes and hepatic steatosis in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. A 2022 RCT (n=71) showed benefit on hepatic steatosis and cardiovascular indices in overweight subjects. However, a 2020 RCT reported no beneficial effects on atherogenic risk factors in some NAFLD patients. Total human evidence comprises 5 primary trials and 4 pooled analyses across approximately 527 documented participants in 7 studies with sample sizes disclosed.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Twelve human studies provide a foundation, but the limited number of primary human trials (5) and smaller pooled evidence base relative to inflammation or cardiovascular outcomes places this at Moderate grade. The 527 verified participants across disclosed studies is substantially smaller than other Strong outcomes, and heterogeneity in patient responses (some trials showing no benefit) indicates the effect is real but less uniformly robust.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Nine independent meta-analyses and 22 human studies show consistent effects on glycemic control and glucose metabolism. A 2022 meta-analysis explicitly titled 'Resveratrol supplementation and type 2 diabetes' confirmed efficacy; a 2022 analysis (n=871) found improvements in glycemic control and cardiometabolic parameters in type 2 diabetes. A 2021 meta-analysis (n=1,476) covering type 2 diabetes, metabolic syndrome, and NAFLD confirmed benefits. A 2020 analysis (n=800) on resveratrol for type 2 diabetes and another (n=388) on metabolic endpoints both supported benefit. A 2019 meta-analysis documented effects across metabolic syndrome components.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Twenty-two human studies with nine converging meta-analyses provide strong consensus. At least 4,027 participants documented across 13 studies with disclosed sizes; the true total is considerably larger. Consistency across nine independent systematic reviews and the breadth of adequately powered trials in type-2 diabetes and related metabolic conditions support Strong grading.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Twelve independent meta-analyses and 21 human studies demonstrate robust effects on lipid profiles. A 2026 meta-analysis (n=2,551) on obesity-related diseases showed lipid benefits; a 2024 meta-analysis explicitly assessed efficacy on lipid profile parameters; a 2022 dose-response meta-analysis examined blood lipid effects across dosing regimens. A 2019 meta-analysis covered lipid components of metabolic syndrome; a 2016 meta-analysis (n=156) examined efficacy in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. Evidence comes primarily from randomized controlled trials in metabolic syndrome, type-2 diabetes, and NAFLD populations.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Twenty-one human studies with twelve converging meta-analyses show strong and consistent effects. At least 4,046 participants documented across 14 studies with disclosed sample sizes; actual total is larger. The number and consistency of independent syntheses, combined with adequately powered individual trials and dose-response analysis, support Strong classification.

resveratrol::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::6.evidence_base: The research base for resveratrol is predominantly human-centered and robustly synthesized. Across all outcomes, 16–22 human studies per outcome are complemented by systematic reviews and meta-analyses (4–12 per outcome), with most major reviews published 2018–2026. Study populations are well-represented in metabolic and cardiovascular disease contexts (type-2 diabetes, metabolic syndrome, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, hypertension), with sample sizes ranging from small pilot trials to meta-analyses combining thousands of participants. The consistency of meta-analytic findings across independent research groups is a key strength, suggesting that observed effects are replicable rather than isolated to single trials.
resveratrol::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::6.emerging_research: A 2025 systematic review examined resveratrol as a candidate for retinal health, suggesting expansion into ophthalmologic outcomes. Recent 2026 meta-analyses continue to focus on obesity-related comorbidities, indicating growing interest in resveratrol's role in broader metabolic dysfunction. Some research explores dose–response relationships and optimal supplementation duration, though these analyses remain early in synthesis. These directions are promising but still accumulating primary evidence.
resveratrol::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::6.open_questions: Among the studies retrieved here, most trials span 8–24 weeks, so long-term safety and sustained efficacy beyond this window are not clearly characterized in the abstracts provided. The retrieved literature concentrates heavily on adults with metabolic or cardiovascular disease; studies in younger, healthy populations or in specific age groups (children, very elderly) are not prominently represented in these records. Additionally, while meta-analyses of blood sugar and lipids are numerous, variation in supplementation dose, duration, and formulation (extract source, purity) across trials is mentioned only occasionally in the abstracts, making it unclear whether all protocols are equally effective. (Note: this characterizes only the ~40 abstracts per outcome retrieved here; the global research landscape may contain additional populations and study designs not reflected in this sample.)
resveratrol::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::6.caveats: Resveratrol supplements vary widely in purity, bioavailability, and actual trans-resveratrol content; third-party testing is advisable. As a polyphenol with mild anticoagulant and estrogenic properties, resveratrol may interact with blood thinners (warfarin) or affect hormone-sensitive conditions; individuals on anticoagulants or with estrogen-dependent cancers should consult a physician before use. Pregnant and nursing women should avoid supplementation due to insufficient safety data, and optimal dosing in individual patients remains an open clinical question.

spermidine::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::35.what_it_is: Spermidine (C₇H₁₉N₃, molecular weight 145.25) is a small aliphatic polyamine—a naturally occurring organic compound found in cells throughout the body and in many foods including aged cheese, mushrooms, whole grains, and legumes. It is a precursor to other polyamines and plays a role in cellular protein synthesis and modification. People typically obtain it through diet or take it as an oral supplement in capsule or powder form.
spermidine::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::35.how_it_works: Spermidine acts primarily through a process called hypusination, in which it is converted to deoxyhypusine (via the enzyme deoxyhypusine synthase) and incorporated into a protein called eIF5A—a translation factor critical for protein synthesis and cellular stress responses. This modification appears to trigger and sustain autophagy, the cell's recycling system that degrades damaged organelles and proteins, which is thought to underlie many of spermidine's potential health effects. Through autophagy and related pathways, spermidine may modulate immune cell aging, reduce markers of inflammation, support mitochondrial function, and protect neurons. The compound also influences the gut microbiota and intestinal barrier function, which feeds back into immune and metabolic regulation.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: One human RCT (n=100, 2022) examining spermidine supplementation in older adults with subjective cognitive decline measured inflammation-related biomarkers alongside cognitive outcomes. Animal studies (2025–2026, various rodent models) showed that spermidine reduced neuroinflammation in vascular dementia models, attenuated microglial activation, and reduced genetic damage in liver and bone marrow; a cardiometabolic study (n=40, 2025) in estrogen-deprived rats found mitigation of cardiac mitochondrial dysfunction. The animal findings align on an anti-inflammatory signal, but human evidence remains limited to a single trial.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The grade reflects one human RCT and consistent directional findings in animal models, but precision is constrained by low human participant numbers (~100 in the verified human trial) and lack of a meta-analysis pooling the animal work. The single human study provides preliminary support, but broader human confirmation is needed to call this established.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: One observational human study (2019) found that spermidine modulates polyamine-dependent pathways regulating B cell senescence reversal via eIF5A hypusination and autophagy. Multiple animal studies (2020–2021, 2026) showed spermidine maintains autophagy in T cells from aged donors, correlating with vaccine response; regulates T cell differentiation; and reduces intestinal oxidative stress and microbiota dysbiosis. These data suggest a mechanism for immune cell rejuvenation and dysbiosis correction, particularly in aging.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: One human observational study and four animal trials provide directional consistency, but sample sizes for the human study could not be verified from abstracts, capping precision. No pooled analysis exists to confirm inter-study agreement, and human mechanistic evidence is limited to a single non-randomized design.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Five human RCTs and clinical trials (2018–2022, sample sizes 30–100 per trial; verified n≈245 across 4 of the 5 studies) tested spermidine in older adults with subjective cognitive decline or early dementia over 3–12 weeks, finding improvements in memory performance and cognition-related biomarkers. Seven animal studies (2018–2026) in rodent models of aging and neurodegeneration showed spermidine enhanced cognition-related outcomes and mitochondrial function in the brain. Human trials were relatively short-term and conducted in at-risk or cognitively impaired populations.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Multiple small human RCTs show consistent benefit in a specific population (older adults with cognitive complaints), but trials were brief (≤3 months), sample sizes modest (30–100 per trial), and no meta-analysis has confirmed they agree. Animal work supports the signal but does not confirm human efficacy in broader or younger populations.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Four animal studies (2017, 2021, 2025, 2026) examined spermidine's effects on liver pathology in rodent models: protection from ethanol-induced ferroptosis via gut-mediated iron homeostasis, enhancement of macrophage regenerative functions, protection of liver endothelium, and arginase-related mechanisms. All are mechanistic or injury-prevention studies in rodents; no human trials of liver health outcomes were retrieved.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Evidence is animal-only and does not translate reliably to human liver disease or health. While the mechanistic findings are interesting, absence of human data and reliance on rodent toxicity models prevents any claim of established efficacy in humans.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: One RCT in piglets (n=54, 2016) found that oral polyamine supplementation pre-weaning improved growth and intestinal characteristics. Three animal studies (2020, 2022, 2026) showed spermidine improves gut barrier integrity, enhances microbiota function in diet-induced obesity, and alleviates alcohol-induced hepatocyte damage via gut-mediated pathways. The signal across studies points to microbiota and intestinal barrier support, but human evidence is limited to a single pre-weaning animal trial.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The grade is supported by consistent directional findings in animal gut models and one animal RCT, but the single human-relevant study used piglets rather than adult humans, and sample size (n=54) is modest. Long-term or dose-response human trials in adults are absent from the retrieved records.

spermidine::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::35.evidence_base: The research base for spermidine is dominated by animal studies (32 of 44 records retrieved), with only 5–6 human RCTs and one observational study, primarily in older adults with cognitive complaints or at-risk populations. Human trials are recent (2018–2022) and mostly short-term (3 months or less); animal studies span 2017–2026 and explore mechanistic pathways in aging, neuroinflammation, and organ protection. The imbalance toward animal work means mechanistic understanding is robust, but human efficacy and safety in general populations remain less certain. Most abstracts omit full sample sizes, making precise participant counts difficult; verified human enrollment across cognition trials is roughly 245 participants.
spermidine::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::35.emerging_research: Recent animal studies (2025–2026) explore spermidine's role in estrogen-dependent cardiometabolic protection, ferroptosis and iron homeostasis in alcohol-induced liver injury, and labor initiation via placental autophagy—suggesting possible applications in reproductive and cardiovascular health. One 2026 study examined metabolite signaling from apoptotic cells in Alzheimer's-type pathology, hinting at a broader role in neurodegenerative disease. These directions are preliminary and animal-only; human trials would be needed to assess clinical relevance.
spermidine::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::35.open_questions: Among the records provided, no human trials of liver health exist, and gut health evidence rests on a single piglet RCT rather than adult humans—neither population directly informs adult human efficacy. Cognition trials are short (≤3 months), raising questions about durability of benefit and optimal dosing in broader age groups or in populations without baseline cognitive complaint. No long-term safety data (>12 weeks in humans) appear in the retrieved records, and no trials in young or healthy adults are evident. It is important to note that this describes only the studies retrieved here (~40 abstracts per outcome); these gaps do not mean such research does not exist globally, only that it is not present in the sample provided.
spermidine::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::35.caveats: Spermidine is derived from biological sources or synthesized; purity and formulation vary by manufacturer, so product quality should be verified. Because most human evidence is in older adults with cognitive or age-related concerns, safety and efficacy in younger, healthy individuals remain uncharacterized in the studies shown. Spermidine can interact with certain medications and diets rich in other polyamines; individuals on specific medications or with unusual dietary restrictions should consult a clinician before supplementing. The evidence as a whole is rated Moderate rather than Strong because human trials are small, short, and limited to specific at-risk populations.

fisetin::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::7166e.what_it_is: Fisetin is a flavonoid—a plant polyphenol with the chemical formula C₁₅H₁₀O₆—found naturally in small amounts in strawberries, apples, onions, and other fruits and vegetables. It is also known as 5-desoxyquercetin and belongs to the class of compounds called 3,7,3',4'-tetrahydroxyflavones. People typically consume it as an oral supplement in capsule or powder form, often in doses ranging from a few hundred milligrams to several grams.
fisetin::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::7166e.how_it_works: Fisetin is a potent antioxidant and anti-inflammatory compound that works through multiple cellular pathways. It scavenges free radicals directly and activates the body's own antioxidant defense systems, including upregulation of enzymes like superoxide dismutase and catalase. Additionally, fisetin has been shown in research to inhibit inflammatory signaling pathways—particularly those triggered by senescent (aged) cells and their inflammatory secretions (a process called SASP inhibition)—which may help reduce chronic inflammation and support cellular health. It also appears to modulate metabolic pathways affecting glucose and lipid handling, though the precise human mechanisms remain incompletely understood.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Research retrieved includes 3 human studies and 10 animal studies. A 2018 randomized trial in 19 participants examined fisetin's effect on inflammatory markers and matrix metalloproteinase enzymes in colorectal cancer contexts. Multiple 2026 studies—including a 12-week RCT on fisetin combined with interval resistance and aerobic training, and an unclassified phase II study in breast cancer survivors—assessed inflammatory biomarkers including Maresin-1. Animal studies from 2025–2026 demonstrated that fisetin, acting as a senolytic (clearing aged cells), reversed age-related endothelial dysfunction and reduced inflammation-related markers (SASP factors) and ferroptosis pathways.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Human evidence exists but is limited: only ~19 participants are verified in the largest single human trial, yielding modest statistical power and unstable effect estimates. The studies are recent and use relevant designs (RCT, controlled), but consistency across the human trials has not been pooled or formally compared, and sample sizes overall remain small for firm efficacy claims.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Only one human study—a 2026 randomized trial combining 12 weeks of fisetin supplementation with interval resistance and aerobic training—directly addressed blood sugar. The exact sample size and detailed results could not be confirmed from the available abstract.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: A single study with unconfirmed sample size is insufficient to establish efficacy. No animal studies on this specific outcome were retrieved, and consistency cannot be assessed. This outcome is promising as a research direction but not yet supported by human evidence robust enough to claim clinical benefit.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Five human studies and 25 animal studies addressed liver health. Human data include the 2026 RCT on fisetin with exercise (examining markers like Asprosin and adipokines), the 2018 RCT in 19 participants, the 2026 phase II breast cancer study, and other unclassified 2025–2026 trials. Animal studies from 2013–2026 investigated fisetin's effects on hepatic lipogenesis, glucose metabolism, and suppression of cellular senescence in doxorubicin-induced vascular aging models.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Human evidence is present but sparse—roughly 19 verified participants in a single trial, with most other abstracts omitting exact sample sizes. No meta-analysis pooling these studies was available to confirm they move in the same direction, so consistency remains unestablished. The grade reflects plausible but not yet robust human support.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: All four retrieved studies were conducted in animals (mice and rats). Studies from 2013, 2024, and 2025–2026 examined fisetin's effects on arterial function, endothelial dysfunction, and cellular senescence. Results showed improvements in arterial stiffness and reversal of age-related endothelial dysfunction via SASP factor reduction and decreased cellular senescence.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Evidence is entirely animal-derived; no human trials on cardiovascular outcomes were retrieved. Animal findings do not reliably translate to human physiology and disease, so the cardiovascular grade cannot advance beyond preliminary until human evidence emerges.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Five human and 25 animal studies addressed endurance or physical performance. Human studies include the 2026 RCT combining fisetin with interval resistance-aerobic training and assessments of physical function in breast cancer survivors (2026, unclassified). The 2018 trial in 19 participants also captured exercise-related outcomes. Animal studies (2025–2026) investigated vascular aging, cellular senescence, and performance-relevant markers following fisetin supplementation.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Human sample sizes are small and verified primarily from one trial (~19 participants); total human N across all studies omits confirmed sizes for most records. No pooled analysis confirms consistency among trials. The grade reflects emerging human support and numerous animal models, but insufficient statistical power and lack of formal comparison between studies prevent a stronger rating.

fisetin::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::7166e.evidence_base: The retrieved literature on fisetin comprises predominantly recent studies (2018–2026), with a mix of human and animal work. Human evidence is limited: approximately 5 randomized or unclassified trials, most with small participant numbers (one verified at n=19), and most from 2026. Animal studies are far more numerous (~50+ total across outcomes) and consistently show anti-inflammatory, senolytic, and antioxidant effects in mice and rats. The overall research base is still young and growing, with most rigorous human data emerging in 2026. This suggests fisetin is attracting increased clinical attention but has not yet generated the large, long-term human trials typical of well-established interventions.
fisetin::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::7166e.emerging_research: Recent 2025–2026 animal and early-phase human studies highlight fisetin's role as a senolytic—a compound that selectively clears senescent cells and their inflammatory secretions (SASP), potentially reversing age-related vascular and metabolic dysfunction. Trials combining fisetin with structured exercise (resistance and aerobic training) are underway, suggesting interest in synergistic effects. A phase II trial in breast cancer survivors indicates expansion into populations recovering from chemotherapy-related injury. These directions are early but suggest fisetin may act not merely as a general antioxidant but as a cell-selective aging intervention.
fisetin::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::7166e.open_questions: Among the studies retrieved here, most human trials are very recent (2026) and follow participants for only 12 weeks or less—long-term safety and durability of effects remain uncharacterized in the provided records. The vast majority of research addresses young healthy animals or small human cohorts; data on older adults, chronic disease populations, or diverse ethnic groups are sparse or absent in this sample. Sample sizes in human trials are consistently modest (one verified at 19 participants), so questions about minimum effective doses, optimal duration, and inter-individual variability cannot yet be answered. Additionally, while animal studies are numerous, the retrieved abstracts do not show whether human findings replicate animal mechanisms or merely correlate with them.
fisetin::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::7166e.caveats: Fisetin is a dietary supplement not regulated as a drug in most countries; quality, purity, and dose accuracy vary by manufacturer and have not been systematically verified across products in the records provided. As a polyphenol, fisetin may interact with certain medications (especially anticoagulants and antiplatelet agents) and can inhibit cytochrome P450 enzymes, potentially altering drug metabolism; consultation with a healthcare provider is advisable, particularly for those on chronic medications. Pregnant and nursing individuals, and those with known allergies to plant polyphenols or flavonoids, should exercise caution pending further safety data in these populations.

quercetin::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::a96.what_it_is: Quercetin (C₁₅H₁₀O₇, molecular weight 302.23) is a plant-derived flavonoid—a type of polyphenol found abundantly in onions, apples, berries, and green tea. It is a yellow crystalline compound classified chemically as 2-(3,4-dihydroxyphenyl)-3,5,7-trihydroxychromen-4-one. People typically take it as an oral supplement in capsule or powder form, often derived from food sources or synthesized.
quercetin::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::a96.how_it_works: Quercetin acts primarily as an antioxidant and anti-inflammatory agent by scavenging free radicals and inhibiting key inflammatory pathways in cells. It crosses cell membranes and can suppress the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines (like TNF-α and IL-6) and modulate nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB), a central regulator of inflammation. The compound also has mild vasodilatory effects—it may improve blood vessel relaxation and endothelial function—which could explain effects on blood pressure and cardiovascular health. Additionally, quercetin appears to influence glucose metabolism and lipid handling, though the precise mechanisms in humans remain incompletely characterized.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Six independent meta-analyses and systematic reviews consistently found that quercetin supplementation reduced blood pressure in human participants. A 2022 meta-analysis (n=841), a 2020 meta-analysis (n=896), a 2019 meta-analysis, a 2016 meta-analysis (n=587), and two systematic reviews (2023 and 2016) all converged on this outcome. Studies included patients with metabolic syndrome and related conditions as well as community-dwelling adults, with supplementation durations and doses varying across trials.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Convergence across six independent syntheses of human data (a marker of replication and robustness) earned this outcome the top grade. Although most individual study abstracts did not report sample sizes, at least 2,571 participants were verified across 8 of the 24 retrieved studies, providing adequate statistical power.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2020 meta-analysis on lipid profiles and inflammatory markers, a 2020 systematic review on polycystic ovary syndrome, and several randomized trials (2021, n=44; 2020, n=33; 2013; 2012) examined effects of quercetin on inflammatory biomarkers and markers of muscle damage after exercise. Studies showed reductions in inflammatory factors and post-exercise muscle inflammation, though outcomes varied.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: While 10 human studies were retrieved, no pooled analysis confirmed consistent agreement across them, and only ~149 participants were verified with reported sample sizes; most abstracts omitted participant numbers. The evidence suggests a real anti-inflammatory signal but lacks the consistency or precision needed for a higher grade.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Meta-analyses from 2026, 2020, 2019, and 2017 and a 2023 systematic review examined quercetin's effects on lipid profiles, blood pressure, endothelial function, and atherosclerosis in humans and rodents. Studies included patients with metabolic syndrome and cardiovascular risk factors; sample sizes ranged from n=116 to n=896 where reported. Results suggested improvements in lipid profiles and endothelial function, though heterogeneity was noted.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Fifteen human studies were retrieved, but only 6 primary human studies and 7 pooled analyses were found—below the threshold for a strong grade. Although ~2,304 participants were verified across 9 of 19 studies, the limited number of independent primary trials and inconsistency in outcomes prevented upgrading to strong.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Meta-analyses from 2020 and 2019, systematic reviews from 2023 and 2016, and randomized trials from 2018 and 2015 examined quercetin's effects on glycemic control and metabolic parameters in patients with metabolic syndrome and related disorders. Studies measured fasting glucose, insulin, and other glycemic markers; sample sizes where reported ranged up to n=896.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Twelve human studies were retrieved with ~1,087 participants verified across 4 studies, but no pooled analysis confirmed consistency across trials. Several studies exist showing benefit, but the inconsistency and modest precision across reported samples held this outcome at moderate pending further synthesis.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Meta-analyses from 2026, 2020 (two separate analyses), and 2017, and randomized trials from 2011 and 2010 (n=60) examined quercetin's effects on serum lipid profiles, total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, and triglycerides. Studies included overweight and community-dwelling adults; results suggested modest improvements in lipid profiles, though responses varied by genotype and population.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only 9 human studies and 4 primary trials with pooled analyses were retrieved—below the threshold for strong. Although ~1,705 participants were verified across 6 of 24 studies, the limited number of independent primary human trials and lack of unified synthesis prevented a higher grade.

quercetin::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::a96.evidence_base: Quercetin's evidence base is dominated by human meta-analyses and systematic reviews (15–17 human studies per outcome), complemented by animal studies (~4–15 per outcome). Most retrieved records date from 2015 onward, with clusters of syntheses appearing in 2019–2023, suggesting active recent research interest. However, many abstracts omit sample sizes, so the true participant pool is substantially larger than verified counts alone indicate. Blood pressure emerges as the best-supported outcome, with six converging syntheses; other outcomes rest on fewer pooled analyses and less consistent individual trials, supporting their moderate grades.
quercetin::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::a96.emerging_research: Recent systematic reviews (2023) have begun mapping quercetin's broader cardiometabolic effects via umbrella reviews of multiple meta-analyses, suggesting a shift toward integrated assessment. Early work on polycystic ovary syndrome (2020 systematic review) and genotype-dependent lipid responses (2010 RCT) hints at personalized approaches. A 2026 meta-analysis on quercetin and hyperuricemia-related outcomes represents a newer direction, though the full scope of such emerging applications remains unclear from the retrieved abstracts.
quercetin::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::a96.open_questions: Among the studies retrieved here, most trials appear to be relatively short-term (weeks to a few months), and none of the abstracts provided reported long-term (multi-year) follow-up data, so durability of effect is unknown from these records. The retrieved studies do not clearly document whether effects differ by age, sex, or disease state, though some examined metabolic syndrome patients or community-dwelling adults. Several outcomes (inflammation, blood sugar, lipids) are held at moderate grade due to inconsistency among trials—the abstracts provided do not explain why some studies diverge, and a complete understanding would require access to full-text analyses of heterogeneity.
quercetin::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::a96.caveats: Quercetin is poorly absorbed orally; bioavailability is typically 1–5% unless formulated with enhancers (e.g., vitamin C), meaning supplement quality and formulation vary widely. It may interact with certain drugs (particularly anticoagulants and some antibiotics) and can act as a mild estrogen agonist, making it inadvisable for people with hormone-sensitive conditions without medical guidance. Pregnant or nursing women and those with kidney disease should consult a healthcare provider before supplementing.

metformin::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::aa1.what_it_is: Metformin (1,1-dimethylbiguanide, molecular formula C₄H₁₁N₅) is a small-molecule oral medication that has been used for over 70 years, primarily to treat type 2 diabetes and prediabetes. It is derived from the plant guanidine alkaloids and is typically taken as metformin hydrochloride tablets by mouth. The compound works systemically, affecting multiple tissues involved in energy metabolism, glucose handling, and inflammatory processes.
metformin::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::aa1.how_it_works: Metformin's primary mechanism involves activating AMPK (adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase), a cellular 'metabolic sensor' that turns on when energy is low and activates pathways that improve insulin sensitivity and glucose uptake. In the liver, it reduces glucose production (gluconeogenesis); in muscle and fat, it increases glucose uptake and improves insulin responsiveness. The drug also modulates the gut microbiota — the trillions of bacteria living in the intestines — which appears to influence systemic inflammation and metabolic health through microbial metabolites and intestinal barrier function. Beyond glucose control, metformin reduces production of pro-inflammatory molecules and may enhance certain immune cell functions, although the breadth and clinical significance of these effects in humans remain incompletely understood.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2022 systematic review compared metformin with glyburide in gestational diabetes, and multiple randomized trials from the 1990s and 2020s demonstrate that metformin improves glucose and insulin responses in type 2 diabetes, hypertensive obese women, and prediabetic populations. Recent studies (2023) examined postprandial glucose kinetics and insulin sensitivity after metformin with and without exercise in prediabetic and diabetic individuals. The records retrieved span roughly 82 participants with verified sample sizes across 2 of the 15 studies shown; the true total is likely substantially larger, though most abstracts do not specify participant numbers.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Multiple human randomized trials confirm metformin improves blood glucose control across different populations and metabolic contexts. The grade is held at Moderate rather than Strong because a single systematic review conclusion is not independently replicated in the retrieved records, and sample size information is missing from most abstracts, limiting precision assessment.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Human trials in 2024–2025 show that metformin, alone or combined with SGLT2 inhibitors or other agents, improves hepatic steatosis (fat accumulation in the liver), liver fibrosis markers, and liver function tests. Studies include a 2022 RCT (n=487) examining metformin's effects on fetal liver circulation in pregnant people with PCOS, a 2024 trial (n=106) on diet-induced obesity, and a 2025 trial (n=80) on metabolic profile and liver fibrosis indexes. Approximately 673 participants appear across 3 of 20 studies with verified sizes; most abstracts lack sample numbers.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Several human trials spanning the past 3–4 years document improvements in liver health outcomes, but no pooled meta-analysis in the retrieved records independently confirms consistency across these studies. Precision is limited because sample sizes are missing from most abstracts. The grade reflects moderate confidence pending a replicable synthesis.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Two human studies are present in the retrieved records: a 2023 RCT comparing gemigliptin-plus-metformin versus glimepiride-plus-metformin on gut function, and a 2024 unclassified study on metformin and linagliptin effects on gut microbiota in prediabetic patients. The majority of the retrieved evidence (18 of 20 studies) comes from animal models published in 2025, demonstrating that metformin activates intestinal AMPK, remodels the microbiota, and reduces markers of intestinal inflammation and metabolic dysfunction. Verified sample sizes exist for only 1 of 20 studies (~18 participants), making precision estimates unreliable.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The Moderate grade reflects a small but consistent body of human and animal evidence that metformin influences gut microbiota and intestinal metabolism. However, very limited human data (only 2 studies) and small verified participant counts make this outcome imprecise and uncertain in clinical translation. Animal studies suggest plausibility but cannot substitute for human evidence.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2020 systematic review assessed metformin's effects on T-cell-mediated inflammation in vitro and in vivo. A 2020 RCT (n=849) in patients on systemic glucocorticoid therapy showed metformin reduced metabolic complications and inflammatory markers. A 2024 study examined metformin's association with reduced coronary artery inflammation via pericoronary adipose tissue imaging. The bulk of the retrieved evidence (19 of 22 studies) consists of animal studies from 2026 showing metformin attenuates oxidative stress-related inflammation, macrophage senescence, and bone-damaging inflammation. Verified human participants span approximately 864 across 2 of 22 studies.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Human evidence includes one independent systematic review and multiple trials showing anti-inflammatory effects, particularly in metabolic and immune contexts. However, only a single meta-analysis synthesis exists in the retrieved records and has not been independently replicated. The strong animal evidence supports plausibility but does not increase confidence in human clinical effects. Grade is Moderate pending confirmation.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Three human studies appear in the retrieved records: a 2025 unclassified study on metformin combined with insulin aspart effects on immune function, a 2023 study on metformin and empagliflozin modulating oxidative stress and vascular function (with immune correlates), and a 2022 study reporting metformin treatment on CD8 T cells (abstract title truncated). Nine animal studies from 2025–2026 report metformin suppressing pro-inflammatory Th17 differentiation, enhancing antitumor immune responses, and modulating immune cell function. No sample sizes were verifiable from any of the human study abstracts.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Very few human studies exist (3 of 12 retrieved), and none report verified sample sizes, making precision unreliable and certainty capped below Moderate. The animal evidence suggests metformin influences immune cell differentiation and function, but human clinical translation remains unproven. This outcome is graded Preliminary—promising but far from established in people.

metformin::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::aa1.evidence_base: The metformin literature retrieved spans roughly 15–22 studies per outcome, with a mix of human trials, animal models, and systematic reviews published primarily in 2020–2026. Most outcomes show 7–8 human studies and 13–19 animal studies, indicating that evidence is heterogeneous: human trials provide the strongest signals for blood sugar and liver health, while inflammation and immune function are dominated by animal or mechanistic work. Sample size reporting is sparse across abstracts, which limits formal precision assessment. Overall, the research is relatively recent (mostly 2020 onward), suggesting active investigation, but the human evidence base remains modest in size and breadth for longevity-specific outcomes.
metformin::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::aa1.emerging_research: Recent 2024–2026 studies are increasingly focused on metformin's microbiota-dependent effects: multiomics studies (2025) reveal metformin's dual role in remodeling the gut microbiome and reprogramming hepatic metabolism, and mechanistic work demonstrates intestinal AMPK activation as a key driver of metabolic improvements. Emerging work on immune function (2025–2026) suggests metformin may suppress pro-inflammatory Th17 responses and enhance antitumor immunity, although human validation is minimal. A 2026 animal study on metformin and chromatin fragmentation in senescence hints at potential cellular aging mechanisms, but this remains purely preclinical.
metformin::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::aa1.open_questions: Among the studies retrieved here, human evidence is concentrated in blood sugar and liver health; immune function and gut/digestion rely heavily on animal or mechanistic data with very few human trials of verified size. Trial durations and long-term follow-up periods are not clearly specified in most abstracts provided, so it is unclear whether the retrieved studies track outcomes beyond weeks or months. Notably, the retrieved records do not specify which populations (age, metabolic status, geographic region, sex) are represented across outcomes, limiting clarity on generalizability. This sample of ~40 abstracts per outcome represents only a fraction of the global metformin literature; the completeness and representativeness of this retrieval cannot be assessed here.
metformin::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::aa1.caveats: Metformin is generally well-tolerated but can cause gastrointestinal side effects (nausea, diarrhea, abdominal discomfort), particularly at high doses or in people with reduced kidney function; it should not be used in severe renal impairment (eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73m²) due to rare risk of lactic acidosis. Metformin may interact with certain medications and contrast agents; discuss with a healthcare provider before starting. While approved for type 2 diabetes and prediabetes, use of metformin for general 'longevity' in people without glucose intolerance remains experimental and is not standard clinical practice.

rapamycin::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::078.what_it_is: Rapamycin (also called sirolimus) is a macrolide antibiotic derived from the bacterium Streptomyces hygroscopicus, with the molecular formula C₅₁H₇₉NO₁₃. It is a small lipophilic compound that crosses cell membranes readily, allowing it to work inside cells. Clinically, it is used as an immunosuppressant in organ transplantation and as a coating on some medical stents; in research and off-label contexts, people take it orally in pill form, and it is sometimes used as an injectable.
rapamycin::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::078.how_it_works: Rapamycin works by binding to a protein called FKBP12, and this complex then inhibits mTORC1 — a master metabolic and growth-control hub in cells. mTORC1 normally activates protein synthesis, cell proliferation, and inflammation; blocking it triggers autophagy (cellular 'housekeeping'), slows aging-related pathways, and dampens immune overactivity. By slowing mTORC1, rapamycin reduces the growth of immune cells (especially T cells), which is why it is an effective immunosuppressant in transplant patients. This same pathway inhibition is theorized to underpin effects on longevity, glucose metabolism, and inflammation, though the net effect depends on context — suppressing immune activation is protective in autoimmunity but can impair vaccine response and infection control.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2023 meta-analysis of 1223 participants found that rapamycin improved resilience against pathogens compared to dietary restriction alone. A 2025 meta-analysis examined rapamycin's impact on delayed graft function in kidney transplant recipients. A 2020 case report documented restoration of regulatory T-cell function in an IPEX patient treated with rapamycin. Animal studies (2024, 2023, 2022) showed improvements in T-cell memory for tuberculosis vaccine, modulation of myeloid-derived suppressor cells in angiogenesis, and immunomodulation in lung tumors.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Three human studies provide clinical evidence, though pooled analysis confirming agreement is pending. The largest human sample size verified is 1223 (from one study); most abstracts omit participant numbers, making a precise denominator uncertain. The mix of transplant data, case reports, and animal work is heterogeneous, preventing strong pooled conclusions at present.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: All 23 retrieved studies are animal models. Recent findings (2026, 2025, 2024, 2023) show rapamycin preserving cardiac function in autoimmune myocarditis, ameliorating intrahepatic inflammation in metabolic fatty liver disease, modulating senescence-related inflammation in arthritis, lowering age-related inflammation via mTORC1 suppression, reducing neuronal injury after cerebral ischemia, and suppressing inflammatory mediators. These span diverse tissue systems and inflammatory contexts in rodents.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: No human trials on inflammation outcomes were retrieved; all evidence is animal-only, and animal inflammation models often do not translate reliably to human disease. Until human studies confirm these pathways in vivo, inflammation outcomes remain preliminary.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Only one human study (2017, observational) examined blood sugar outcomes, comparing mTORC1 inhibitors rapamycin and metformin on cardiovascular markers, with modest sample size (~15 participants verified). Animal studies (2019, 2018, 2017) reported rapamycin improving insulin resistance and hepatic steatosis in type 2 diabetes rats through autophagy activation, rescuing metabolic deficits in apolipoprotein E4 transgenic mice, and showing differential effects in diabetic versus healthy rat hearts. One 2019 study examined rapamycin in ischemic and drug-induced kidney injury.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only one small human observational study exists (n~15); no randomized controlled trials in humans were retrieved. Animal studies suggest plausible metabolic benefit, but the human evidence base is too sparse and the designs too observational to support clinical claims. This warrants further human investigation.

rapamycin::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::078.evidence_base: The research landscape is mixed: immune function has 3 human studies (including one large meta-analysis of 1223 transplant and pathogen-resilience data) and 12 animal studies, providing moderate confidence in a real signal. Inflammation and blood sugar effects rely almost entirely on animal models — 23 animal studies for inflammation (zero human) and 8 of 9 blood sugar studies animal-based. Most human evidence comes from transplant populations or observational designs rather than randomized trials. Studies span 2017–2026, so the field is active, but human evidence for longevity and metabolic outcomes remains thin.
rapamycin::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::078.emerging_research: Recent animal work (2025–2026) is exploring rapamycin's role in specific inflammatory states: cardiac autoimmunity via Cxcl9 reprogramming, metabolic fatty liver via macrophage lipid metabolism, and arthritis via neuropeptide Y. One 2024 study linked S6K inhibition (downstream of mTORC1) to lifespan extension and endolysosomal autophagy in mice. These directions suggest rapamycin may work partly through metabolic reprogramming of immune and lipid-handling cells, but none constitute human evidence yet.
rapamycin::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::078.open_questions: Among the studies retrieved here, human evidence is concentrated in transplant and one meta-analysis; very few studies on inflammation or blood sugar in humans appear in this sample. No retrieved studies followed participants beyond typical clinical timescales (e.g., long-term longevity trials are absent). Whether rapamycin's immune effects in transplant patients — where it is an active immunosuppressant — generalize to non-transplant populations seeking immune resilience is unclear from this record sample. The retrieved abstracts do not specify whether any human studies included aging populations or focused on age-related outcomes directly.
rapamycin::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::078.caveats: Rapamycin is a prescription immunosuppressant with significant toxicity: it increases infection risk, can cause mouth ulcers, elevated cholesterol, and bone loss, and is contraindicated in certain cancers. It is not approved by regulatory agencies for longevity or metabolic indications, and off-label use requires medical supervision and monitoring. People considering rapamycin should consult a physician and understand it may impair immune response to vaccines and infections — a double-edged effect that is protective in transplant rejection but dangerous in healthy individuals trying to prevent infection.

ca-akg::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::e64d60.what_it_is: Ca-AKG (calcium alpha-ketoglutarate) is the calcium salt of alpha-ketoglutarate (α-KG), a small organic molecule with the formula C₅H₆O₅ found naturally in cells as a key intermediate in the citric acid cycle—the central metabolic pathway that generates energy. It is derived from the amino acid glutamate and is sold as an oral supplement in powder or capsule form. The calcium salt form is chosen for improved absorption and stability compared to alpha-ketoglutarate alone.
ca-akg::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::e64d60.how_it_works: Alpha-ketoglutarate acts as a cofactor and substrate in several critical cellular processes. In mitochondria, it participates directly in energy production (the citric acid cycle) and serves as a precursor for the amino acid glutamate, which supports protein synthesis and acts as a neurotransmitter. α-KG also functions as a cosubstrate for a family of enzymes called dioxygenases, which regulate cellular signaling, collagen synthesis (via prolyl hydroxylase), and the epigenetic marks on DNA (via ten-eleven translocation enzymes that modify methylated cytosines). At the cellular level, it helps maintain redox balance—the ratio of oxidized to reduced molecules—which influences inflammatory tone and metabolic stress responses. In theory, by supporting these pathways, α-KG might improve energy metabolism, tissue repair, and cellular resilience with age, though human evidence remains sparse.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Among the three studies retrieved, one human clinical trial (2023, n=120 middle-aged adults, the ABLE-intervention study) examined alpha-ketoglutarate supplementation and biological age; the two animal studies (2011 in aged mice; 2026 in ruminants) observed effects on redox homeostasis and arterial properties, which relate indirectly to tissue quality and elasticity. The human trial appears to be protocol or early-stage reporting rather than completed outcome analysis, and the animal studies examined different endpoints (arterial elasticity, rumen fermentation) rather than direct skin or appearance measures.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Evidence is graded Emerging because human data is minimal (one trial, n=120) and the animal studies, while suggestive of cellular benefits to tissue structure, do not directly measure skin appearance or aging markers in humans. The modest sample size and heterogeneous endpoints across studies introduce imprecision and instability in any effect estimate.

ca-akg::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::e64d60.evidence_base: The research landscape shown here is heavily weighted toward animal models (2 of 3 studies), with only one human trial retrieved and that appearing to be early-stage reporting. The studies span from 2011 to 2026, indicating some sustained interest, but human-level evidence remains sparse and recent. The studies focus on mechanistic endpoints—redox status, arterial properties, microbial composition—rather than validated clinical outcomes in aging or appearance, which limits confidence in translation to human benefit. Overall, this reflects a compound with established biochemical roles in metabolism but insufficient human data to support specific claims about skin, appearance, or longevity outcomes.
ca-akg::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::e64d60.emerging_research: Recent work (2026) has begun examining α-KG's effects on health parameters beyond energy metabolism, including immune and microbial effects in ruminants, suggesting interest in its broader systemic benefits. The ABLE-intervention study (2023) represents an attempt to measure biological age directly in middle-aged humans, a sophisticated endpoint that may help clarify whether α-KG influences aging rate. Mechanistically, ongoing interest in α-KG's role in epigenetic regulation and dioxygenase activity may eventually connect its biochemistry to validated aging and tissue health markers, but such links remain preliminary in humans.
ca-akg::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::e64d60.open_questions: Among the studies retrieved here, the human evidence is limited to one trial of middle-aged adults with no reported endpoint data yet; it is unknown whether skin or appearance measures were primary or secondary outcomes, or how long participants were followed. Neither of the animal studies directly measured skin characteristics or appearance, so any translation to dermatological benefit remains speculative. The retrieved records do not show how long-term supplementation (beyond weeks or months) affects human aging markers, nor do they clarify dose-response relationships or which populations might benefit most—these absences reflect the early stage of human investigation in this sample, though they do not indicate whether such research exists elsewhere in the broader literature.
ca-akg::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::e64d60.caveats: Ca-AKG is generally recognized as safe at supplemental doses because alpha-ketoglutarate is an endogenous metabolite; however, people with kidney disease, certain genetic metabolic disorders (e.g., glutaric acidemia), or those taking medications that interact with glutamate metabolism should consult a healthcare provider before use. The purity and bioavailability of commercial products vary; look for third-party tested supplements. Because human efficacy data for skin and appearance is currently Emerging and based on very limited trials, claims of anti-aging benefit are premature and should not replace established dermatological care or medical evaluation of aging-related concerns.

urolithin a::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::2.what_it_is: Urolithin A (C₁₃H₈O₄, molecular weight 228.20) is a polyphenol metabolite produced by gut bacteria when you consume foods rich in ellagic acid, such as pomegranate, berries, and walnuts. It is not present in food directly, but rather generated in your colon as a byproduct of microbial metabolism. Most commercial urolithin A supplements are synthetic versions taken orally, designed to bypass the need for your microbiota to produce it.
urolithin a::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::2.how_it_works: Urolithin A appears to work primarily by enhancing mitochondrial function and reducing inflammatory signaling in cells. It activates pathways involved in mitophagy (the selective removal of damaged mitochondria) and mitochondrial biogenesis (the creation of new, healthy mitochondria), processes that naturally decline with age. In research models, it inhibits several inflammatory pathways—including NF-κB and mTOR signaling—and modulates how immune cells and tissue cells respond to stress. This combination of mitochondrial renewal and reduced inflammation is theorized to support muscle function, exercise capacity, and tissue resilience, though the full cascade of effects in human bodies remains incompletely mapped.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Five animal studies (from 2017 to 2026) reported that urolithin A reduced intestinal injury and improved gut barrier function in mice exposed to toxins (hexavalent chromium, arsenic) or inflammatory challenges (colitis). A 2023 mouse study found it restored healthy gut microbiota composition and altered tryptophan metabolism in colitis models. No human trials of urolithin A's effects on gut health were among the studies retrieved.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: All evidence is from animal models or cell culture, which does not reliably predict human outcomes. While the findings are consistent in direction, they cannot yet confirm whether urolithin A produces similar gut or digestive benefits in people.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Two human randomized controlled trials (a 2025 trial of n=42 athletes and a 2022 trial) reported improvements in biomarkers of mitochondrial health and recovery. Thirteen animal studies from 2022–2025 showed that urolithin A reduced inflammatory markers and tissue injury in models of liver aging, sepsis, rheumatoid arthritis, and neuroinflammation associated with Parkinson's disease. Human evidence is limited to performance and mitochondrial biomarkers rather than direct inflammatory markers.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The evidence rests on only ~42 confirmed participants in human trials, and most study abstracts did not specify sample sizes. While animal work is consistent, no pooled meta-analysis confirms agreement across studies. The human data addresses mitochondrial and performance outcomes rather than inflammation directly, creating some inconsistency in outcome measurement.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2026 systematic review of randomized controlled trials in humans summarized effects on muscle health; two RCTs (2025, n=42; and 2022) reported urolithin A improved muscle strength and exercise performance with associated changes in mitochondrial biomarkers. One 2023 mouse study showed that urolithin A inhibited NF-κB and mTOR signaling in a D-galactose aging model, improving muscle outcomes in aged mice.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Verified human participant counts are modest (~42 from one trial), and effect estimates may be unstable with such small samples. A single systematic review exists but has not been independently replicated; human and animal evidence come from different methodologies.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Five human studies were identified, including two RCTs with verified sample sizes (2025, n=42; 2022, n=66) and a 2026 systematic review. Together, ~108 participants across the identified trials showed improvements in muscle endurance and performance markers after urolithin A supplementation. All five studies were human-based; no animal studies on endurance were among the records retrieved.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Verified participant counts across reported trials are modest (~108 total), limiting the stability of effect estimates. Only one systematic review exists and has not been independently verified; consistency across the small number of trials has not been formally pooled or confirmed.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Three human studies were retrieved: a 2025 RCT (n=42) on running performance and recovery, a 2022 RCT on overall exercise performance and mitochondrial health, and a 2025 unclassified study in academy soccer players. All three reported improvements in exercise performance or related biomarkers after urolithin A supplementation.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Verified sample size is modest (~42 from one trial); the total across all three studies is small, making effect estimates potentially unstable. No animal studies on this outcome were retrieved, and the human trials are few and not yet pooled in a robust meta-analysis.

urolithin a::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::2.evidence_base: The research on urolithin A is mixed in maturity. Inflammation and muscle outcomes rest on a foundation of numerous animal studies (13 and 1, respectively) paired with small human randomized trials (2 and 3 confirmed trials per outcome), totaling roughly 42–108 verified human participants across the records shown. Endurance and exercise performance evidence is exclusively human-based, while gut/digestion has only animal support. Most human trials are recent (2022–2025), but sample sizes remain modest and no large-scale or long-term human studies appear in the records provided. This means confidence in human efficacy is moderate—plausible but not yet robust.
urolithin a::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::2.emerging_research: Recent work (2025–2026) has expanded focus to neuroinflammation in Parkinson's disease, sepsis-induced lung injury, and rheumatoid arthritis, all in animal models. A 2026 systematic review on muscle health in humans suggests the field is beginning to synthesize human trial data. Soccer player and aging populations are now represented in human trials, broadening the tested demographics. These directions are early and mostly unconfirmed in humans, but suggest clinicians and researchers are exploring urolithin A beyond simple performance enhancement.
urolithin a::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::2.open_questions: Among the studies retrieved here, human evidence is concentrated in young or middle-aged athletes; long-term safety and efficacy in older adults, children, or people with specific diseases remain largely absent from the records. No human trials longer than the durations implied in the study titles (typically weeks to a few months) appear in the data provided. Gut and digestive outcomes rest entirely on animal models; the mechanisms seen in mice may or may not apply to human microbiota and intestinal physiology. The retrieved records do not allow assessment of whether such research exists elsewhere—only that it is not present in the ~40 abstracts shown per outcome.
urolithin a::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::2.caveats: Urolithin A is typically a synthetic, orally bioavailable supplement; quality and purity vary by manufacturer, and it is not FDA-approved for medical claims. It may interact with medications that affect inflammation or mitochondrial function (e.g., some statins, NSAIDs), and people with severe gastrointestinal disease or those taking immunosuppressants should consult a clinician before use. Pregnant and nursing individuals should avoid supplementation due to lack of safety data in these populations.

sulforaphane::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::.what_it_is: Sulforaphane (C₆H₁₁NOS₂, molecular weight 177.3) is an isothiocyanate compound found naturally in cruciferous vegetables, especially broccoli sprouts. It is produced when the plant enzyme myrosinase breaks down the glucosinolate glucoraphanin—a process triggered by chewing, chopping, or digestion. People typically consume it either by eating broccoli sprouts raw, taking broccoli sprout extracts, or using purified sulforaphane supplements in powder or capsule form.
sulforaphane::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::.how_it_works: Sulforaphane activates the cellular stress-response pathway centered on the protein Nrf2 (nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2). In healthy cells, Nrf2 is normally bound to a protein called Keap1, which keeps it inactive in the cytoplasm. Sulforaphane disrupts this binding, freeing Nrf2 to enter the cell nucleus, where it switches on genes that produce antioxidant and detoxifying enzymes—including NAD(P)H quinone oxidoreductase (NQO1) and glutathione S-transferases (GSTs). This upregulation increases the cell's capacity to neutralize reactive oxygen species and clear damaged proteins, which is why sulforaphane is thought to reduce oxidative stress and inflammation. The compound also appears to influence other stress-sensing pathways, including PI3K/Akt signaling and possibly NF-κB (a key inflammatory transcription factor), though human evidence for the latter remains inconsistent.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Among the 8 studies retrieved (2 human, 6 animal), human evidence comes from a 2025 meta-analysis of 333 participants investigating sulforaphane in autism spectrum disorder and a 2024 randomized controlled trial (n=30) in hemodialysis patients. The autism meta-analysis found sulforaphane associated with reduced inflammatory markers, while the hemodialysis trial found no significant change in NRF2 or NF-κB mRNA expression—suggesting the anti-inflammatory mechanism does not always translate in this population. Animal studies from 2021–2019 showed sulforaphane reduced skin aging and liver damage through Nrf2 pathway activation, and attenuated arsenic-induced kidney toxicity.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Two human studies with ~363 verified participants provide direct evidence, but they show mixed results and cover narrow populations (autism and hemodialysis); a single meta-analysis supports the effect but lacks independent replication. The true sample size across human studies is larger than verified (most abstracts omit numbers), but consistency remains uncertain because one controlled trial in hemodialysis found no effect on the proposed inflammatory markers.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Of 13 retrieved studies (4 human, 9 animal), human evidence includes a 2025 meta-analysis of 333 participants (autism spectrum disorder), a 2025 phase II RCT in former smokers at high risk for lung cancer, a 2024 RCT (n=30) in hemodialysis patients, and an unclassified 2021 study on muscle soreness in young adults. The autism meta-analysis and phase II lung cancer trial support anxiolytic or stress-reducing effects, though details on anxiety-specific outcomes in the lung cancer trial and muscle-soreness study are not specified in the abstracts. Animal studies (2023–2021) examined behavioral and reproductive stress responses.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Four human studies with ~363 verified participants across anxiety or stress-related outcomes provide Moderate support, but a single meta-analysis forms the main efficacy claim without independent replication. Heterogeneous study designs (autism, oncology, exercise recovery) and inconsistent outcome reporting limit confidence in generalizability; the true total sample is likely larger, but precision across the field remains unclear from the records provided.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Only 3 studies were retrieved (1 human, 2 animal/in vitro). The single human study was a 2024 RCT (n=30) in hemodialysis patients examining NRF2 and NF-κB expression but not direct cardiovascular outcomes. Animal and in vitro studies from 2020 and 2023 explored reductive stress in myogenic differentiation and sulforaphane's effects on platelet mitochondrial dysfunction via the glycoprotein VI pathway, suggesting a plausible mechanism but no human cardiovascular efficacy data.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Evidence is scarce and lacks direct human cardiovascular outcomes. The single human study (n=30) does not measure blood pressure, cholesterol, arterial function, or other clinical cardiovascular endpoints. Animal and in vitro data hint at potential mechanisms but do not reliably translate to human cardiovascular benefit.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Only 1 study was retrieved, a 2021 animal study in which dietary sulforaphane ameliorated skin aging through activation of the Keap1-Nrf2 pathway in mice. No human studies on skin appearance or aging are present in the records.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Evidence is animal-only and does not include human trials. Findings in mice do not reliably translate to human skin physiology, and the single study is insufficient to establish even preliminary human efficacy.

sulforaphane::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::.evidence_base: The retrieved literature comprises 25 studies: 11 human (including 2 meta-analyses, 4 RCTs, 1 phase II trial, and several unclassified designs) and 14 animal or in vitro studies. Most human evidence clusters around two topics—autism spectrum disorder and hemodialysis—reflected in the same meta-analysis and RCT appearing across multiple outcomes. Studies span 2017–2025, with a concentration in recent years (2023–2025). The dominance of animal research (56% of studies retrieved) and reliance on a single human meta-analysis for much of the Moderate-grade evidence indicate that human efficacy is supported but narrow in scope and not yet independently replicated across independent trials. Confidence is therefore Moderate overall, not Strong.
sulforaphane::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::.emerging_research: Recent directions include sulforaphane's role in autism spectrum disorder (2025 meta-analysis), its investigation in former smokers at high risk for lung cancer (2025 phase II trial), and its effects on reproductive and meiotic health in animal models (2023 studies on semen storage and oocyte function). A 2021 study examined muscle soreness recovery after eccentric exercise in humans. These areas suggest expanding clinical interest beyond traditional antioxidant/anti-inflammatory claims, though human evidence remains preliminary or absent in most of these applications.
sulforaphane::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::.open_questions: Among the records retrieved, no studies follow participants beyond a few weeks to months—long-term safety and sustained efficacy are not visible. Human evidence concentrates on autism and hemodialysis; other populations (healthy adults, aging, athletes) appear minimally if at all in the sample. The skin / appearance outcome rests on a single animal study, and cardiovascular outcomes have no human trials despite plausible mechanism. It is important to note that the app has retrieved only a ~40-abstract sample per outcome; these gaps describe what is absent *in the provided records*, not necessarily what is missing from the broader literature.
sulforaphane::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::.caveats: Sulforaphane supplements are widely available but vary in concentration and bioavailability; broccoli sprouts must be fresh or properly processed to retain glucoraphanin and myrosinase activity. The compound is generally well tolerated, but individuals taking warfarin or other anticoagulants should consult their healthcare provider, as cruciferous vegetables can interact with vitamin K metabolism. Quality and purity of supplements vary; third-party testing is advisable. Pregnant or breastfeeding individuals should seek medical guidance before supplementing beyond dietary intake.

astaxanthin::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::3.what_it_is: Astaxanthin (C₄₀H₅₂O₄, molecular weight 596.8) is a red carotenoid pigment produced naturally by microalgae, krill, and other marine organisms. It is the same molecule that gives salmon and flamingos their characteristic pink-red color. People typically consume it as a supplement derived from cultivated microalgae (Haematococcus pluvialis) or from krill oil, in oral capsule form.
astaxanthin::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::3.how_it_works: Astaxanthin is a lipophilic (fat-soluble) antioxidant that crosses cell membranes and the blood–brain barrier, allowing it to scavenge free radicals throughout the body. It has an unusually long conjugated polyene chain (nine conjugated double bonds) that makes it exceptionally efficient at quenching reactive oxygen species and singlet oxygen. Additionally, astaxanthin appears to modulate inflammatory signaling pathways—including NF-κB and MAPK cascades—and can upregulate the body's own antioxidant defenses like superoxide dismutase and catalase. This dual action against oxidative stress and inflammation is the basis for its proposed effects on cardiovascular, metabolic, and immune outcomes.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2022 meta-analysis of 380 participants found that astaxanthin supplementation mildly reduced oxidative stress and inflammatory biomarkers. Multiple RCTs conducted between 2023–2024 (including a 28-participant trial on serum inflammatory markers and ER stress-related gene expression, and a study in endometriosis patients) reported reductions in inflammatory markers. A 2021 systematic review examined skin aging outcomes, and a 2024 systematic review assessed reproductive outcomes, both retrieving human evidence on inflammatory endpoints.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Eighteen human studies and nine animal studies were retrieved, but human evidence is concentrated in 8 primary trials and 3 pooled analyses—below the threshold for a Strong grade. Verified sample sizes across disclosed studies total approximately 802 participants, and many abstracts lack sample-size reporting, so true total enrollment is substantially higher; however, the relative scarcity of large, independently replicated trials and absence of consensus on clinical magnitude of benefit keep this at Moderate.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Fourteen human studies and seven animal studies were retrieved. A 2008 RCT (n=66) in renal transplant patients showed astaxanthin reduced arterial stiffness, oxidative stress, and inflammation versus placebo. Two 2024 RCTs examined cardiovascular markers during structured exercise (CrossFit training and high-intensity functional training), with one 12-participant trial reporting decreased adipokines and improved cardiovascular markers. A 2022 systematic review focused on microRNA expression in cardiovascular disease, and a 2026 systematic review characterized astaxanthin's antioxidant and anti-inflammatory roles in human health.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Verified participant counts across disclosed studies total approximately 215, with most abstracts omitting exact sample sizes. No pooled meta-analysis confirms consistency among the available trials; individual studies show benefit but lack independent replication at scale. This yields Moderate confidence rather than Strong.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Six human and ten animal studies were retrieved. A 2018 RCT (n=44) in type 2 diabetes patients reported that astaxanthin improved glucose metabolism and reduced blood pressure. A 2024 RCT examined impacts on insulin resistance, lipid profile, blood pressure, and oxidative stress. Two meta-analyses (2021 and 2020) pooling data from human obesity and metabolic disease models described astaxanthin's effects on glycemic biomarkers. A 2023 unclassified human study reported reduced carbohydrate oxidation rates during exercise in overweight individuals, and a 2025 study described microRNA and lysophosphatidylcholine modulation in type 2 diabetes.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Verified participants across disclosed studies total approximately 186 across 4 trials; most studies do not report sample sizes in their abstracts. Multiple trials exist but no pooled analysis has confirmed consistency of effect. Heterogeneity and modest trial volume hold this at Moderate pending larger or more uniform evidence.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Seven human and seven animal studies were retrieved. A 2018 RCT (n=44) in type 2 diabetes patients showed astaxanthin improved glucose metabolism and lipid markers. A 2021 RCT (n=53) in healthy volunteers reported beneficial effects on glucose metabolism and modified LDL. A 2024 RCT examined lipid profile changes alongside insulin resistance and blood pressure. A 2021 meta-analysis pooled obesity-associated disease models, and a 2026 unclassified study (n=80) assessed lipid profile changes with inflammatory markers.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Verified participant counts total approximately 177 across 3 disclosed trials; most abstracts omit sample sizes. Only a single meta-analysis or systematic review conclusion is available in the retrieved records, and it has not yet been independently replicated or verified by another pooled analysis. This limits confidence to Moderate.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Three human studies were retrieved, with no animal studies in this category. A 2023 RCT reported that astaxanthin supplementation did not affect markers of muscle damage or inflammation after exercise-induced injury. A second 2023 unclassified study found astaxanthin reduced subjective markers of muscle soreness following eccentric exercise in resistance-trained participants. A third 2023 unclassified study reported that astaxanthin supplementation countered exercise-induced decreases in immune-related plasma proteins.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only three human studies are available, and sample sizes could not be verified from the abstracts; this imprecision prevents a higher grade. Results are also mixed—one trial found no effect on muscle damage markers, while others reported benefits for soreness and immune protein preservation. The evidence base is too small and findings too inconsistent for strong confidence.

astaxanthin::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::3.evidence_base: The retrieved literature on astaxanthin comprises 81 total records across the five outcomes, with 48 human studies and 33 animal studies. Human evidence dominates and comes primarily from RCTs and meta-analyses conducted between 2008 and 2026, with most trials appearing in the past five years. The studies focus heavily on inflammation, cardiovascular, metabolic, and lipid outcomes; most trials are small to moderate in size (verified samples range from 12 to 380 per study), and many abstracts do not disclose exact participant numbers, making the true cumulative enrollment substantially larger than verified counts. This recent, human-centered evidence base suggests moderate confidence in astaxanthin's anti-inflammatory and metabolic effects, but lacks the scale and consistency of pooled evidence required for a higher tier.
astaxanthin::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::3.emerging_research: Recent work (2024–2026) has expanded beyond broad antioxidant endpoints to mechanistic targets: microRNA modulation in cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes, lysophosphatidylcholine remodeling, and ER stress-mediated apoptosis pathways. A 2024 systematic review examined reproductive outcomes in endometriosis and female fertility, suggesting astaxanthin may influence hormone-related inflammation. Exercise-focused trials are exploring whether astaxanthin enhances recovery and immune resilience during high-intensity training, though early data are mixed. These directions remain preliminary in humans and warrant larger, longer-term confirmation.
astaxanthin::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::3.open_questions: Among the studies retrieved here, no trial followed participants beyond 12 weeks, and most studies do not specify trial duration in their abstracts; long-term safety and efficacy over months to years remain uncharacterized in the provided records. Sample sizes vary widely (from 12 to 380), and most abstracts omit exact participant counts, making it difficult to assess whether observed benefits persist across diverse populations and doses. The retrieved records show very few trials in certain subgroups (e.g., pediatric, elderly, or disease-specific populations beyond type 2 diabetes and transplant recipients), and it is unclear whether benefits generalize. Note: this assessment reflects only the ~40 studies per outcome provided to me; the full astaxanthin literature may be substantially larger.
astaxanthin::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::3.caveats: Astaxanthin is a dietary supplement and is not FDA-regulated as a drug; quality, purity, and dose consistency vary across commercial products. It is fat-soluble and may accumulate in fatty tissues; long-term safety at high doses is not well-characterized in the retrieved studies. Astaxanthin may theoretically interact with anticoagulants, antiplatelet agents, or immunosuppressants; individuals on these medications, pregnant or nursing women, and those with shellfish allergy should consult a healthcare provider before supplementing. The retrieved evidence is insufficient to establish efficacy in any condition as a substitute for medical treatment.

dhea::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::faf04644.what_it_is: DHEA (dehydroepiandrosterone) is a steroid hormone naturally produced by the adrenal glands in both men and women.
