It is a precursor to testosterone and estrogen, meaning the body can convert it into these sex hormones. DHEA is available as an over-the-counter oral supplement in the United States, derived synthetically from plant sources (usually wild yam or soy), and declines with age — DHEA levels peak in the 20s and drop significantly by age 70.
dhea::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::faf04644.how_it_works: DHEA circulates in the bloodstream and crosses the blood-brain barrier, where it and its metabolite DHEAS (dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate) interact with multiple receptor systems. It acts partly as a direct hormone and partly as a prohormone — the body converts some DHEA into testosterone and estrogen, amplifying those hormonal signals. It also appears to modulate glucocorticoid and mineraloocorticoid receptors, affect inflammatory pathways, and influence neurotransmitter function in the brain. These overlapping mechanisms explain why DHEA touches so many body systems: reproduction, metabolism, cognition, and immune regulation.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Four human randomized controlled trials and one animal study examined DHEA's effect on testosterone. A 1999 RCT in young men (n=19) showed acute DHEA administration raised free testosterone; a 2016 RCT (n=32) examined testosterone supplementation alongside DHEA; and a 2013 RCT measured free testosterone response in middle-aged and young men after high-intensity exercise. A 2018 clinical trial (NCCTG N10C1) studied systemic and local effects of vaginal DHEA. Across these studies, DHEA does elevate testosterone levels, but sample sizes in two trials (verified at ~51 participants total) were modest, making the size of the effect uncertain.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: This outcome earned Moderate rather than Strong because the verified sample is small and spread across few studies, creating imprecision; the effect direction is clear (DHEA does raise testosterone), but the magnitude is unstable. The included animal study did not contradict the human findings.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Seven human studies—three systematic reviews (2023, 2014, 2000) and four randomized or observational trials—examined DHEA and mood/depression outcomes. A 2000 RCT studied DHEA treatment in HIV-positive patients and measured mood effects; a 2015 RCT examined DHEA and DHEAS in relation to emotional processing; and a 2023 systematic review surveyed the association between endogenous DHEA and depression in postmenopausal women. One trial with verified sample size (n=16) was small, making the overall effect estimate unstable, though the body of evidence suggests an association between DHEA and mood regulation.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The Moderate grade reflects consistent human evidence across multiple study types but imprecision from a very small verified sample in one trial (n=16); the effect on depression and mood has not been definitively quantified, though the direction is promising. No animal studies contradicted the findings.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: One human RCT (2000, part of the DHEAge study) and one animal study examined cardiovascular outcomes. The animal study (2013) found DHEA prevented glucocorticoid and mineraloocorticoid receptor-induced heart effects in isolated tissues, suggesting a protective mechanism. The human RCT contributed to the DHEAge observational and interventional work on aging and cardiovascular parameters, though sample sizes could not be verified from the abstracts provided.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: This outcome is graded Moderate because sample sizes are unconfirmed and the human evidence base is very thin (one trial). The direction of effect is plausible from animal data and one human study, but precision is unconfirmed, preventing a higher grade despite consistent findings.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Eight human studies and one animal study addressed cognition and DHEA. Three systematic reviews (2020 on Alzheimer's disease, 2000 on cognition and well-being) and multiple RCTs were included: a 2001 RCT (n=46) in older men measured salivary cortisol, DHEA, and cognitive measures; a 2012 RCT examined DHEA in HIV-positive patients with depression; a 2006 RCT studied DHEA in postmenopausal women; and a 2015 RCT assessed DHEA/DHEAS and emotional processing. Verified samples across two trials totaled ~70 participants, and the studies varied in design and population, suggesting DHEA may support cognition but with uncertain effect size.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The Moderate grade reflects consistent human evidence across multiple study designs (systematic reviews and RCTs) but imprecision from modest verified sample sizes (~70 across 2 trials) and heterogeneous populations. The cognitive effect is suggestive but not yet precisely quantified.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Six human trials and four animal studies examined DHEA's effect on fasting glucose, insulin, and insulin resistance. A 2020 meta-analysis summarized the influence of DHEA on these metabolic parameters; six RCTs followed, including studies in 2006 (elderly men and women), 2004 (n=56 in elderly, and n=13 in patients), 1999 (n=19 young men), and 1998 (n=10) with a 100 mg daily DHEA dose for six months. Verified samples across five trials totaled ~108 participants. The meta-analysis showed an association, but its conclusion has not been independently replicated in the records provided here, and animal models showed similar metabolic effects.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderate reflects multiple human trials with consistent direction (DHEA improves insulin sensitivity and glucose regulation) but modest and fragmented sample sizes, and reliance on a single meta-analysis without independent replication. The effect is not precisely quantified, and heterogeneity in study designs and populations limits certainty.

dhea::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::faf04644.evidence_base: The research base for DHEA includes 26 human studies (dominated by randomized controlled trials and systematic reviews from 1998–2023) and 6 animal studies across five major health domains. The human evidence is more substantial than animal work, and most studies are from the past two decades, lending reasonable currency. However, sample sizes are typically modest (median verified samples under 50 per trial), and studies often involve small subpopulations (HIV patients, postmenopausal women, elderly adults, young men), meaning results may not generalize broadly. The consistency of direction across outcomes and study types is a strength; the fragmentation and imprecision of individual trials is a limitation.
dhea::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::faf04644.emerging_research: Recent work (2020–2023) has focused on DHEA's role in Alzheimer's disease and cognitive aging, with systematic reviews examining the link between endogenous DHEA levels and depression in specific populations like postmenopausal women. Animal studies continue to probe mechanisms—particularly DHEA's effects on cardiac and metabolic receptor signaling—suggesting ongoing interest in its protective or regulatory roles in aging-related disease. These directions are early and have not yet translated into large, definitive human trials.
dhea::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::faf04644.open_questions: Among the studies retrieved here, most human trials lasted weeks to months (the longest verified continuous treatment was 6 months in 1998); none of the records show long-term safety or efficacy data beyond one year, leaving questions about sustained benefit and safety with prolonged use. The studies retrieved involve older adults, postmenopausal women, HIV-positive patients, and young men, but coverage of other populations (children, premenopausal women, non-Western populations, people with specific metabolic disorders) is absent from these records. This sample of ~40 abstracts per outcome does not represent the complete literature, so gaps apparent here may be filled elsewhere in the broader field.
dhea::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::faf04644.caveats: DHEA is a hormone precursor and can elevate testosterone and estrogen; it should be used cautiously by individuals with hormone-sensitive conditions (breast cancer, prostate cancer, endometriosis) without medical supervision. Quality and purity of supplements vary widely since DHEA is not FDA-regulated as a drug; look for third-party testing. DHEA may interact with other medications and can cause side effects including acne, hair loss, and mood changes at higher doses; pregnant and breastfeeding women should avoid it, and anyone with liver disease should consult a physician before use.

pregnenolone::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::.what_it_is: Pregnenolone (C₂₁H₃₂O₂) is a steroid hormone synthesized primarily in the mitochondria of the adrenal glands and gonads, and also produced in the brain. It serves as a precursor to other steroid hormones including DHEA, progesterone, and cortisol. People typically take pregnenolone as an oral supplement in capsule or tablet form, often derived from wild yam or soy sources, though the body must convert these plant sterols to pregnenolone.
pregnenolone::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::.how_it_works: Pregnenolone is a neurosteroid — a steroid hormone that acts directly in the central nervous system — and crosses the blood–brain barrier to affect neural function. It enhances the activity of NMDA receptors (glutamate receptors involved in learning and memory) and modulates GABAergic signaling (the brain's main inhibitory system), which can influence cognition, mood regulation, and stress response. The compound also promotes neuroplasticity and may protect neurons from stress-induced damage. These mechanisms suggest it could support memory formation, emotional stability, and cognitive resilience, though the clinical significance of these effects in healthy or diseased populations remains to be fully established.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Two human randomized controlled trials (one in 2010 with n=70 in dual diagnosis patients, and one in 2009 with n=21 in schizophrenia patients) reported cognitive improvements with pregnenolone supplementation. A 2014 animal study in adult male rats found that pregnenolone sulphate enhanced spatial orientation and object discrimination. Across the human trials, the combined sample was modest (~91 participants), and improvements were observed in cognition and negative symptoms in the schizophrenia cohort and in dual-diagnosis populations.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The evidence grade reflects human data showing benefit, but the sample size is small and spread across only two trials, making the effect estimate prone to statistical instability. The grade 'Moderate' indicates meaningful preliminary human support without the larger or longer evidence base needed for a 'Strong' rating.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Three human randomized controlled trials totaling ~161 participants examined pregnenolone for mood and depression: a 2014 trial (n=80) in bipolar depression showed benefit, a 2010 trial (n=70) in dual diagnosis patients reported mood improvements, and a 2017 trial (n=11) measured changes in a biomarker (microtubule-associated protein 2) linked to bipolar depression. A 2013 animal study examined pregnenolone sulphate's role in spatial orientation and cognition. The human trials involved primarily bipolar or dual-diagnosis populations.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The 'Moderate' grade reflects consistent findings across three human trials, but the combined sample remains modest (~161 participants) and scattered across different patient groups, limiting confidence in the true effect size and generalizability. Imprecision is the main limitation noted.

pregnenolone::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::.evidence_base: The research base for pregnenolone consists mostly of small to modest-sized randomized controlled trials conducted between 2009 and 2017, predominantly in psychiatric populations (schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, dual diagnosis). Human studies outnumber animal work, though the total human sample across outcomes remains under 200 participants. The trials are relatively recent but not numerous; most are single-center proof-of-concept or early-phase designs rather than large, multi-site confirmatory trials. This pattern suggests early promise in specific neuropsychiatric conditions, but confidence in effect size and durability is limited by sample modesty and the lack of large-scale replication.
pregnenolone::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::.emerging_research: Recent work has focused on pregnenolone's role as a neuromodulator in psychiatric disorders, particularly examining its effects on specific biomarkers (such as microtubule-associated protein 2 in bipolar depression) and its interaction with glutamatergic and GABAergic signaling. Animal studies continue to explore pregnenolone sulphate in cognition and spatial learning, suggesting a potential role in age-related or stress-related cognitive decline. These directions remain early; translation to broader clinical populations and longer-term outcomes has not yet been extensively studied in the retrieved literature.
pregnenolone::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::.open_questions: Among the studies retrieved here, all human trials were conducted in psychiatric patient populations (schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, dual diagnosis); no trials in healthy volunteers or other disease groups (e.g., age-related cognitive decline, healthy aging) appear in the sample provided. Trial durations were not specified in the available abstracts, but the modest sample sizes and early-phase design suggest short-term follow-up is likely. It is unclear from these records whether pregnenolone's benefits persist over months or years, or how it performs against standard treatments. Note: you are seeing only a sample of ~40 abstracts per outcome, so other published or unpublished work may exist in the broader literature.
pregnenolone::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::.caveats: Pregnenolone is a hormone precursor and may affect endocrine balance; long-term safety in humans is not well characterized in the retrieved studies. Quality and purity of commercial supplements vary widely and are often unregulated; content should be verified through third-party testing. Pregnant women, individuals with hormone-sensitive cancers, and those taking other hormonal medications (including birth control or HRT) should consult a healthcare provider before use, as pregnenolone may interact with endocrine function.

vitamin d::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::a4b.what_it_is: Vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol, C27H44O) is a fat-soluble steroid hormone precursor synthesized in skin upon sun exposure or obtained from dietary sources like fatty fish, egg yolks, and fortified milk. The body converts it first in the liver to 25-hydroxyvitamin D (the storage form, used to assess status), then in the kidneys to 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (the active hormone form). People typically obtain it through diet, supplements (tablets, capsules, oral solutions), or sunlight exposure.
vitamin d::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::a4b.how_it_works: Vitamin D functions as a hormone by binding to the vitamin D receptor (VDR), a nuclear receptor present in nearly all cell types. Once activated, the VDR-vitamin D complex enters the nucleus and regulates the expression of hundreds of genes involved in calcium and phosphate homeostasis, immune function, inflammation, and vascular health. In the kidneys specifically, vitamin D receptor activation modulates how the kidneys reabsorb and excrete minerals, regulate blood pressure, and manage inflammatory pathways—processes directly relevant to kidney function. This hormonal signaling affects parathyroid hormone regulation, endothelial cell stability, and production of inflammatory markers like cytokines, all of which influence kidney disease progression.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Five randomized controlled trials in humans examining vitamin D receptor activation—via paricalcitol, ergocalciferol, and other vitamin D compounds—in patients with chronic kidney disease show effects on inflammatory markers, microcirculatory function, and endothelial stability. A 2017 RCT (n=12) found vitamin D receptor activation reduced inflammatory cytokines and plasma microRNAs in moderate chronic kidney disease; a 2014 RCT (n=38) examined ergocalciferol's effects on microcirculation in CKD with concurrent vitamin D deficiency. One 2018 animal study in uremic rats demonstrated vitamin D attenuates endothelial dysfunction and maintains human endothelial stability in vitro. A 2018 animal mechanistic study examined serum 24,25-dihydroxyvitamin D and kidney disease associations.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The evidence is graded Moderate rather than Strong because the human trial sample sizes are modest (the two largest verified studies reported only ~50 participants combined), and effect estimates may be unstable. While multiple RCTs show plausible benefits on kidney-relevant biomarkers (inflammation, endothelial function) in CKD patients, the small sample sizes limit confidence that results are reproducible and applicable broadly.

vitamin d::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::a4b.evidence_base: The retrieved records for kidney function comprise five human studies (mostly RCTs) and one animal study conducted between 2008 and 2018. The human studies are relatively small, focused on chronic kidney disease populations, and primarily measure intermediate outcomes (cytokines, microRNAs, microcirculatory markers, endothelial function) rather than hard clinical endpoints like disease progression or mortality. This is a hormone-based intervention with a mechanistically plausible link to kidney health, but the evidence base as shown here is narrow in scope and modest in scale, reflecting early-stage clinical investigation rather than large, long-term confirmatory trials.
vitamin d::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::a4b.emerging_research: Recent work has explored vitamin D's effects on specific pathways in kidney disease—including endothelial dysfunction and systemic inflammation—suggesting that vitamin D receptor activation may slow progression in early to moderate CKD. Animal models continue to demonstrate protective effects on vascular stability and inflammatory markers. However, these findings remain preliminary in humans; the research shown here does not yet establish whether vitamin D supplementation materially slows kidney disease decline or improves clinical outcomes in larger, longer trials.
vitamin d::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::a4b.open_questions: Among the studies retrieved here, trial sizes are small (n=12 to ~38 in the largest RCTs) and most were conducted over relatively short periods; none of the records retrieved specify long-term follow-up duration or hard clinical outcomes (e.g., progression to dialysis, change in glomerular filtration rate over years). The retrieved studies focus on chronic kidney disease populations; whether vitamin D has similar effects in other kidney conditions or in people with normal kidney function is not clear from these records. This sample of ~6 studies represents only a portion of the literature; conclusions about what is or is not known in the field overall cannot be drawn from these records alone.
vitamin d::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::a4b.caveats: Vitamin D is generally well-tolerated at physiologic doses, but excessive supplementation (>10,000 IU daily long-term) can cause hypercalcemia and hyperphosphatemia, which are particularly risky in chronic kidney disease patients who cannot excrete excess minerals efficiently; people with CKD should have vitamin D status monitored and supplementation guided by a nephrologist. Quality varies among supplements; third-party testing (USP, NSF, ConsumerLab) helps verify dose accuracy. Vitamin D interacts with medications affecting calcium absorption and corticosteroid metabolism; inform your healthcare provider if using high-dose supplements, especially if you have kidney disease, take bisphosphonates, or use certain anti-seizure drugs.

progesterone::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::.what_it_is: Progesterone (C₂₁H₃₀O₂) is a naturally occurring steroid hormone produced primarily by the ovaries and adrenal glands in people with female reproductive anatomy. It is also synthesized pharmaceutically from plant sources (most commonly wild yam or soy) and is available as oral tablets, vaginal gels, intramuscular injections, and transdermal creams. In the body, progesterone acts as a key regulator of the menstrual cycle, pregnancy, and mood—and declines sharply after menopause.
progesterone::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::.how_it_works: Progesterone works by binding to progesterone receptors (PR-A and PR-B) located in the brain, uterus, breasts, and other tissues, where it modulates gene expression and cellular signaling. In the brain specifically, it influences neurotransmitter systems—particularly GABA (a calming neurotransmitter) and serotonin—and may enhance sleep-promoting pathways. It also interacts with other hormonal systems, including estrogen signaling and the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, which governs stress and circadian rhythm regulation. These overlapping mechanisms could plausibly affect mood, cognition, sleep architecture, and even testosterone balance, though the precise clinical significance remains incompletely characterized.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Among the three studies retrieved, one human observational study (2011) examined effects of progesterone and testosterone on cocaine self-administration and discrimination in female subjects, while two animal studies (2011, 2006) investigated progesterone's interactions with testosterone in brain injury models and cultured cells. The human study did not report direct testosterone measurements, and animal work focused on neuroprotection rather than hormonal outcomes per se, limiting direct evidence of progesterone's effect on circulating testosterone levels.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Evidence is split between a single human observational study and animal models, neither directly establishing progesterone's effect on testosterone in typical physiological conditions. Sample sizes could not be verified from abstracts, introducing imprecision; this combination of limited human data and unconfirmed sample precision keeps the grade at Moderate rather than Strong.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Four studies were retrieved: a 2005 meta-analysis (n=108) on estrogen for schizophrenia, a 2023 systematic review (n=457) on progesterone derivatives for catamenial epilepsy, a 2008 RCT (n=33) on hormone therapy effects on sleep and cognition in postmenopausal women, and a 2025 animal study on estrogen–progesterone combination therapy in behavioral impairment. The human work primarily addresses cognition indirectly through seizure control or sleep improvement rather than direct cognitive testing, and the largest pooled analysis focused on estrogen rather than progesterone alone.

The retrieved human evidence consisted of one primary RCT and two pooled analyses. The cognition outcome is not directly isolated in most studies; instead, it emerges as a secondary benefit related to improved sleep or seizure suppression in women with epilepsy or menopausal symptoms. Only one animal study (2025) directly examined cognition in a progesterone combination model.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Limited primary human evidence (one RCT with n=33, plus pooled analyses) falls below the threshold for a Strong grade. Cognition is often inferred indirectly from other outcomes (seizure frequency, sleep quality) rather than measured with dedicated cognitive scales, and the animal study does not independently replicate the human pattern.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Six human studies were retrieved, spanning 2005–2026: a 2012 systematic review, a 2021 RCT on vaginal and intramuscular progesterone in pregnancy, a 2011 RCT showing progesterone prevented sleep disturbances and modulated melatonin/GH/TSH in postmenopausal women, a 2008 RCT (n=33) on estrogen/progesterone effects on sleep pattern, a 2005 RCT on estradiol/progesterone and mood, and a 2026 study (n=36) on micronized progesterone in menopausal hormone replacement. Collectively, these studies report improvements in sleep onset, maintenance, and hormone secretion patterns, particularly in postmenopausal and pregnant populations.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Although six human studies support sleep benefit, verified sample sizes from only two studies totaled ~69 participants, introducing imprecision; effect estimates may be unstable with such modest confirmed numbers. Additionally, a single meta-analysis or systematic review exists but has not been independently replicated or verified in the retrieved records. This combination of modest sample confirmation and lack of independent replication holds the grade at Moderate.

progesterone::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::.evidence_base: The retrieved evidence is predominantly human (9 of 13 studies), concentrated in observational designs, RCTs, and systematic reviews published between 2005 and 2026. Most human work involves postmenopausal women, pregnant women, or women with epilepsy; animal studies are few and focus on neuroprotection or behavior in rodent models. The research is moderately recent but not uniformly large-scale: verified sample sizes are often small or unconfirmed from abstracts. This mix of real-world human data and controlled trials, combined with limitations in sample size transparency and consistency of independent replication, suggests a reasonable but cautious evidence base—stronger for sleep than for hormonal or cognitive claims.
progesterone::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::.emerging_research: A 2025 animal study examined combined estrogen–progesterone therapy for behavioral impairments via circLrp1b and autophagy pathways, suggesting a mechanistic angle for neuroprotection that has not yet been tested in humans. Recent work (2021, 2026) has focused on different delivery routes (vaginal, intramuscular, micronized formulations) in pregnancy and menopausal hormone replacement, hinting at refinements in clinical application rather than fundamentally new outcomes. These directions remain early-stage and mostly unconfirmed in large human trials.
progesterone::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::.open_questions: Among the studies retrieved here, almost all human work enrolled postmenopausal or pregnant women; evidence in other populations (e.g., younger cycling women, men, or those with primary hormone disorders) is absent from this sample. Trial durations range from short-term (weeks to months in most RCTs) to longer follow-up in systematic reviews, but no study in the retrieved records appears to examine progesterone beyond 6–12 months, limiting knowledge of long-term safety or sustained efficacy. The mechanism by which progesterone improves sleep (e.g., via GABA, melatonin, or circadian pathways) is inferred but not directly proven in the human studies provided.
progesterone::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::.caveats: Progesterone is a hormone and should be prescribed and monitored by a healthcare provider; dosing, route, and duration vary widely and depend on individual health status and goals. Quality and purity of over-the-counter or compounded progesterone products can vary; pharmaceutical-grade formulations (e.g., micronized progesterone, transdermal patches) have more consistent bioavailability. Progesterone may interact with other medications (e.g., those metabolized by cytochrome P450 enzymes) and carries documented risks in certain populations (e.g., history of blood clots, breast cancer); it is not appropriate for all users and requires informed discussion with a clinician.

omega-3::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::47c90.what_it_is: Omega-3 (specifically eicosapentaenoic acid, EPA; molecular formula C₂₀H₃₀O₂) is a long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acid with five double bonds. It occurs naturally in fatty cold-water fish, algae, and certain plant oils, and is sold as a dietary supplement in capsule or liquid form. Omega-3 fatty acids are essential nutrients—your body cannot synthesize them, so they must come from diet or supplements.
omega-3::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::47c90.how_it_works: Omega-3 fatty acids integrate into cell membranes throughout the body, where they influence membrane fluidity and the behavior of embedded proteins. They are precursors to signaling molecules called eicosanoids (including prostaglandins and leukotrienes) that regulate inflammation, immune responses, and vascular tone. Omega-3s also activate specific ion channels (such as large-conductance potassium channels) in blood vessel walls, which can lower blood pressure, and they modulate gene expression through nuclear receptors involved in glucose and lipid metabolism. By shifting the balance of pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory mediators, omega-3s help tune down excessive inflammatory responses.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2024 meta-analysis of 2,385 participants found that omega-3 improved endothelial function (the health of blood vessel linings). Additional meta-analyses from 2023 and 2021 examined broad cardiovascular outcomes and the dose–response relationship in intervention trials. A 2021 study reviewed omega-3 effects in patients with hypertriglyceridemia and atherosclerosis. Studies were predominantly pooled analyses of existing trials rather than large new randomized trials.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The evidence base includes four human studies (mostly meta-analyses rather than primary trials) and one animal study, with verified sample sizes in only two of the five records. The reliance on pooled analyses rather than large primary trials limits confidence to the Moderate tier.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Seven human studies examined omega-3's effect on inflammatory markers. A 2026 meta-analysis looked at inflammation and recovery in sports; a 2024 meta-analysis of 853 participants measured inflammatory markers and endothelial function in patients with cardiovascular disease; a 2021 meta-analysis of 751 participants examined long-term effects on inflammatory bowel disease. Two randomized controlled trials (2025 and 2011) directly tested omega-3 supplementation, with the 2011 trial showing reduced inflammation and anxiety in medical students.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Although all seven retrieved studies were human (no animal evidence), only two were primary randomized trials; the others were pooled analyses. Verified participant counts are available for only two studies. This mix of design types and incomplete sample size reporting limits the certainty to Moderate.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Two randomized human trials examined omega-3 with exercise: a 2022 study combined omega-3 with high-protein diet and resistance/vibration exercise, and a 2019 trial studied omega-3 in gastric cancer patients tracking immune and inflammatory profiles. Three animal studies (2018, 2015, 2014) tested omega-3 in models of muscle wasting (Duchenne muscular dystrophy, lipopolysaccharide-induced weight loss, and dexamethasone-induced atrophy). Sample sizes for the human trials could not be verified from the abstracts.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The evidence is split between human and animal studies, with only two human trials and no verified sample sizes reported in the retrieved abstracts. The mixed study types and unconfirmed precision cap the grade at Moderate.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Four human studies addressed blood pressure: a 2024 meta-analysis of 489 participants examined metabolic syndrome and cardiovascular disease; a 2022 meta-analysis of 4,973 participants performed a dose–response analysis of randomized controlled trials; and a landmark 1994 randomized trial of 43 treated hypertensives showed reduction in blood pressure and triglycerides. A 2018 unclassified study reported omega-3 reduced blood pressure but not renal vasoconstriction. Two animal studies examined mechanisms (prenatal omega-3 and blood-brain barrier integrity, and direct activation of potassium channels).
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Four human studies were retrieved, but only one was a primary trial; the others were meta-analyses. The oldest primary trial is from 1994, and the more recent studies rely on pooling prior data. This evidence structure—dominated by meta-analyses—places the grade at Moderate rather than Strong.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Ten human studies (no animal evidence) addressed cognition. A 2023 meta-analysis of 1,135 participants examined the relationship between omega-3 and dementia/cognitive decline in prospective cohorts. A 2020 meta-analysis of 4,247 participants assessed domain-specific effects on cognitive performance in youths. A 2025 systematic review with dose–response meta-analysis focused on cognitive function. Additional systematic reviews (2022, 2021, 2020) examined omega-3 effects during menopause, pregnancy/lactation, and childhood, with one 2020 review including only 10 participants.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Although all ten studies were human and some included large cohorts (up to 4,247), only three were primary studies; six were meta-analyses and systematic reviews. The evidence base leans heavily on pooling and observational data, which is why it achieves Moderate rather than Strong certainty.

omega-3::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::47c90.evidence_base: The research on omega-3 is predominantly human (27 of 33 studies retrieved), reflecting its long history of nutritional and clinical investigation. Most retrieved studies are meta-analyses or systematic reviews—pooled analyses of prior trials and cohort studies—rather than large primary randomized trials. The evidence spans recent work (2025, 2026) back to a foundational 1994 trial, suggesting ongoing interest but also that no recent mega-trials have substantially changed the landscape. This mix of meta-analyses and older primary trials is why most outcomes land at Moderate rather than Strong.
omega-3::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::47c90.emerging_research: Recent studies (2025–2026) show renewed focus on omega-3 in sports recovery and inflammation, as well as refined dose–response analyses to pinpoint optimal intakes. Systematic reviews on pregnancy/lactation and childhood neurodevelopment are expanding the evidence in vulnerable populations. Animal research continues to clarify mechanisms—such as potassium channel activation in vascular smooth muscle and molecular pathways in muscle atrophy—though these have not yet led to new human trials that would elevate overall confidence.
omega-3::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::47c90.open_questions: Among the studies retrieved here, sample sizes are explicitly reported for only 13 of 33 records, making it difficult to assess the overall precision of the evidence base. The retrieved human studies in cognition, inflammation, and cardiovascular outcomes do not distinguish by age group, sex, or baseline health status in a systematic way, so it remains unclear whether effects differ in older adults, younger adults, or disease-specific populations. No studies in the provided records followed participants beyond a few months or years, so long-term safety and durability of benefit are not visible in this sample of the literature.
omega-3::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::47c90.caveats: Omega-3 supplements are generally well tolerated, but high doses may increase bleeding risk (particularly in people on anticoagulants or antiplatelet agents) and can cause gastrointestinal upset. Quality and purity vary among commercial products; users should look for third-party testing (e.g., USP or NSF certification). Fish-based omega-3 may contain mercury or other contaminants if sourced from contaminated waters, whereas algae-based alternatives avoid this risk. Pregnant women, people on blood thinners, or those scheduled for surgery should consult a healthcare provider before supplementing.

fish oil::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::e25e.what_it_is: Fish oil is a lipid-rich extract from fatty fish tissues, containing high concentrations of omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids, particularly eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA, C20H30O2, MW 302.5) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA). It is commonly consumed as a dietary supplement in liquid, capsule, or softgel form. Fish oil has been used in traditional medicine and modern nutrition for decades, with growing research interest in its metabolic and cardiovascular effects.
fish oil::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::e25e.how_it_works: Fish oil's EPA and DHA are incorporated into cell membranes and serve as substrates for specialized signaling molecules called resolvins and protectins, which actively dampen inflammation. These omega-3 fatty acids also displace pro-inflammatory omega-6 polyunsaturates in membrane phospholipids, shifting the balance toward anti-inflammatory eicosanoid production. EPA and DHA activate GPR120 (a G-protein coupled receptor) on immune and epithelial cells, triggering reduced NF-κB signaling and IL-6 secretion. Additionally, fish oil influences hepatic lipid metabolism and cholesterol clearance pathways, and may modulate vascular endothelial function through improved nitric oxide bioavailability and reduced oxidative stress.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Nine human randomized controlled trials and five animal studies examined fish oil's effects on cardiovascular biomarkers and function. Studies ranged from 2007 to 2026 and included populations such as middle-aged and older adults, healthy volunteers (n=26–34 in two trials), and individuals exposed to air pollution. Outcomes measured vascular endothelial function, neurovascular reactivity to stress, and cardiovascular disease markers. Results consistently pointed toward improvements in endothelial markers and cardiovascular stress responses, though the magnitude of benefit varied across trials.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderate grade reflects nine human studies with RCT designs, providing substantive evidence of benefit. However, precision is limited: only 2 of 14 studies disclosed sample sizes (~60 verified participants), and the true total across all trials is substantially larger but unspecified. Inconsistency across trials has been noted but no pooled meta-analysis was retrieved to confirm agreement, so the grade is held at Moderate pending formal synthesis.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Ten human studies (including meta-analyses and systematic reviews from 2020–2025, plus RCTs) and six animal studies evaluated fish oil's anti-inflammatory effects. Human trials examined adults undergoing hemodialysis, patients with psoriasis, those with multiple sclerosis, HIV-positive individuals (n=37 in one trial), and healthy adults performing eccentric exercise. Meta-analyses reviewed 18 randomized controlled trials in psoriasis and multiple systematic reviews in MS. Results generally favored fish oil in reducing inflammatory biomarkers and clinical inflammation, though effect sizes and patient populations varied substantially.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderate grade is supported by 10 human studies, including pooled analyses and RCTs across diverse inflammatory conditions. Precision is limited: only 5 of 16 studies reported sample sizes (~156 verified participants), and most abstracts omitted N values, making the true total unknown. No single pooled analysis confirmed agreement across all retrieved studies, so the grade remains Moderate pending further synthesis and evidence of consistency.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Eight human studies (three primary RCTs, three meta-analyses, and two additional trials spanning 1990–2024) and 12 animal studies examined fish oil's effects on serum lipids and cholesterol. Human trials included patients with type 2 diabetes (meta-analysis of 12 trials), individuals with hyperlipidemia (systematic review and meta-analysis), women with metabolic syndrome (n=14 RCT), and healthy volunteers. Meta-analyses consistently reported modest reductions in triglycerides and LDL cholesterol, with variable effects on HDL. One 2024 systematic review compared fish oil to corn oil on lipid profiles.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderate grade reflects eight human studies including multiple meta-analyses and RCTs. However, precision is substantially limited: only 3 of 20 studies provided verifiable sample sizes (~1,029 participants total), and most abstracts omitted N values. Critically, only 3 primary human studies and 3 pooled analyses were retrieved—below the threshold for the top tier. This reflects limited human-level evidence relative to the volume of animal work, warranting a Moderate rather than Strong classification.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: One human RCT (n=40, 2015) and 13 animal studies (2018–2025) investigated fish oil's effects on liver function and disease. The human trial measured serum lipids, glucose, and fibroblast growth factor-23 (a marker of metabolic health linked to liver function) in patients receiving fish oil supplementation. Animal studies in rodent models examined mechanisms in chronic alcohol-induced liver injury, fatty liver disease, and the effects of paternal obesity on offspring liver health. Results in animal models showed attenuation of liver injury, reduced steatosis, and favorable microbiota shifts; the single human trial showed reductions in serum lipids and glucose.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderate grade is based on a small human evidence base: only 1 human RCT (n=40) and 13 animal studies were retrieved. This imbalance—13 animal versus 1 human study—limits confidence in translating findings to humans. Precision is low: only 2 of 14 studies reported sample sizes (~70 participants), and abstracts for most omitted N values. No pooled analysis of human trials was retrieved, and inconsistency has been noted, so the grade is held at Moderate pending more human evidence.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Four human RCTs (spanning 2003–2025, n=57–871 per trial) and two animal studies examined fish oil's effects on depression and mood symptoms. Human trials included men with angina (n=452), adults with clinical depression (n=77 in a double-blind placebo-controlled trial, 2005), individuals comparing fish oil to krill oil (n=57, 2025), and a large trial of vitamin D supplementation (n=871, 2020) in which fish oil was evaluated. Results showed modest improvements in depressive symptoms in some trials, though effect sizes were variable. Animal studies in postpartum depression and anxiety models demonstrated anti-inflammatory and BDNF-related mechanisms.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderate grade is justified by four human RCTs with designs ranging from small focused trials to large population studies. However, inconsistency is notable: while some trials showed benefit, others were less conclusive, and no pooled meta-analysis of the retrieved studies confirmed consistent agreement. The sample includes only four human studies and two animal studies, a relatively sparse base. The grade reflects meaningful human evidence without strong consensus across trials, appropriate for a Moderate classification pending further synthesis.

fish oil::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::e25e.evidence_base: The evidence base for fish oil spans approximately 14–20 retrieved studies per outcome, predominantly human RCTs and meta-analyses (published 1990–2026), with supplementary animal research. Most human studies are small to moderate in size (n=26–871 per trial); however, sample sizes are omitted in the majority of abstracts, making precise participant counts uncertain. The field is dominated by cardiovascular, inflammatory, and lipid outcomes; human evidence for liver health is sparse (1 RCT, 13 animal studies). Overall, the evidence is recent and increasingly rigorous (several 2024–2026 trials and systematic reviews), though formal pooled analyses confirming consistency across outcomes are limited.
fish oil::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::e25e.emerging_research: Recent work (2023–2026) explores fish oil's potential in autoimmune and metabolic contexts—including multiple sclerosis management, resistance exercise combined effects on physical function, and acute muscle soreness after eccentric contraction. Mechanistic studies highlight the role of omega-3-derived resolvins and protectins in inflammasome inhibition and microbiota modulation in liver disease. A 2025 trial directly compared fish oil to krill oil in mood and cardiometabolic outcomes, suggesting ongoing refinement of which omega-3 sources may be most effective. These directions remain preliminary in humans and require further confirmation.
fish oil::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::e25e.open_questions: Among the retrieved studies, only a handful reported complete sample sizes—most abstracts omitted N values, obscuring the true precision of the evidence base. The liver health outcome is notably underpowered in humans (1 RCT of 40 participants) relative to animal work, leaving human efficacy uncertain. No studies retrieved here extended follow-up beyond typical RCT windows (most appear ≤12 weeks, though this cannot be confirmed uniformly from abstracts alone); long-term safety and durability of benefit remain unclear in the records provided. Pediatric and adolescent populations do not appear in the retrieved studies; the evidence base reflects primarily adult cohorts.
fish oil::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::e25e.caveats: Fish oil is generally well-tolerated but may cause mild gastrointestinal upset, fishy aftertaste, or increased bleeding risk at very high doses or in combination with anticoagulants (warfarin, aspirin) or antiplatelet medications. Quality and purity vary widely among commercial supplements; third-party certification (USP, NSF, ConsumerLab) is recommended to verify EPA/DHA content and screen for contaminants (mercury, PCBs). Individuals on blood thinners or with bleeding disorders, upcoming surgery, or fish allergies should consult a healthcare provider before starting fish oil supplementation.

krill oil::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::32c.what_it_is: Krill oil is a lipid extract from Antarctic krill (Euphausia superba), small shrimp-like crustaceans harvested from Southern Ocean waters. It is rich in omega-3 fatty acids (EPA and DHA), phospholipids, and astaxanthin, a potent antioxidant that gives it a reddish color. People typically consume it as a softgel supplement, often marketed as a marine alternative to fish oil.
krill oil::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::32c.how_it_works: Krill oil's omega-3 fatty acids (EPA and DHA) integrate into cell membranes and serve as precursors for anti-inflammatory signaling molecules called resolvins and protectins, which help dial down excessive inflammation. The phospholipid structure of krill oil may allow better absorption and tissue delivery compared to triglyceride-based fish oils. Astaxanthin, a carotenoid antioxidant unique to krill oil, crosses the blood–brain barrier and scavenges reactive oxygen species that damage lipids and proteins. Together, these components are thought to improve endothelial function (the lining of blood vessels), reduce triglycerides and other blood lipids, lower blood glucose, and dampen joint inflammation—all pathways linked to cardiovascular and metabolic health.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Two independent meta-analyses (2023, n=1458; 2017, n=662) examining randomized controlled trials consistently found that krill oil supplementation improves cardiovascular health markers, including lipid profiles and related outcomes in humans. Recent RCTs (2025–2026) in older adults and adults with familial hypercholesterolemia or overweight/obesity also reported cardiovascular benefits. The evidence spans diverse populations and durations, with over 2400 participants verified across identified studies, though the true total is substantially larger given incomplete reporting in abstracts.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: This grade reflects convergence across 14 human studies including 2 independent meta-analyses that reached consistent conclusions, plus adequate sample sizes. The consistency of findings across different trial designs and populations supports a 'Strong' classification.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Three human trials (2024, n=39 with systemic lupus; 2022, n not fully reported; 2015, n=17) tested krill oil on inflammatory markers, with mixed but encouraging results—notably a 2024 RCT showing improvement in disease activity in lupus patients. Animal studies (12 retrieved) consistently showed anti-inflammatory effects via mechanisms like TLR4/MyD88/NF-κB signaling and reduction in exercise-induced muscle inflammation. However, no pooled human meta-analysis yet confirms these findings agree, and human trial numbers remain small (~56 participants verified across 2 studies).
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Despite promising animal and early human data, the human evidence is limited in volume and lacks independent replication through meta-analysis. The grade is held at Moderate pending larger or confirmatory human trials.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2025 meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (n=730 total participants) examined krill oil for knee osteoarthritis and found benefit. A 2016 RCT showed krill oil improved mild knee joint pain. One animal study (2010) demonstrated that krill oil supplementation protects against experimental rheumatoid arthritis. The human evidence comes primarily from the single meta-analysis and one dedicated RCT, with one animal proof-of-concept study.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The single meta-analysis (n=730) provides reasonable precision for this outcome, but it lacks independent replication—no second meta-analysis or large confirmatory trial is present in the retrieved records. This limits confidence to Moderate despite the promising aggregate finding.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Three meta-analyses (2023, 2017, and 2024) involving over 2600 pooled participants from randomized trials found that krill oil improves lipid profiles, including triglycerides and related lipoprotein markers. Recent RCTs (2026, n=300; 2025; 2015, n=47) in hyperlipidemia and overweight/obese populations examined lipid outcomes, though one 2015 trial (n=47 blended krill–salmon oil) reported increased metabolic risk. A 2004 trial (n=120) in hyperlipidemia also showed benefit. About 3200 participants are verified across identified studies.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Multiple meta-analyses and a solid body of primary RCT data (12 human studies total) support this outcome, but the evidence base includes only 7 primary studies and 3 pooled analyses—below the threshold for 'Strong' where more independent corroboration would be expected. Some inconsistency (one trial showing negative lipid change) also tempers confidence.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Six human trials (ranging from 2004 to 2022, with verified sample sizes of 27–120 participants in several) examined krill oil effects on blood glucose and related metabolic markers. A 2022 RCT (n=102) in older adults, a 2015 trial (n=47) with blended krill–salmon oil, a 2004 trial (n=120) in hyperlipidemia, and smaller 2012–2018 studies reported mixed improvements in glucose, insulin sensitivity, or anthropometric parameters. Ten animal studies supported metabolic benefits. However, no human meta-analysis exists, and trial durations and consistency are not yet pooled.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Human evidence exists across multiple small-to-moderate trials (~343 participants verified), but no meta-analysis confirms agreement, and inconsistency is noted. Animal support is substantial, yet the human data remain fragmented, justifying Moderate rather than Strong.

krill oil::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::32c.evidence_base: The research base includes 37 human studies (14 trials and meta-analyses on cardiovascular outcomes, 12 on lipids, 6 on blood sugar, 3 on inflammation, 2 on joints) alongside 37 animal studies, for a total of approximately 4700 study records retrieved. The bulk of human evidence comes from randomized controlled trials and systematic reviews/meta-analyses conducted between 2004 and 2026, with the most robust findings in cardiovascular and lipid outcomes. Most abstracts omit precise participant numbers, so true sample sizes are substantially larger than the ~2407–3224 participants verified across single outcomes. Recent trials (2023–2026) increasingly include diverse populations (older adults, familial hypercholesterolemia, systemic lupus, obesity) and reflect growing clinical interest. The field remains dominated by relatively short-duration trials and small-to-moderate sample sizes; long-term safety and durability of benefits are less well characterized.
krill oil::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::32c.emerging_research: Recent 2024–2026 work has expanded krill oil investigation into autoimmune disease (systemic lupus, n=39), acute dietary interventions (alternate-day fasting, n=25), and sex-stratified responses in older adults (n=49). Mechanistic animal studies are exploring krill oil's effects on sortilin signaling in liver and adipose tissue, and on TLR4/MyD88/NF-κB inflammatory pathways in exercise contexts—suggesting potential for metabolic syndrome and post-exercise recovery. A 2026 RCT (n=300) specifically paired krill oil with culturally adapted heart-healthy diets, pointing toward combination intervention research. These directions are promising but remain early; human evidence for these specific applications is thin.
krill oil::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::32c.open_questions: Among the studies retrieved here, the vast majority of human trials are short-term (most ≤3 months; few exceed 6 months), so durability and safety over years remain uncharacterized in these records. The retrieved studies do not include large pediatric or pregnant populations, nor do they systematically report long-term adherence or adverse events. For inflammation and blood sugar outcomes, the human sample is small (3 and 6 human studies, respectively) and no meta-analysis yet pools these findings, making it unclear whether results will replicate at scale. Animal studies vastly outnumber humans for inflammation (12 vs. 3), widening the translational gap. Note: you are seeing only a SAMPLE of approximately 40 abstracts per outcome—research beyond these retrieved records may exist in the literature, so absence of evidence here does not mean the field lacks such work.
krill oil::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::32c.caveats: Krill oil is not a medication and is not regulated with the same rigor as pharmaceuticals; quality, purity, and omega-3 potency vary among commercial products. It may interact with anticoagulants (warfarin, apixaban) and antiplatelet agents (aspirin, clopidogrel) by enhancing blood thinning; people on such medications should consult a doctor before use. Those with shellfish or crustacean allergies should avoid krill oil. The 2015 trial reporting increased metabolic risk in a blended krill–salmon oil formulation raises a flag about certain combinations; the mechanisms and generalizability of this finding are not yet clear. Pregnant or nursing women lack adequate human safety data and should seek medical advice before supplementing.

algae oil::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::870.what_it_is: Algae oil is a lipid extract derived from marine microalgae, typically rich in omega-3 fatty acids—particularly docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) and eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA). Unlike fish oil, which comes from fish tissues, algae oil is harvested directly from algae species that naturally produce these long-chain polyunsaturated fats. It is sold as a liquid supplement or in capsule form, making it a plant-based alternative to fish oil for obtaining marine omega-3s.
algae oil::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::870.how_it_works: Algae oil's bioactive compounds, especially DHA and EPA, are incorporated into cell membranes throughout the body, where they influence membrane fluidity and function. These omega-3 fatty acids serve as precursors to specialized molecules called resolvins and protectins, which are potent regulators of inflammation; they dampen the production of pro-inflammatory signaling molecules (cytokines like TNF-α and IL-6) and promote the resolution phase of immune responses. DHA also crosses the blood-brain barrier and accumulates in neural tissue, where it may support neuronal membrane health and cell signaling. At the mechanistic level, omega-3 fatty acids compete with omega-6 arachidonic acid for incorporation into membranes and conversion to lipid mediators, thereby shifting the balance away from excess inflammation.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Two animal studies examined algae oil's effects on inflammatory markers and immune function. A 2026 study investigated docosahexaenoic acid-rich algae oil supplementation in milk replacer and measured blood inflammatory markers. A 2018 study compared sex-based differences in gut microbiota composition following tuna oil and algae oil supplementation in animals. Both used animal models, and neither provides direct human evidence.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Evidence rests entirely on animal models and does not yet include any human trials. Animal findings are useful for identifying plausible mechanisms, but inflammatory responses in animals often differ from those in humans in terms of magnitude, timing, and clinical relevance, limiting confidence in translating these results to human health outcomes.

algae oil::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::870.evidence_base: The research base for algae oil's anti-inflammatory effects shown here consists entirely of animal studies, with no human trials present in the retrieved records. The studies span recent years (2018–2026) and suggest investigators are actively exploring algae oil's immunomodulatory potential. Because human evidence is absent, confidence in efficacy remains low; animal work can illuminate mechanisms and guide human research design, but cannot establish clinical benefit in people.
algae oil::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::870.emerging_research: Recent work (2026) is beginning to examine algae oil's delivery via functional foods—such as fortified milk replacer—as a route to evaluate physiological effects. Concurrent investigation of sex-based differences in microbiota responses (2018) hints at potential interactions between algae oil, gut microbial composition, and immune function, a frontier of growing interest. These early directions suggest researchers are probing both delivery methods and individual variation, but human data are still needed to determine relevance.
algae oil::clarity-engine-v2::rich4::870.open_questions: Among the studies retrieved here, both are animal-based, and neither includes human participants. The retrieved records do not show human trials of algae oil for inflammation, nor do they specify the dose range, duration, or intensity of inflammatory markers studied in the animal models.
